questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese securities firm is validating a booked correlation swap whose term sheet is missing the fixed correlation. The firm was the fixed-rate receiver on a notional of JPY 600,000,000 on three Nikkei constituents and received JPY 90,000,000 at maturity. The realised pairwise correlations were:

|  | Stock 1 | Stock 2 | Stock 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stock 1 | 1 | 0.55 | 0.40 |
| Stock 2 | 0.55 | 1 | 0.25 |
| Stock 3 | 0.40 | 0.25 | 1 |

Which of the following is closest to the fixed correlation in the swap?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Realised correlation**

$$\rho_{\text{realised}} = \frac{2}{3^{2} - 3}(0.55 + 0.40 + 0.25) = \frac{1.20}{3} = 0.40$$

⇒ Average pairwise co-movement over the swap life was 40%.

**Step 2 – Return per unit notional**

$$\frac{\text{Payoff}_{\text{receiver}}}{N} = \frac{90{,}000{,}000}{600{,}000{,}000} = 0.15$$

⇒ The firm earned 15 correlation points; a positive receiver payoff means realised correlation came in below the fixed rate.

**Step 3 – Reverse-solve the receiver’s payoff**

$$\frac{\text{Payoff}_{\text{receiver}}}{N} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} - \rho_{\text{realised}} \Rightarrow\rho_{\text{fixed}} = 0.40 + 0.15 = 0.55$$

⇒ The firm had sold correlation at 55%.

**Interpretation**

The booked receipt is consistent only with a 55% strike. A term sheet showing a lower fixed correlation alongside a positive JPY 90 million receipt would be an exception for the auditor to escalate, because a receiver with a strike below realised correlation pays rather than receives.

**LO:** MR-8 d: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap. • **Reference:** Meissner, Ch.1, 8.5 Trading and Correlation, Equations 8.6 and 8.7

**Source:** Workbook A8.3 • S3 • Map #8 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-8 d.6)

a.reason: Intermediate result: reported the return per unit notional, 90/600 = 0.15, as if it were the strike.

b.reason: Party flip: treated the firm as the payer, $\rho_{\text{fixed}} = \rho_{\text{realised}} - 0.15 = 0.25$.

questions.question: A risk analyst is preparing a case-study note on correlation positions in credit and on how correlation swaps are valued. Which of the following statements in the note is correct?

options.text: In 2012 the “London Whale” sold CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and bought CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if volatility and correlation fell in a recovering economy.
In 2012 the “London Whale” bought CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and sold CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if correlation rose in a recovering economy.
Correlation swaps are valued with an industry-standard model that discounts the fixed leg off a market term structure of correlation.
The present value of a correlation swap rises for the fixed-rate receiver when realised correlation increases during the life of the swap.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The London Whale trade**

Bruno Iksil sold CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 bond index and “hedged” it by buying CDS on individual bonds. In a recovering economy volatility and correlation typically decrease, so the sold index CDS should outperform the losses on the single-name CDS.

⇒ It was a short-correlation position in credit, the mirror of buying index puts and selling single-stock puts.

**Step 2 – Valuation**

GARP: no industry-standard valuation model exists and no term structure of correlation exists; traders use historical data or emerging stochastic correlation models.

**Step 3 – Who gains from rising correlation**

The present value rises for the correlation buyer (fixed-rate payer) when realised correlation increases.

**Interpretation**

The case is a reminder that a hedge built on index versus components is a correlation bet. The trade went wrong in a short squeeze that cost JP Morgan over USD 2 billion.

**LO:** MR-8 d: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap. • **Reference:** Meissner, Ch.1, 8.5 Trading and Correlation

MR-8 • Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, 8.5 (London Whale, valuation) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-8 d.7)

b.reason: Sibling swap: reverses both legs and the correlation view; Iksil sold index protection and expected correlation to fall.

c.reason: True-fact-wrong-claim: there is no industry-standard model and no market term structure of correlation.

d.reason: Party flip: rising realised correlation raises the value for the fixed-rate payer, not the receiver.

questions.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.topic: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.question:
A credit risk manager at a German commercial bank is reviewing a proposal from the corporate lending desk. Today the bank has a single EUR 20 million loan to one borrower. The desk proposes to replace it with two loans of EUR 10 million each to two unrelated borrowers, X and Y, in different sectors. The manager’s inputs are:

- One-year default probability of X: 8%; of Y: 12%
- Default correlation between X and Y (binomial Pearson correlation): 0.25
- Expected recovery on either loan: 40%

Using Meissner’s framework, which of the following correctly states the bank’s concentration ratio after the change and the probability of the worst-case scenario in which both X and Y default?

options.text: Concentration ratio 0.50; joint default probability 3.16%
Concentration ratio 0.50; joint default probability 0.96%
Concentration ratio 0.50; joint default probability 2.20%
Concentration ratio 2.00; joint default probability 3.16%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Concentration ratio**

Concentration ratio $= \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.50$

⇒ Two loans of equal size halve the ratio from 1 (a single loan) to 0.50: the default risk is more diversified, provided the default correlation is below 1.

**Step 2 – Standard deviations of the binomial default variables (Equation 8.12)**

$$\sigma_{X} = \sqrt{0.08 \times0.92} = 0.2713, \sigma_{Y} = \sqrt{0.12 \times0.88} = 0.3250$$

**Step 3 – Joint default probability (Equation 8.11)**

$$P (X \cap Y ) = \rho_{XY} \sigma_{X}\sigma_{Y} + P_{X}P_{Y} = 0.25 \times0.2713 \times0.3250 + 0.08 \times0.12$$

= 0.0220 + 0.0096 = 3.16%

⇒ There is a 3.16% chance that both borrowers default within the year, the bank’s worst case.

**Interpretation**

Under the old single loan the worst case (default of the one borrower) had the full PD of that borrower; after splitting, losing both loans requires a joint default, here 3.16%. The benefit comes from both levers Meissner links: a lower concentration ratio and a correlation below 1. If X and Y were in the same sector, intra-sector default correlation would be higher and the joint probability would rise. The 40% recovery is a red herring: it changes the size of the loss, not its probability.

**LO:** MR-8 g: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk. • **Reference:** Meissner, Ch.1, 8.8 Correlation Risk and Concentration Risk, Example 8.3, Equations 8.11 and 8.12

**Source:** Workbook A8.4 • S5 • Map #8 • Map #76 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-8 g.4)

b.reason: Dropped term: assumed independence and kept only $P_{X}P_{Y} = 0.08 \times0.12 =$ 0.96%, ignoring the 0.25 default correlation.

c.reason: Dropped term: kept only the correlation term 0.25 × 0.2713 × 0.3250 = 2.20% and forgot to add $P_{X}P_{Y}$ .

d.reason: Polarity flip on the ratio: reported $n/1 = 2.00$ instead of $1/n$; a higher number would wrongly signal more concentration after diversifying.

questions.question: A credit oﬀicer is reviewing two equal loans to borrowers X and Y. Each borrower has a one-year default probability of 10%, so the binomial standard deviation of each default indicator is 30%. Which of the following statements in the oﬀicer’s memo is correct?

options.text: With a default correlation of −0.1 the joint default probability is still positive, at about 0.1%, so a slightly negative correlation does not eliminate the worst case.
With any negative default correlation the joint default probability is zero, so a negatively correlated pair removes the worst case entirely.
With a default correlation of 1, splitting one loan into these two equal loans halves the worst-case probability from 10% to 5%.
Lending to two borrowers in the same sector reduces concentration risk more than lending across sectors, because intra-sector default correlations are lower.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Joint PD as a function of correlation**

$$P (X \cap Y ) = \rho\times0.3 \times0.3 + 0.1 \times0.1 = 0.09 \rho+ 0.01$$

**Step 2 – Evaluate the statements**

$\rho= -0.1$: −0.009 + 0.01 = 0.001 = 0.1%, still positive. It reaches zero only at $\rho=$ −0.01/0.09 = −0.111.

$\rho= 1$: 0.09 + 0.01 = 10%, the same as one 10m loan with a 10% PD.

⇒ A is GARP’s own observation: even a slightly negative correlation can leave a positive joint default probability when the PDs are high.

**Interpretation**

The worst case shrinks as correlation falls, but it is not eliminated by a small negative correlation, and the concentration ratio buys nothing when $\rho= 1$ (Figure 5).

**LO:** MR-8 g: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk. • **Reference:** Meissner, Ch.1, 8.8 Correlation Risk and Concentration Risk, Example 8.3, Equation 8.11

MR-14 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, 8.8 (Example 8.3) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-8 g.6)

b.reason: Absolute qualifier: “any” negative correlation is wrong; the joint PD is positive down to $\rho= -0.111$ here.

c.reason: At $\rho= 1$ the loans default together or survive together: the worst case stays at 10%, there is no benefit from the lower ratio.

d.reason: Polarity flip: intra-sector default correlations are higher, so lending across sectors diversifies more.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a Malaysian bank uses Model 1 ($dr = \sigma dw$) to describe the MYR short rate for the ALCO pack. The current short rate is 4.50% and the annual basis-point volatility is 150 bp. The pack needs two figures: the standard deviation of the change in the short rate over the next month, and the standard deviation of the short rate five years from now. Which pair is closest?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – SD of the one-month change**

$$\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.50\% \times\sqrt{1/12} = 1.50\% \times0.28868 = 0.433\%$$

⇒ About 43 bp a month, the same calculation as GARP’s 32.6 bp for $\sigma= 1.13\%$.

**Step 2 – SD of the rate in five years**

$$\sigma\sqrt{T} = 1.50\% \times\sqrt{5} = 3.354\%$$

⇒ Monthly variances add over 60 steps: $60 \times\sigma^{2}/12 = 5\sigma^{2}$.

**Interpretation**

The current rate is not needed: Model 1’s dispersion depends only on $\sigma$ and the horizon. With a 4.50% rate and a 3.354% SD, a shock of only 1.34 SD would take the rate below zero after five years.

**LO:** MR-14 b: Calculate the short-term rate change and standard deviation of the rate change using a model with normally distributed rates and no drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat 3e, Ch.9, 14.1, eq. 14.4 and the 10-year terminal SD example

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.1 (eqs. 14.3, 14.4) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 b.6)

a.reason: Scaled the monthly figure by $dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$: 1.50%/12 = 0.125%.

c.reason: Scaled the five-year SD linearly with time: 1.50% × 5 = 7.50%.

d.reason: Reported the annual volatility as the monthly SD: 1.500%.

questions.question: A quant builds a Model 1 short-rate tree with quarterly steps ($dt = 0.25$), starting from $r_{0} =$ 3.00% with annual basis-point volatility of 90 bp and probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on every branch. Which of the following is closest to the standard deviation of the short rate after two steps, and to the distance between the highest and the lowest node on date 2?

options.text: Standard deviation 0.636%; distance 0.900%
Standard deviation 0.636%; distance 1.800%
Standard deviation 0.900%; distance 1.800%
Standard deviation 0.450%; distance 0.900%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – One step**

$$\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 0.90\% \times\sqrt{0.25} = 0.45\%$$

**Step 2 – Standard deviation after two steps: variances add**

SD $= \sigma\sqrt{2dt} = 0.90\% \times\sqrt{0.5} = 0.636\%$

⇒ Check on the tree: nodes ±0.90% with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ each and 0 with $\frac{1}{2}$ give variance $\frac{1}{2}(0.90\%)^{2}$, SD 0.636%.

**Step 3 – Highest minus lowest node**

$$(r_{0} + 2\sigma\sqrt{dt}) - (r_{0} - 2\sigma\sqrt{dt}) = 4\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.80\%$$

**Interpretation**

The outer nodes sit $2\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ from the centre, but the standard deviation grows only with $\sqrt{n}$ because half of the two-step paths (up-down, down-up) cancel. $r_{0}$ is not needed.

**LO:** MR-14 b: Calculate the short-term rate change and standard deviation of the rate change using a model with normally distributed rates and no drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat 3e, Ch.9, 14.1, eqs. 14.3 and 14.4

MR-14 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.1 (tree moments) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 b.7)

a.reason: Correct SD, but measured the distance on date 1 ($2\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 0.90\%$).

c.reason: Added the step SDs linearly (2 × 0.45% = 0.90%) and called it the standard deviation.

d.reason: Gave the one-step SD (0.45%) and the date-1 distance.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at an Australian bank is building a monthly Ho-Lee short-rate tree for AUD swaps. The current one-month rate is 3.20%, annual basis-point volatility is 120 basis points, the calibrated drift for the first month is $\lambda_{1} = 0.60\%$ and for the second month is $\lambda_{2} = 0.90\%$. Which of the following is closest to the short rate in the up state at the end of the first month?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Time step**

$$dt = \frac{1}{12} = 0.08333, \sqrt{dt} = 0.28868$$

⇒ One monthly step, measured in years.

**Step 2 – Drift over the first step**

$$\lambda_{1}dt = 0.60\% \times\frac{1}{12} = 0.050\%$$

⇒ The risk-neutral drift lifts the rate by 5 basis points over the month in both states.

**Step 3 – Volatility perturbation**

$$\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.20\% \times0.28868 = 0.3464\%$$

⇒ One standard deviation of the monthly rate change is about 34.6 basis points.

**Step 4 – Up-state node**

$$r_{u} = r_{0} + \lambda_{1}dt + \sigma\sqrt{dt} = 3.20\% + 0.050\% + 0.3464\% = 3.596\%$$

⇒ If the shock is up, the one-month rate one month from now is about 3.60%.

**Interpretation**

$\lambda_{2}$ is irrelevant until date 2. The node is the date-1 building block from which $\lambda_{2}$ is later chosen so the model reprices the market three-month spot rate.

**LO:** MR-14 d: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee Model with time-dependent drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.9, 14.3, eq. 14.7

**Source:** Workbook A7.1 • S2, S5, S7 • Aug-2026 • Map #7 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 d.2)

b.reason: $dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$ on volatility: 3.20% + 0.050% + 1.20%/12 = 3.350%.

c.reason: Dropped the drift (used Model 1): 3.20% + 0.3464% = 3.546%.

questions.question:
A rates quant at a Canadian pension fund is extending a monthly Ho-Lee tree for CAD to the end of the second month, to check how wide the range of short rates becomes. Inputs:

- Current one-month rate $r_{0}$: 1.50%; annual basis-point volatility $\sigma$: 160 basis points
- Calibrated drift: $\lambda_{1} = 0.60\%$ for month 1 and $\lambda_{2} = 1.20\%$ for month 2 (annualised)

Which of the following is closest to the short rate in the top node after two months, and to the gap between the top and bottom nodes on that date?

options.text: Top node 2.112%; gap 0.924%
Top node 2.524%; gap 1.848%
Top node 2.574%; gap 0.924%
Top node 2.574%; gap 1.848%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cumulative drift to date 2**

$$(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2}) dt = (0.60\% + 1.20\%) \times\frac{1}{12} = 0.150\%$$

⇒ The two monthly drifts together shift every date-2 node up by 15 basis points.

**Step 2 – Volatility perturbation per step**

$$\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.60\% \times0.28868 = 0.4619\%$$

⇒ Each monthly up or down move is about 46 basis points.

**Step 3 – Top node (two up moves) and node-2** $\Delta r$

$r_{uu} = r_{0}+(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})dt+2\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.50\%+0.150\%+0.9238\% = 2.574\%, \Delta r = +107.4$ bp

⇒ After two up shocks the one-month rate is about 2.57%.

**Step 4 – Bottom node and the gap**

$$r_{dd} = 1.650\% - 0.9238\% = 0.726\%, r_{uu} - r_{dd} = 4\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.848\%$$

⇒ The date-2 nodes are 2.574%, 1.650% and 0.726%. The drift cancels in the gap; only volatility sets the width.

**Interpretation**

The range still stays above zero at two months, but in a normal model the probability of negative rates rises with the horizon (MR-14 c): the width grows with $\sqrt{t}$ while the drift grows with $t$.

**LO:** MR-14 d: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee Model with time-dependent drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.9, 14.3

**Source:** Workbook A7.2 • S1, S2, S3, S4, S5 • Map #7 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 d.4)

a.reason: Placed the date-2 top node only one $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ above the centre (the date-1 picture): 1.650% + 0.4619% = 2.112%, gap $2\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 0.924\%$.

b.reason: Used $\lambda_{1}$ for both months ($2\lambda_{1}dt = 0.10\%$) instead of $(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2})dt$: 1.50% + 0.10% + 0.9238% = 2.524%.

c.reason: Correct top node, but measured the gap as $2\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 0.924\%$, the spread between the two date-1 nodes, not the date-2 range.

questions.question: A model validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing a monthly Ho-Lee tree for SGD. The documentation is missing $\lambda_{1}$, but the tree shows $r_{0} = 2.50\%$ and date-1 nodes of 2.8887% (up) and 2.3113% (down). The model’s two-year par rate is 2.95%. Which of the following is closest to the annualised drift $\lambda_{1}$?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Average of the date-1 nodes**

$$\frac{1}{2}(r_{u} + r_{d}) = \frac{1}{2}(2.8887\% + 2.3113\%) = 2.6000\%$$

⇒ The $\pm\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ shocks cancel in the average, leaving $r_{0} + \lambda_{1}dt$.

**Step 2 – Drift over the step**

$$\lambda_{1}dt = 2.6000\% - 2.5000\% = 0.1000\%$$

⇒ The month’s drift raises the expected short rate by 10 basis points.

**Step 3 – Annualise**

$$\lambda_{1} = \frac{0.1000\%}{1/12} = 1.20\%$$

$\Rightarrow\lambda_{1}$ is quoted per year, like every parameter in $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma dw$.

**Check – Implied volatility (not asked)**

$$\sigma= \frac{r_{u} - r_{d}}{2\sqrt{dt}} = \frac{0.5774\%}{2 \times0.28868} = 1.00\%$$

**Interpretation**

A 1.20% annualised drift for month 1 is what makes the model reprice the market two-month spot rate. The two-year par rate is irrelevant to this step.

a.reason: Intermediate result: the monthly shift $\lambda_{1}dt = 0.10\%$, not annualised.

questions.question: A rates analyst is checking a quarterly Ho-Lee tree ($dt = 0.25$) built by a colleague. The tree starts from $r_{0} = 2.00\%$ with annual basis-point volatility of 100 bp. The calibrated drift for the first quarter is $\lambda_{1} = 0.40\%$, and the middle node on date 2 shows 2.30%. Which of the following is closest to the annualised drift for the second quarter, $\lambda_{2}$, and to the rate in the top node on date 2?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the cumulative drift off the middle node**

$(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2}) dt = r_{\text{mid},2} - r_{0} = 2.30\% - 2.00\% = 0.30\% \Rightarrow\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2} = \frac{0.30\%}{0.25} = 1.20\%$

⇒ The shocks cancel on the middle node, so it carries pure drift.

**Step 2 – Second-quarter drift**

$$\lambda_{2} = 1.20\% - 0.40\% = 0.80\%$$

**Step 3 – Top node on date 2**

$$\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.00\% \times\sqrt{0.25} = 0.50\%, r_{uu} = 2.30\% + 2 \times0.50\% = 3.30\%$$

**Interpretation**

This is the calibration logic run backwards: the middle node pins down the drift, the node spread pins down the volatility. Here $\lambda_{2} > \lambda_{1}$, which Ho-Lee allows and Model 2 would not.

questions.question: A swap dealer calibrates a Ho-Lee model to the EUR swap curve every morning. Overnight, a large bank liquidates its book of swaps with about seven years to maturity, pushing 7-year swap rates up by 12 bp while neighbouring maturities barely move. After recalibration, the fitted drift for years six to eight jumps. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion for the dealer’s model risk manager?

options.text: The recalibrated drift correctly signals that the market now expects short rates around year seven to be higher, so hedges should be adjusted for that expectation.

Fitting to the distorted prices attributes a liquidity effect to the interest rate process; the 7-year swaps are fair given the liquidation, not fair with respect to expected rates and the risk premium.
Because Ho-Lee is arbitrage-free, its recalibrated prices are fair values and its hedges remain accurate by construction.
An equilibrium model would be forced to reproduce the higher 7-year rate as well, so the choice between model types does not matter here.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What moved the 7-year rate**

A forced liquidation: a supply and demand imbalance unrelated to expected rates or the risk premium.

**Step 2 – What fitting does with it**

An arbitrage-free model takes the new 7-year price as fair and changes the drift to reproduce it, attributing a liquidity effect to the rate process. The jump in the fitted drift is the warning sign: a risk-neutral drift arises only from expectations and risk premium, and neither plausibly jumped overnight at year seven.

⇒ The 7-year swaps are fair given the liquidity event, not fair with respect to the expected evolution of rates.

**Interpretation**

This is GARP’s own example. Traders might buy the cheapened 7-year swaps and hold them past the liquidity event. An equilibrium model would flag them as cheap instead of absorbing the move.

c.reason: Absolute claim: matching market prices does not imply fair values or accurate hedges.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK insurer is reviewing a GBP rates desk that uses the Ho-Lee model to quote odd-maturity swaps and Model 3 (time-dependent volatility, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$) to quote caplets. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the review?

options.text: Because its drift varies with time, the Ho-Lee model produces a humped term structure of volatility that matches market implied volatilities.
Because $\lambda(t)$ is calibrated to market spot rates, the Ho-Lee model rules out negative short-term rates.
The Ho-Lee drift can match all input spot rates, but the model remains a parallel-shift model with a flat term structure of volatility.
The exponential decay in Model 3’s volatility introduces mean reversion, so Model 3 is no longer a parallel-shift model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What time-dependent drift buys**

The free parameters $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \dots$ are chosen one at a time to match the two-, three-, … -period spot rates, so the rate curves match all the rates input into the model (MR-14 d, e).

**Step 2 – What it does not change**

Adding a constant drift (Model 2) or a time-dependent drift (Ho-Lee) does not affect the shape of the term structure of volatility nor the parallel-shift characteristic of the model. Volatility is $\sigma$ at every term.

**Step 3 – Model 3 contrast**

Time-dependent volatility fits caplet prices across expiries, but as for any model without mean reversion, Model 3 is a parallel-shift model with a flat term structure of volatility, flat at levels that change over time (MR-15 a, c).

**Interpretation**

Calibration buys fit, not structure. If the desk’s hedges rely on non-parallel moves, neither model fixes that: a mediocre model cannot be rescued by calibrating it to market prices.

**LO:** MR-14 e: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices. MR-15 c: Assess the eﬀicacy of time-dependent volatility models. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.9, 14.3 and 14.4; Ch.10, 15.1

MR-14 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A7.5 • S6, S7 • Aug-2026 • Map #7 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 e.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: a humped volatility structure is a Gauss+ feature (no shock on $r$); drift has no effect on the volatility shape in Ho-Lee.

b.reason: Scope/condition error: calibrating the drift fits prices but leaves the distribution normal, so negative rates remain possible; ruling them out needs a different distribution (CIR or lognormal) or setting negative shadow rates to zero.

d.reason: Sibling swap: Model 3 can mimic the Vasicek terminal distribution, but it has no mean reversion and stays a parallel-shift model.

questions.question: A junior quant’s two-step monthly Vasicek tree does not recombine: the up-down and down-up paths end 2 bp apart. Which of the following describes the procedure GARP presents for turning it into a recombining tree?

options.text: Keep probabilities of $\frac{1}{2}$ on every branch and replace the two middle nodes by their average; the outer nodes on date 2 are left as first computed.

Fix the centre node on date 2 at the expected rate after two steps, then choose the outer nodes and the branch probabilities so that, from each date-1 node, the tree matches the process’s expected rate and standard deviation.
Drop the mean-reversion drift in the second step so that the up-down and down-up paths cancel exactly, as they do in Model 2.
Set the branch probabilities so that the tree’s expected rate equals $\theta$ on every date, keeping the move per step at $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Fix the centre**

Since the expected shock is zero, the drift alone fixes the expected rate after two steps; GARP sets the date-2 centre node equal to it (5.1635% in its example; numerically the same as averaging the two middle nodes).

**Step 2 – Free the probabilities and outer nodes**

From the up node, choose $r_{uu}$ and $p$ so that $p r_{uu} + (1 - p)r_{\text{mid}}$ equals the process’s expected rate from that node and the branch SD equals $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$; likewise $r_{dd}$ and $q$ from the down node.

⇒ GARP’s solution: $r_{uu} = 5.8909\%$, $p = 0.4990$; $r_{dd} = 4.4361\%$, $q = 0.5011$.

**Interpretation**

The tree recombines and still honours the Vasicek process at every node: mean reversion is kept, and the probabilities absorb the asymmetry.

**LO:** MR-14 f: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat 3e, Ch.9, 14.5, eqs. 14.12 to 14.21

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.5 (recombining tree) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 f.5)

a.reason: Averaging alone, with outer nodes and $\frac{1}{2}$ probabilities unchanged, no longer matches the expected rate and volatility from each date-1 node.

c.reason: Removing the mean-reverting drift turns the model into something else; recombination must be achieved with the drift kept.

d.reason: Wrong target: the expected rate is not $\theta$ on each date; it moves gradually toward $\theta$ at speed $k$.

questions.question: A model validation analyst at a Japanese bank is asked to recommend a one-factor short-rate model for the bank’s interest rate desk. The desk sets three requirements: (i) the short rate cannot become negative; (ii) the basis-point volatility of the short rate rises with the level of the rate, but less than proportionally; and (iii) the short rate is pulled toward a long-run level. Which recommendation, with its justification, should the analyst make?

options.text: The Vasicek model, because mean reversion pulls the short rate toward its long-run level and therefore prevents the short rate from becoming negative.
The CIR model, because its basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the rate and falls to zero at a zero rate, where the drift is positive.
The Black-Karasinski model, because the logarithm of the rate mean-reverts and its basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the rate.
The Ho-Lee model, because fitting its time-dependent drift to market bond prices guarantees that no node of the rate tree becomes negative.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Requirement (ii) sorts the volatility specifications**

Normal models (Ho-Lee, Vasicek) have constant basis-point volatility; lognormal models (Courtadon, Model 4, Salomon Brothers, Black-Karasinski) have basis-point volatility $\sigma r$, proportional to the rate; CIR has $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, rising less than proportionally.

**Step 2 – Requirement (i)**

CIR: basis-point volatility is zero at a zero rate and the drift $k(\theta- 0)$ is positive there, so the rate cannot go negative.

**Step 3 – Requirement (iii)**

CIR’s drift $k(\theta- r)$ pulls the rate toward $\theta$. Only CIR meets all three.

**Interpretation**

The Vasicek option is the one tied to this LO: mean reversion is a pull, not a floor. (CIR and lognormal models are MR-15 d, f.)

**LO:** MR-15 d: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models. MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models. MR-14 f: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 3e, Ch.10, 15.2 to 15.4; Ch.9, 14.3 and 14.4

MR-14 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D1.2 • S2, S3, S4, S5 • Map #39 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 f.7)

a.reason: Scope/condition error. Vasicek does mean-revert, but its basis-point volatility is constant and rates are normally distributed, so negative rates remain possible; mean reversion only damps the spread of future rates.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Black-Karasinski does mean-revert in the log rate and stays positive, but as a lognormal model its basis-point volatility is proportional to the rate, the property CIR does not have.

d.reason: Absolute claim. Ho-Lee rates are normal with constant volatility; fitting the drift matches bond prices but does not stop low nodes from going negative, and Ho-Lee has no long-run level at all.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank prices BRL rate products with a Vasicek model. The economist’s real-world view and the desk’s risk premium are:

- Current short rate $r_{0}$: 2.00%; speed of mean reversion $k$: 0.15
- Real-world long-run value of the short rate $r_{\infty}$: 4.00%
- Risk premium entering as a constant drift $\lambda$: 0.30% per year

For pricing, which of the following is closest to the expected short rate in 5 years under the risk-neutral process, and to the expected change in the short rate over the next month?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Risk-neutral long-run value**

$$\theta= r_{\infty} + \frac{\lambda}{k} = 4.00\% + \frac{0.30\%}{0.15} = 6.00\%$$

⇒ Prices reflect expectations plus risk premium; the risk-neutral process reverts to 6.00%, not to the economist’s 4.00%.

**Step 2 – Decay factor**

$$e^{-kT} = e^{-0.15\times5} = e^{-0.75} = 0.47237$$

⇒ After 5 years, 47.2% of today’s 4-point gap to $\theta$ remains.

**Step 3 – Expected rate in 5 years**

$$E[r_{5}] = r_{0}e^{-kT} + \theta(1 - e^{-kT} ) = 2.00\%(0.47237) + 6.00\%(0.52763)$$

= 0.9447% + 3.1658% = 4.11%

⇒ Equivalently, $\theta$ minus the remaining gap: 6.00% − 4.00% × 0.47237 = 4.11%.

**Step 4 – One-month expected change**

$E[dr] = k(\theta- r_{0}) dt = 0.15 \times(6.00\% - 2.00\%) \times\frac{1}{12} = 0.050\% = +5.0$ bps

**Interpretation**

The half-life is ln 2/0.15 = 4.6 years, so after 5 years the expected rate has covered a little more than half the distance to $\theta$. Because the drift shrinks as the gap closes, the 5-year move (211 bps) is far less than 60 months of today’s 5 bp drift.

**LO:** MR-14 g: Calculate the Vasicek Model rate change, standard deviation of the rate change, expected rate in T years, and half-life. MR-16 b: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.9, 14.5 eqs. 14.9, 14.10, 14.23; 4e, Ch.9, 16.1 eqs. 16.2 to 16.4

**Source:** Workbook A25.4 • S1, S3, S4 • Map #40 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 g.4)

a.reason: Wrong-input twin: reverted to the real-world $r_{\infty} = 4.00\%$ instead of $\theta$: 2.00%(0.47237) + 4.00%(0.52763) = 3.06%; drift 0.15 × 2.00%/12 = 2.5 bps.

b.reason: Dropped the division by $k$: $\theta= 4.00\% + 0.30\% = 4.30\%$, giving 3.21% and 0.15 × 2.30%/12 = 2.9 bps.

c.reason: Swapped the weights: 2.00%(0.52763) + 6.00%(0.47237) = 3.89%; the one-month drift is unaffected.

questions.question: A risk consultant at an Australian bank is explaining to the board risk committee how long rate shocks persist in the bank’s Vasicek model. Parameters: $r_{0} = 3.50\%$, $\theta= 5.00\%$, $k = 0.08$, $\sigma= 110$ bps per year. Which of the following is closest to the half-life of the short rate, and to the standard deviation of the short rate 10 years from now?

options.text: Half-life 8.66 years; standard deviation 2.04%
Half-life 8.66 years; standard deviation 2.46%
Half-life 8.66 years; standard deviation 3.48%
Half-life 12.50 years; standard deviation 2.46%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Half-life**

$h = \frac{\text{ln} 2}{k} = \frac{0.69315}{0.08} = 8.66$ years

⇒ A shock to the short rate takes about 8.7 years to decay halfway toward $\theta$. $r_{0}$ and $\theta$ do not enter.

**Step 2 – Variance factor**

$$\frac{1 - e^{-2kT}}{2k} = \frac{1 - e^{-1.6}}{0.16} = \frac{1 - 0.20190}{0.16} = 4.9881$$

**Step 3 – Terminal standard deviation**

SD $= \sigma\sqrt{4.9881} = 1.10\% \times2.2334 = 2.46\%$

⇒ The short rate in 10 years is normal with a standard deviation of about 246 bps around its expectation.

**Interpretation**

Without mean reversion the standard deviation would be $1.10\%\sqrt{10} = 3.48\%$: the pull toward $\theta$ dampens dispersion, particularly at long horizons, and the same effect makes the volatility term structure slope downward. For the committee, an 8.7-year half-life means rate news is fairly long-lived in this calibration.

**LO:** MR-14 g: Calculate the Vasicek Model rate change, standard deviation of the rate change, expected rate in T years, and half-life. MR-14 h: Describe the effectiveness of the Vasicek Model. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.9, 14.5 eqs. 14.25 to 14.27, Figure 14.5

MR-15 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A25.5 • S2, S3 • Map #40 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 g.6)

a.reason: Dropped the 2 in the exponent: $1.10\%\sqrt{(1 - e^{-0.8})/0.16} = 2.04\%$.

c.reason: Ignored mean reversion: $\sigma\sqrt{T} = 1.10\%\sqrt{10} = 3.48\%$.

d.reason: Used $1/k = 12.5$ years (the exponential time constant) instead of ln $2/k$.

questions.question: A rates desk replaces its Ho-Lee model with Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t) dt + \sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t} dw$ with $\alpha> 0$, so that it can quote caplets across expiries. The head of market risk asks how the short-rate process has changed. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Because volatility decays over time, a shock to the short rate now moves short-term rates more than long-term rates, so Model 3 produces non-parallel shifts.
At any given date the term structure of volatility is flat, but its level changes over time as $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ declines.
Because volatility now depends on the level of the short rate, basis-point volatility falls when rates fall, which prevents negative rates.
Setting $\alpha= 0$ turns Model 3 into the Vasicek model with constant volatility.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Model 3 adds**

Only the volatility term changes: $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ instead of a constant $\sigma$. It depends on calendar time, not on the level of $r$.

**Step 2 – What it keeps**

There is still no mean reversion, so a shock to the short rate moves all rates equally: a parallel-shift model. At any date, volatility is the same across maturities, so the term structure of volatility is flat; because $\sigma(t)$ falls with time, the level of that flat structure falls with time.

⇒ “Flat at levels that change over time, but still always flat.”

**Interpretation**

Decay in volatility is easy to mistake for mean reversion. It changes how wide future shocks are, not where rates are pulled to, so it cannot create non-parallel shifts.

**LO:** MR-15 a: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.10, 15.1, eq. 15.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15 (Tuckman 15.1) and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 a.6)

a.reason: Polarity of the model class: without mean reversion, shocks move all rates equally. Non-parallel shifts need mean reversion (Vasicek).

c.reason: Sibling swap: rate-level dependence is CIR ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$) or lognormal ($\sigma r$). Model 3 is normal, so negative rates remain possible.

d.reason: Wrong nesting: with $\alpha= 0$ the volatility is a constant $\sigma$ and the drift is still $\lambda(t)$, which is Ho-Lee. Vasicek needs a drift $k(\theta- r)$.

questions.question: A model validator compares a Vasicek model, $dr = k(\theta- r) dt + \sigma dw$, with a Model 3 implementation in which the initial volatility equals the Vasicek $\sigma$, the decay rate $\alpha$ equals the Vasicek mean-reversion speed $k$, and the time-dependent drift $\lambda(t)$ is set to match the average path of rates in the Vasicek model. Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: The two models produce identical terminal distributions of the short rate, yet Model 3 remains a parallel-shift model while Vasicek does not.
Because the terminal distributions are identical, the two models imply identical yield curve shifts and therefore identical hedge ratios.
The terminal standard deviations would match only if $\alpha$ were set equal to half of $k$, so the two terminal distributions differ.
Model 3 has a wider terminal distribution than Vasicek at every horizon, because Model 3 has no mean reversion.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Terminal standard deviation**

With Model 3’s initial volatility and decay rate equal to Vasicek’s $\sigma$ and $k$, the standard deviations of the terminal distributions are identical (Tuckman, Section 15.1).

**Step 2 – Terminal mean**

With Model 3’s drift matched to Vasicek’s average rate path, the means match too, so the terminal distributions are identical.

**Step 3 – What still differs**

Model 3 has no mean reversion: it is a parallel-shift model with a flat volatility term structure. Vasicek is a non-parallel shift model with a downward-sloping volatility term structure.

⇒ Same terminal distribution, different dynamics.

**Interpretation**

Matching terminal distributions makes the two models agree on anything that depends only on the distribution of the short rate at a date. Anything that depends on how the whole curve moves (hedge ratios across maturities, curve trades) still differs.

**LO:** MR-15 a: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.10, 15.1 and Figure 15.1

MR-15 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15 (Tuckman 15.1) and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 a.7)

b.reason: Identical terminal distributions do not imply identical curve dynamics; Model 3 shifts in parallel, Vasicek does not.

c.reason: Wrong condition: GARP sets $\alpha$ equal to $k$, not $k/2$, and the terminal standard deviations then match exactly.

d.reason: With the parameters matched there is no difference in width; the decay in Model 3’s volatility does the job mean reversion does in Vasicek.

questions.question: A fixed-income analyst models the short rate with GARP’s Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t) dt + \sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t} dw$, using monthly steps. The parameters are $r_{0} = 4.0\%$, $\sigma= 1.50\%$ per year, $\alpha= 0.25$, and drift $\lambda(t) = 0.20\%$ per year. What is the standard deviation of the rate change over the one-month step that begins at $t = 3$ years?

options.text: 5.9 bp

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Volatility in force at** $t = 3$

$\sigma(3) = 1.50\% \times\text{e}^{-0.25\times3} = 1.50\% \times0.47237 = 0.70855\%$ per year

⇒ Three years in, the volatility has decayed to less than half its starting value.

**Step 2 – Scale to one month**

SD $= \sigma(3)\sqrt{dt} = 0.70855\% \times\sqrt{1/12} = 0.70855\% \times0.28868 = 0.2045\% \approx20.5$ bp

**Interpretation**

Only the volatility term matters for the standard deviation of a step. $r_{0} = 4.0\%$ and $\lambda= 0.20\%$ are given but not needed: the drift shifts the mean of the change, not its dispersion.

**LO:** MR-15 b: Calculate the short-term rate change and determine the behavior of the standard deviation of the rate change using a model with time-dependent volatility. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.10, 15.1, eq. 15.2

c.reason: Left out the decay, using the initial $\sigma$: 1.50% × 0.28868 = 0.4330% = 43.3 bp (the Ho-Lee answer).

d.reason: Left out the time scaling: $\sigma(3) = 0.7086\% = 70.9$ bp is an annual figure.

questions.question:
An interest rate options market maker at a Japanese bank quotes caplets off Model 3, $dr =$ $\lambda(t)dt + \sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}dw$, on a quarterly tree ($dt = 0.25$). For each quarter the desk uses the volatility at the start of that quarter, $\sigma(0)$ for the first step and $\sigma(0.25)$ for the second. Inputs (annualised):

- $r_{0} = 2.40\%$; $\lambda_{1} = 0.80\%$; $\lambda_{2} = 1.00\%$
- Initial basis-point volatility $\sigma= 150$ bps; decay rate $\alpha= 0.60$

Which of the following is closest to the short rate in the upper node after two quarters, and to the standard deviation of the short rate after two quarters?

options.text: Upper node 4.246%; standard deviation 0.990%
Upper node 4.246%; standard deviation 1.396%
Upper node 4.350%; standard deviation 1.061%
Upper node 4.696%; standard deviation 0.990%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Volatility for each step**

$$\sigma(0) = 1.50\%, \sigma(0.25) = 1.50\% \times\text{e}^{-0.60\times0.25} = 1.50\% \times0.8607 = 1.2911\%$$

⇒ Volatility decays from 150 to about 129 bp per year over the first quarter.

**Step 2 – Perturbations per step**

$\sigma(0)\sqrt{dt} = 1.50\% \times0.5 = 0.7500\%, \sigma(0.25)\sqrt{dt} = 1.2911\% \times0.5 = 0.6455\%$

**Step 3 – Drift over two quarters**

$$(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2}) dt = (0.80\% + 1.00\%) \times0.25 = 0.450\%$$

**Step 4 – Upper node**

$$r_{uu} = 2.40\% + 0.450\% + 0.7500\% + 0.6455\% = 4.246\%$$

⇒ Two up moves, each sized by the volatility in force during that quarter.

**Step 5 – Standard deviation after two quarters**

SD $= \sqrt{dt} \sqrt{\sigma(0)^{2} + \sigma(0.25)^{2}} = 0.5 \times\sqrt{1.50^{2} + 1.2911^{2}} \% = 0.5 \times1.9791\% = 0.990\%$

⇒ The two independent steps add in variance. Because volatility decays, the SD rises more slowly with horizon than $\sigma\sqrt{t}$.

**Interpretation**

A constant-volatility Ho-Lee tree with the same $\sigma$ gives a wider distribution (1.061%); the decay is what lets the desk match caplets that expire later at lower volatilities. With $\sigma$ changing between steps the up-down and down-up nodes no longer coincide (2.954% and 2.746%), and Model 3 remains a parallel-shift model with a flat (time-varying) volatility term structure.

**LO:** MR-15 a: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility. MR-15 b: Calculate the short-term rate change and determine the behavior of the standard deviation of the rate change using a model with time-dependent volatility. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.10, 15.1, eqs. 15.1 and 15.2, Figure 15.1

**Source:** Workbook A7.4 • S2, S3 • Map #7 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 b.5)

b.reason: Correct node, but added the standard deviations linearly, 0.7500% + 0.6455% = 1.396%: this is the upper node’s distance from $r_{0}$ plus drift, not a standard deviation.

c.reason: Ignored the decay and used $\sigma= 1.50\%$ in both steps (Ho-Lee): 2.85% + 2 × 0.75% = 4.350%, SD $1.50\%\sqrt{0.5} = 1.061\%$.

d.reason: Scaled the drift by $\sqrt{dt}$ instead of $dt$: 2.40%+1.80%×0.5+1.3955% = 4.696%.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a pension fund runs a coarse annual tree ($dt = 1$) for Model 3 to sense-check the dispersion of the short rate three years ahead. For each year the tree uses the volatility at the start of that year. The inputs are:

- Current short rate: 3.10%; drift $\lambda(t)$: 0.25% per year
- Initial basis-point volatility $\sigma= 120$ bps per year; decay rate $\alpha= 0.20$

Which of the following is closest to the standard deviation of the short rate after three years on this tree?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Volatility at the start of each year**

$\sigma(0) = 1.20\%, \sigma(1) = 1.20\% \text{e}^{-0.20} = 0.9825\%, \sigma(2) = 1.20\% \text{e}^{-0.40} = 0.8044\%$

**Step 2 – Add the variances (**$dt = 1$**)**

SD $= \sqrt{1} \times\sqrt{1.20^{2} + 0.9825^{2} + 0.8044^{2}} \% = \sqrt{3.0523} \% = 1.747\%$

⇒ About 1.75%: each later year adds less variance because its volatility has decayed.

**Interpretation**

A constant-volatility model would give $1.20\%\sqrt{3} = 2.08\%$; the decay narrows the three-year distribution by about a sixth. The current rate and the drift move the centre of the distribution, not its width, so they are not needed. (On a fine grid the same inputs approach $\sigma\sqrt{(1 - \text{e}^{-2\alpha T} )/(2\alpha)} = 1.59\%$; the coarse annual tree overstates it because it holds each year’s volatility at its starting value.)

**LO:** MR-15 b: Calculate the short-term rate change and determine the behavior of the standard deviation of the rate change using a model with time-dependent volatility. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.10, 15.1, eq. 15.2, Figure 15.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15 and Workbook A7 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 b.6)

a.reason: Used the volatility at the end of each year, $\sigma(1)$, $\sigma(2)$, $\sigma(3)$: $\sqrt{0.9653 + 0.6470 + 0.4337} = 1.43\%$. The stem says start of year.

c.reason: Ignored the decay (Ho-Lee): $1.20\% \times\sqrt{3} = 2.08\%$.

d.reason: Added the standard deviations linearly: 1.20 + 0.98 + 0.80 = 2.99%.

questions.question: A market maker in interest rate options uses Model 3 with $\sigma= 126$ bps per year and $\alpha= 0.025$, the parameters of GARP’s Figure 15.1. A junior analyst asks how the standard deviation of the terminal distribution of the short rate behaves as the horizon lengthens. Which of the following is the correct answer?

options.text: It declines toward zero, because the volatility $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ decays to zero.
It grows in proportion to $\sqrt{T}$, reaching about 6.90% at 30 years, as in a constant-volatility model.
It rises rapidly at first and then more slowly, levelling off toward about 5.63%, so it is about 4.97% at 30 years.
It rises rapidly at first and then levels off at the initial volatility of 1.26%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Separate the two standard deviations**

The instantaneous volatility $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ falls toward zero. The terminal standard deviation adds up the variance of every step from today to $T$ , so it can only rise with $T$ .

**Step 2 – How fast it rises**

Early steps carry nearly the full $\sigma$, so the terminal SD rises rapidly at first; later steps add less and less, so it rises more slowly. GARP’s Figure 15.1 shows exactly this shape.

**Step 3 – Where it levels off**

$\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\alpha}} = \frac{1.26\%}{\sqrt{0.05}} = 5.63\%,$ SD$(r_{30}) = 1.26\%\sqrt{\frac{1 - \text{e}^{-1.5}}{0.05}} = 4.97\%$

**Interpretation**

The shape mirrors the effect of mean reversion on horizon standard deviation in Vasicek, which is why matching $\alpha$ to $k$ makes the two models’ terminal standard deviations identical (MR-15 a).

**LO:** MR-15 b: Calculate the short-term rate change and determine the behavior of the standard deviation of the rate change using a model with time-dependent volatility. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 3e, Ch.10, 15.1, Figure 15.1

MR-16 • The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, Figure 15.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 b.7)

a.reason: Confuses the instantaneous volatility at a date with the dispersion of the terminal distribution: the first declines, the second accumulates.

b.reason: Ignores the decay: $1.26\% \times\sqrt{30} = 6.90\%$ is the constant-volatility answer.

d.reason: Right shape, wrong ceiling: the initial annual volatility is not the limit of the accumulated standard deviation.

questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16 (Tuckman 16.2) and Vardeez
questions.question: A risk manager is reviewing a rates desk’s new Gauss+ implementation, in which $dr_{t} =$ $-\alpha_{r}(r_{t} - m_{t})dt$, $dm_{t} = -\alpha_{m}(m_{t} - l_{t})dt + \sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$ and $dl_{t} = -\alpha_{l}(l_{t} -$ $\mu)dt + \sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$. Which of the following statements about the model’s structure is correct?

options.text: The model has three state variables but only two sources of risk, because the short-term rate has no random shock of its own.
The model has three sources of risk, one for each of $r$, $m$ and $l$, and the “+” in its name refers to this third source.
The short-term rate carries its own volatility term, which makes short-end volatility the highest point of the volatility term structure.
Rates are lognormally distributed in Gauss+, which keeps the short-term rate above zero at all horizons.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Count the state variables**

Describing the state of the world requires knowing $r$, $m$ and $l$: three factors.

**Step 2 – Count the sources of risk**

Only $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ appear; $dr$ has no random term.

⇒ Three factors, two sources of risk: that is the “+”.

**Interpretation**

The missing shock on $r$ is deliberate. It reflects a central bank pegging the policy rate, keeps short-rate volatility low and lets the model produce the hump-shaped volatility term structure seen in the data.

**LO:** MR-16 a: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16 (Tuckman 16.2) and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 a.3)

b.reason: Miscounts the sources of risk: there are only two. The “+” marks a state variable that is not a source of risk.

c.reason: Polarity: the short rate has no volatility term, which makes short-end volatility low, not the highest point.

d.reason: Wrong distribution: “Gauss” means rates are normally distributed, so negative rates are possible.

questions.question: A quantitative analyst is explaining to a portfolio manager how the mean-reversion parameters of the Gauss+ model shape the way factor changes pass through to the term structure of rates. Which of the following statements is consistent with the model?

options.text: A larger $\alpha_{r}$ makes changes in the factors $m$ and $l$ make their way into the term structure of rates faster.
A larger $\alpha_{m}$ makes $m$ converge to $l$ more slowly and increases the effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.
A smaller $\alpha_{l}$ makes the effect of $l$ on longer-term yields less parallel across terms.
A larger $\alpha_{l}$ lengthens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ persist longer.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Role of** $\alpha_{r}$

$r$ reverts to $m$ at speed $\alpha_{r}$. The faster it does so, the faster changes in $m$ (and, through $m$, in $l$) show up in the short rate and hence in the term structure.

**Step 2 – Check the other speeds**

Larger $\alpha_{m}$: $m$ converges to $l$ faster and affects longer-term yields less. Smaller $\alpha_{l}$: $l$ converges to $\mu$ more slowly, so its effect on all longer-term yields is more parallel. Half-life is ln $2/\alpha$, so a larger $\alpha_{l}$ shortens it.

⇒ Only A matches Tuckman.

**Interpretation**

This is why the estimated $\alpha_{l} = 0.0165$ (half-life 42 years) makes the long factor behave almost like a parallel shift of the long end, while $\alpha_{r} = 1.0547$ confines the short factor to the very short end.

**LO:** MR-16 a: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.3, Figure 16.7

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16 (Tuckman 16.3) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 a.6)

b.reason: Polarity flip twice: a larger $\alpha_{m}$ means faster convergence and a smaller effect on longer yields.

c.reason: Polarity flip: a smaller $\alpha_{l}$ makes the effect of $l$ more parallel.

d.reason: Half-life is inversely related to speed: ln $2/\alpha_{l}$ falls as $\alpha_{l}$ rises.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a US asset manager is presenting the Gauss+ model to a group of newly hired analysts, using the book’s estimated parameters: $\alpha_{r} = 1.0547$, $\alpha_{m} = 0.6358$, $\alpha_{l} = 0.0165$, $\sigma_{m} = 109.2$ bps, $\sigma_{l} = 96.4$ bps. Today the short-term rate is $r = 5.25\%$ and the medium-term factor is $m = 4.10\%$. The desk’s previous one-factor Vasicek implementation used a short-rate volatility of 95 bps, and this month’s realised increment is $dw = +0.20$ (already scaled by $\sqrt{dt}$). Which of the following is closest to the short-term rate one month from now ($dt = 1/12$) under Gauss+?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – State the equation**

$dr_{t} = -\alpha_{r}(r_{t} - m_{t}) dt ($Equation 16.9, no random term)

⇒ The short-term rate is pushed only toward the medium-term factor, the way a central bank moves its policy target gradually.

**Step 2 – Gap to the target**

$$r - m = 5.25\% - 4.10\% = 1.15\%$$

⇒ The short rate sits 115 bps above where the medium-term factor says it is heading.

**Step 3 – Annualised drift**

$$-\alpha_{r}(r - m) = -1.0547 \times1.15\% = -1.2129\%$$

⇒ At the current gap, the short rate would fall about 121 bps over a full year.

**Step 4 – One-month change and new level**

$$dr = -1.2129\% \times\frac{1}{12} = -0.1011\%, r_{1/12} = 5.25\% - 0.1011\% = 5.149\%$$

⇒ With no shock in Equation 16.9, the short rate’s path over $dt$ is deterministic: the expected and actual moves coincide.

**Interpretation**

The short rate falls about 10 bps toward the medium-term factor, reflecting a market that expects easing. Neither $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ nor the Vasicek volatility and $dw$ enter: the absence of a shock on $r$ is what keeps short-rate volatility low and lets Gauss+ match the hump-shaped volatility term structure.

**LO:** MR-16 c: Calculate changes in the short-term, medium-term, and long-term interest rate factors under the Gauss+ model. MR-16 a: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.2 eq. 16.9, Table 16.1

MR-16 • The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A25.1 • S5, S6 • Aug-2026 • Map #40 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 a.7)

b.reason: Wrong speed (sibling swap): used $\alpha_{m} = 0.6358$: 5.25%−0.6358×1.15%/12 = 5.189%.

c.reason: Added a Vasicek-style shock to the short rate: 5.149% + 0.95% × 0.20 = 5.339%. Equation 16.9 has no random term.

d.reason: Sign flip: wrote the drift as $+\alpha_{r}(r - m)dt$, so the rate moves away from its target: 5.25% + 0.1011% = 5.351%.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
questions.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
questions.topic: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
questions.question: The head of rates at an insurer is deciding which applications of the Vasicek and Gauss+ models to approve. Which of the following proposed uses is consistent with Tuckman’s assessment of the two models?

options.text: Using Vasicek to price, compare and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years, calibrated to match 10- to 30-year noncallable bonds and the 10-year rate volatility.
Using Vasicek to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds, because a single factor explains most term structure variability at every maturity.
Restricting Gauss+ to classroom use, because practitioners avoid it for proprietary trading since its factors cannot be recovered from market data.
Using Gauss+ for caps across the curve because, unlike Vasicek, it adds a random shock to the short-term rate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where Vasicek is reasonable**

GARP: the model “can reasonably be used, for example, to price, compare values, and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years”, because it can match noncallables from 10 to 30 years and the volatility of 10-year rates.

**Step 2 – Check the other proposals**

Vasicek needs more than one factor to hedge intermediate and shorter bonds. Gauss+ is well known among practitioners for proprietary trading, and its factors are fitted daily to the fed funds rate and the two- and 10-year forwards. Gauss+ removes the shock on the short rate.

⇒ Only A is consistent with Tuckman.

**Interpretation**

A good comparison answer names what each model is for. Vasicek: simple long-end pricing and hedging. Gauss+: relative-value and macro trading and products spread across the curve.

**LO:** MR-16 b: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.1, 16.3 and 16.4

MR-16 • The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16 (Tuckman 16.1, 16.4) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 b.6)

b.reason: One factor explains a lot of variability mainly at longer maturities; more than one factor is needed for intermediate and shorter bonds.

c.reason: Reversed: Gauss+ is popular for proprietary trading, and its factors are recovered from market data every day.

d.reason: Sibling swap: Vasicek has the short-rate shock; Gauss+ is defined by its absence.

questions.question: A rates strategist at a hedge fund is simulating one monthly step ($dt = 1/12$) of the Gauss+ medium-term factor with the book’s parameters: $\alpha_{m} = 0.6358$, $\sigma_{m} = 109.2$ bps (1.092% per year), $\rho= 0.212$. Current factor values are $r = 1.75\%$, $m = 3.00\%$ and $l = 4.20\%$. The realised increments for the month are $dW^{1} = -0.2309$ and $dW^{2} = -0.3464$. Which of the following is closest to the change in the medium-term factor?

options.text: +6.4 bps

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – State the equation**

$dm_{t} = -\alpha_{m}(m_{t} - l_{t}) dt + \sigma_{m} (\rho dW^{1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}) ($Equation 16.10)

$\Rightarrow m$ reverts to the long-term factor $l$, not to $r$ and not to $\mu$; the short rate $r = 1.75\%$ is irrelevant here.

**Step 2 – Drift over the month**

$$-\alpha_{m}(m - l) dt = -0.6358 \times(3.00\% - 4.20\%) \times\frac{1}{12} = +0.0636\%$$

$\Rightarrow m$ is 120 bps below $l$, so the trend pulls it up by about 6.4 bps this month.

**Step 3 – Loading on the second shock**

$$\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} = \sqrt{1 - 0.212^{2}} = 0.97727$$

⇒ This weight gives the medium-term fluctuation volatility $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$ and correlation exactly $\rho$ with the long-term factor (Equations 16.13 to 16.15).

**Step 4 – Combined standardised shock**

$$\rho dW^{1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2} = 0.212 \times(-0.2309) + 0.97727 \times(-0.3464)$$

= −0.04895 − 0.33853 = −0.38748

⇒ Most of the medium-term move comes from the factor’s own independent shock $dW^{2}$.

**Step 5 – Scale by volatility**

$$\sigma_{m} \times(-0.38748) = 1.092\% \times(-0.38748) = -0.4231\%$$

**Step 6 – Total change**

$dm = 0.0636\% - 0.4231\% = -0.3595\% \approx-36.0$ bps

⇒ The negative shock overwhelms the upward drift toward $l$.

**Interpretation**

The medium-term factor, the market’s “forward shadow rate” for where the short rate will be in two to three years, fell about 36 bps. Since $r$ reverts quickly to $m$ ($\alpha_{r} = 1.0547$), this lowers the expected path of the short rate over the next year or so.

**LO:** MR-16 c: Calculate changes in the short-term, medium-term, and long-term interest rate factors under the Gauss+ model. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.2 eqs. 16.10 and 16.13 to 16.15, Table 16.1

**Source:** Workbook A25.2 • S5, S6 • Aug-2026 • Map #40 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 c.5)

a.reason: Dropped the correlation loadings and added the raw increments: 0.0636% + 1.092% × (−0.2309 − 0.3464) = −56.7 bps.

b.reason: Wrong target (sibling swap): reverted $m$ to $r$ instead of $l$: −0.6358 × (3.00% − 1.75%)/12 − 0.4231% = −48.9 bps.

d.reason: Intermediate result: the drift alone, +6.4 bps, treating $m$ like the shock-free short rate.

questions.question: A model validator at a European bank is checking a monthly ($dt = 1/12$) simulation step of the long-term factor in a EUR implementation of the Gauss+ model that reuses the book’s parameters: $\alpha_{l} = 0.0165$, $\alpha_{m} = 0.6358$, $\sigma_{l} = 96.4$ bps (0.964% per year), $\mu= 10.555\%$ and $\rho= 0.212$. The long-term factor is $l = 3.50\%$ and the medium-term factor is $m = 2.80\%$. The realised increment for the month is $dW^{1} = +0.15$ (already scaled, so it includes $\sqrt{dt}$). Which of the following is closest to the change in the long-term factor?

options.text: +5.1 bps

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – State the equation**

$dl_{t} = -\alpha_{l}(l_{t} - \mu) dt + \sigma_{l} dW^{1} ($Equation 16.11)

$\Rightarrow l$ reverts to the constant $\mu$ at speed $\alpha_{l}$ and loads only on $dW^{1}$; $m$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $\rho$ do not enter.

**Step 2 – Gap to the target**

$$l - \mu= 3.50\% - 10.555\% = -7.055\%$$

**Step 3 – Drift over the month**

$$-\alpha_{l}(l - \mu) dt = -0.0165 \times(-7.055\%) \times\frac{1}{12} = +0.0097\%$$

⇒ Despite the 7-point gap, the slowest speed in the cascade (half-life ln 2/0.0165 = 42.0 years) moves $l$ up by only about 1 bp a month.

**Step 4 – Random fluctuation**

$$\sigma_{l} dW^{1} = 0.964\% \times0.15 = 0.1446\%$$

⇒ The shock adds about 14.5 bps; the monthly standard deviation of this term is 0.964% × $\sqrt{1/12} = 27.8$ bps.

**Step 5 – Total change**

$dl = 0.0097\% + 0.1446\% = 0.1543\% \approx+15.4$ bps

**Interpretation**

Because $\alpha_{l}$ is so small, $l$ behaves almost like a random walk: its effect on longer-term forwards is nearly parallel and, beyond 10 years, it is the sole factor driving forward-rate changes. A 15 bp rise in $l$ lifts the long end almost one-for-one.

**LO:** MR-16 c: Calculate changes in the short-term, medium-term, and long-term interest rate factors under the Gauss+ model. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.2 eq. 16.11, Table 16.1

**Source:** Workbook A25.3 • S2, S5, S6 • Aug-2026 • Map #40 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 c.6)

a.reason: Double $\sqrt{dt}$: multiplied the already-scaled increment by $\sqrt{1/12}$ again: 0.97 + 14.46 × 0.28868 = 5.1 bps.

c.reason: Dropped $dt$ on the drift: 0.0165 × 7.055% = 11.64 bps plus 14.46 bps = 26.1 bps.

d.reason: Wrong speed (sibling swap): used $\alpha_{m}$: 0.6358 × 7.055%/12 = 37.38 bps plus 14.46 bps = 51.8 bps.

questions.question:
A rates strategist steps the Gauss+ model forward one month ($dt = 1/12$) using GARP’s Table 16.1 parameters:

|  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\alpha_{r}$ | 1.0547 | $\sigma_{m}$ | 109.2 bps |
| $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.6358 | $\sigma_{l}$ | 96.4 bps |
| $\alpha_{l}$ | 0.0165 | $\rho$ | 0.212 |
| $\mu$ | 10.555% |  |  |

Today $r = 2.00\%$, $m = 3.00\%$ and $l = 4.00\%$. The realised increments for the month, already scaled by $\sqrt{dt}$, are $dW^{1} = +0.10$ and $dW^{2} = -0.05$. Which of the following is closest to the changes in the three factors $(dr, dm, dl)$, in basis points?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Short rate, drift only**

$dr = -1.0547 \times(2.00\% - 3.00\%) \times\frac{1}{12} = +0.0879\% = +8.8$ bp

**Step 2 – Medium factor, drift plus both shocks**

drift $= -0.6358 \times(3.00\% - 4.00\%) \times\frac{1}{12} = +0.0530\%, \sqrt{1 - 0.212^{2}} = 0.9773$

shock = 1.092% × \[0.212 × 0.10 + 0.9773 × (−0.05)\] = 1.092% × (−0.02767) = −0.0302% $dm = 0.0530\% - 0.0302\% = +0.0228\% = +2.3$ bp

**Step 3 – Long factor, drift plus** $dW^{1}$

drift $= -0.0165\times(4.00\%-10.555\%)\times\frac{1}{12} = +0.0090\%, \text{shock} = 0.964\%\times0.10 = 0.0964\%$ $dl = +0.1054\% = +10.5$ bp

⇒ (+8.8, +2.3, +10.5) bp.

**Interpretation**

The long factor moves most even though it has by far the slowest mean reversion, because its move is almost all shock. The short rate moves 8.8 bp with no randomness at all. Compare MR-16 c.2: without shocks the ranking is the reverse.

**LO:** MR-16 c: Calculate changes in the short-term, medium-term, and long-term interest rate factors under the Gauss+ model. • **Reference:** Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.9, 16.2 eqs. 16.9 to 16.11, Table 16.1

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16, Table 16.1 and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 c.7)

a.reason: Used $\alpha_{m}$ for the short rate: 0.6358 × 1%/12 = 5.3 bp.

b.reason: Reverted $l$ to $m$ instead of $\mu$: drift −0.0165 × 1%/12 = −0.14 bp, so $dl = 9.5$ bp.

d.reason: Swapped the loadings in $dm$, putting $\rho$ on $dW^{2}$ and $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ on $dW^{1}$: shock +9.5 bp, so $dm = 14.8$ bp.

questions.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
questions.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
questions.topic: Volatility Smiles
questions.source: Workbook A3.1 • S1, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #4
questions.question: A senior equity derivatives analyst at a Hong Kong bank is presenting implied volatilities of European options on a stock index to a group of newly hired analysts. Short-dated implied volatilities on the index are currently at historically low levels. Which of the following statements should the analyst include in the presentation?

options.text: Implied volatility rises as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.
Implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises toward both lower and higher strikes, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.
Implied volatility falls as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to decrease with option maturity.
Implied volatility falls as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Strike: the equity skew**

For equity options (stocks and indices) the volatility decreases as the strike price increases (Hull 17.3). Low-strike options, deep OTM puts and deep ITM calls, carry the highest implied volatilities.

**Step 2 – Maturity: the term structure**

Implied volatility tends to be an increasing function of maturity when short-dated volatilities are historically low, because volatilities are then expected to increase (Hull 17.5). The stem sets that condition.

**Step 3 – The second maturity effect**

Across a surface, the skew itself becomes less pronounced as maturity increases: jumps are averaged out over long horizons and the impact of non-constant volatility on implied volatility usually shrinks.

**Interpretation**

D is the only statement with both directions right. If short-dated volatilities were historically high instead, the same skew would sit on a term structure that decreases with maturity.

**LO:** MR-17 e: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape. questions.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles

questions.question: A volatility trader at a Dutch bank holds a European call and a European put on a non-dividend-paying index, with the same strike price and the same time to maturity. Over a short period the index level and interest rates are unchanged, but implied volatility rises from $\sigma_{1}$ to $\sigma_{2}$. A junior colleague argues that the two options must change in value by different amounts. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The call gains and the put loses value, because the two options have deltas of opposite sign.
Both options gain by the same dollar amount, because $c -p = S_{0} -K\text{e}^{-rT}$ does not depend on volatility.
Both options gain value, but the call gains more because its payoff is unlimited on the upside.
Both options gain by the same dollar amount only if they are at the money.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Parity before and after**

At $\sigma_{1}$: $c_{1} - p_{1} = S_{0} - K\text{e}^{-rT}$ . At $\sigma_{2}$: $c_{2} - p_{2} = S_{0} - K\text{e}^{-rT}$ (same right-hand side, since $S_{0}$, $K$, $r$, $T$ are unchanged and volatility does not appear).

**Step 2 – Subtract**

$c_{2} - c_{1} = p_{2} - p_{1}$.

⇒ Both options change by the same dollar amount: call vega equals put vega. Both gain, since vega is positive.

**Interpretation**

This is the price-change version of “one implied volatility for the call and the put”. Holding the parity right-hand side fixed is what makes it work: over a short period with the index unchanged, only volatility moves.

**LO:** MR-17 b: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.1; Practice Question 17.26

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17 Q17.26 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 b.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap: opposite signs belong to delta (sensitivity to the index), not to vega.

c.reason: Payoff asymmetry does not change the parity difference, which contains no volatility term.

d.reason: Scope error: the result holds at every strike, not only at the money.

questions.question: An options trader at a Swiss bank observes European call and put options on a non-dividend-paying stock with the same strike price and the same maturity. Using BSM, the call’s implied volatility is 24% and the put’s implied volatility is 27%. The head of market risk asks what the discrepancy means. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: No action is needed, because the equity skew assigns higher implied volatilities to puts than to calls.
An arbitrage exists only if the stock price is lognormally distributed, because the implied volatilities come from BSM.
The call is expensive relative to the put, so the trader should sell the call, buy the put and buy the stock, borrowing at the risk-free rate.
The put is expensive relative to the call, so the trader should sell the put, buy the call and short the stock, investing the proceeds at the risk-free rate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What parity implies**

Put-call parity $p + S_{0} = c + K\text{e}^{-rT}$ holds for BSM prices and for market prices, so $p_{BS} - p_{mkt} =$ $c_{BS} - c_{mkt}$ (17.2). At any volatility the dollar pricing errors are equal, so a European call and put with the same strike and maturity must have the same implied volatility.

**Step 2 – Which leg is rich**

A higher implied volatility means a higher price relative to BSM. At 27% versus 24%, the put is priced too high relative to the call: $p_{mkt} + S_{0} > c_{mkt} + K\text{e}^{-rT}$ .

**Step 3 – The arbitrage**

Sell the put, buy the call and short the stock: the cash received $p - c + S_{0}$ exceeds $K\text{e}^{-rT}$ . Invest it at the risk-free rate. At $T$ the long call and short put together buy the stock for $K$ whatever happens, which closes the short; the invested proceeds exceed $K$.

**Interpretation**

Parity is a no-arbitrage relation with no assumption about the asset price distribution, so the profit is locked in whether or not prices are lognormal. This is why the smile is the same for calls and puts.

**LO:** MR-17 b: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20, 17.1, eqs. 17.1 and 17.2, Example 17.1; Practice Questions 17.8 and 17.17

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A3.4 • S7 • Map #4, #71 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 b.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the skew relates implied volatility to the strike, across strikes. At the same strike and maturity the call and put must share one implied volatility.

b.reason: Scope/condition error: put-call parity does not require any assumption about the probability distribution; it is true both when the distribution is lognormal and when it is not.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the put, with the higher implied volatility, is the expensive leg. Selling the call and buying the put would buy the overpriced side.

questions.question: A junior trader at a Canadian dealer prices every European option on a stock index, and every European option on USD/CAD, with a single lognormal volatility per underlying equal to that underlying’s at-the-money implied volatility. A market risk analyst compares the resulting model prices with market prices of options with the same maturity. Which of the following conclusions should the analyst reach?

options.text: Deep out-of-the-money index puts are priced below market, because the implied distribution has a heavier left tail than the lognormal.
Deep out-of-the-money index calls are priced below market, because the implied distribution has a heavier right tail than the lognormal.
Deep out-of-the-money USD/CAD puts are priced above market, because the implied distribution has a thinner left tail than the lognormal.
Options at every strike are priced at market, because put-call parity forces one implied volatility on every option with the same maturity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a single lognormal volatility assumes**

BSM with one volatility assumes a lognormal distribution. The market prices with a smile, which corresponds to the implied distribution (Hull 17.2, 17.3 and Appendix).

**Step 2 – Index options**

The equity implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a less heavy right tail than the lognormal. A deep OTM put pays off only in the left tail, so the market prices it relatively high, at an implied volatility above the at-the-money level. The trader’s at-the-money volatility therefore prices it below market. A deep OTM call pays off only in the thin right tail and is priced relatively low by the market, so the trader prices it above market.

**Step 3 – FX options**

The FX implied distribution has heavier tails on both sides. Both deep OTM puts and deep OTM calls carry implied volatilities above the at-the-money level, so the trader prices both wings below market. Table 17.1 supports the market: 3 SD daily moves occur on 1.30% of days versus 0.27% under the lognormal model.

**Interpretation**

The trader is selling tail protection too cheaply on index puts and on both FX wings: the trade Business Snapshot 17.1 describes, from the wrong side.

**LO:** MR-17 c: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset. MR-17 d: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20, 17.1 to 17.3, Table 17.1, Business Snapshot 17.1

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A3.3 • S2, S3, S4, S5, S7 • Map #4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 c.8)

b.reason: Sibling swap: a heavier right tail is the FX property, not the equity one. The index implied distribution has a less heavy right tail, so deep OTM index calls are priced above market by the lognormal.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the FX implied distribution has a heavier, not thinner, left tail, so deep OTM USD/CAD puts are priced below market.

d.reason: Scope error: put-call parity makes a call and a put with the same strike and maturity share one implied volatility; it does not equalise implied volatilities across strikes.
