questions.question:
A currency options strategist at a Japanese bank studies daily moves in 10 exchange rates against the USD over ten years and compares the frequencies with those predicted by a lognormal model:

| Daily move | Real world | Lognormal model |
|---|---|---|
| > 1 SD | 23.32% | 31.73% |
| > 3 SD | 1.30% | 0.27% |
| > 5 SD | 0.24% | 0.00% |

Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the data?

options.text: Exchange rate distributions are more peaked and have heavier tails than the lognormal, so deep out-of-the-money calls and puts should trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.
Exchange rate distributions have heavier tails than the lognormal only on the downside, so only deep out-of-the-money puts should trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.

Moves larger than 1 SD occur less often than the lognormal predicts, so exchange rate distributions have thinner tails and deep out-of-the-money options should trade at lower implied volatilities than at-the-money options.
Moves larger than 3 SD occur about five times as often as the lognormal predicts, so the at-the-money implied volatility should be raised while implied volatility stays flat across strikes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the tails**

Beyond 3 SD: 1.30% versus 0.27% (about 4.8×). Beyond 5 SD: 0.24% versus essentially zero. Large moves are far more frequent than lognormal: heavy tails.

**Step 2 – Read the centre**

Beyond 1 SD: 23.32% versus 31.73%. More days than predicted fall inside 1 SD: the distribution is more peaked.

**Step 3 – Implication for options**

Heavy tails on both sides make deep OTM calls and puts worth more than BSM at the ATM volatility, so their implied volatilities are higher: a smile.

**Interpretation**

Hull’s point is that the table supports the smile traders use. The table counts moves of either sign, which is why the conclusion is about both wings.

**LO:** MR-17 d: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.2, Table 17.1, Business Snapshot 17.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17 Table 17.1 and Business Snapshot 17.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 d.2)

b.reason: Sibling swap: a heavy downside only is the equity picture; the data measure moves in both directions.

c.reason: Misreads the first row: fewer moves beyond 1 SD reflects a more peaked centre, while the 3 to 5 SD rows show heavier tails.

d.reason: True fact, wrong conclusion: raising one volatility for all strikes keeps the lognormal shape and still underprices the wings relative to the ATM option.

questions.question: A central bank has credibly committed to keep an exchange rate between 0.97 and 1.03, and the rate currently trades at 1.00. An FX options trader at a Brazilian bank is asked what pattern of implied volatilities to expect for 3-month options on the rate. Which of the following is the most appropriate answer?

options.text: Implied volatility is highest at the money and lower for strikes near or beyond 0.97 and 1.03, because the band makes both tails thinner than the lognormal.
Implied volatility is lowest at the money and higher for strikes near or beyond 0.97 and 1.03, because central bank actions make the rate jump.
Implied volatility falls steadily as the strike rises, because the central bank defends the lower edge of the band more strongly.
Implied volatility is flat across strikes, because the band reduces the volatility of the rate by the same amount at every strike.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the band does to the distribution**

A credible band truncates the distribution at 0.97 and 1.03: both tails are much thinner than a lognormal with the same ATM volatility.

**Step 2 – Implication for prices**

Options struck near or beyond the band edges have far less chance of paying off than BSM implies, so they are cheap and their implied volatilities are low.

⇒ Implied volatility is highest at the money and falls toward the wings: a frown, the inverse of the usual FX smile.

**Interpretation**

The same rule as always: less probability in a tail than the lognormal means lower implied volatility for options that pay off there.

**LO:** MR-17 d: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), Practice Question 17.15

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17 Q17.15 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 d.5)

b.reason: Applies the free-floating FX story (jumps on central bank actions) to a rate the central bank is holding inside a band; that gives a smile only when tails are heavy.

c.reason: Sibling swap: a downward skew needs a heavier left tail and thinner right tail; a symmetric band thins both.

d.reason: A band changes the shape of the distribution, not just its scale, so implied volatility cannot stay flat.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the options desk of a German bank that trades EUR/USD options and options on a European equity index. The desk prices the two books with differently shaped volatility smiles, and the consultant is preparing a report explaining why. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the report?

options.text: The FX smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are negatively correlated.
The FX smile is U-shaped because of the leverage effect and crashophobia, while the equity skew slopes downward because volatility is not constant and prices jump on central bank actions.
The FX smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are positively correlated.
The FX smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward in a pattern that was equally marked before the October 1987 crash.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – FX shape and reason**

Implied volatility is relatively low at the money and progressively higher into or out of the money (Hull 17.2). Two lognormal conditions fail: volatility is far from constant and exchange rates frequently jump, sometimes on central bank actions. Both make extreme outcomes, in either direction, more likely.

**Step 2 – Equity shape and reason**

Volatility decreases as the strike increases (Hull 17.3). There is a negative correlation between equity prices and volatility, explained by leverage, the volatility feedback effect and crashophobia, so declines bring higher volatility (heavy left tail) and rises bring lower volatility (thin right tail).

**Interpretation**

The consultant should explain each smile by its own market’s mechanism; the two shapes are not interchangeable even though both depart from the lognormal.

**LO:** MR-17 d: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility. MR-17 e: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20, 17.2 and 17.3, Business Snapshot 17.2

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A3.2 • S2, S3, S6 • Map #4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 d.7)

b.reason: Sibling swap: the explanations are exchanged. Leverage and crashophobia explain the equity skew; non-constant volatility and jumps (including central bank actions) explain the FX smile.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the equity correlation between prices and volatility is negative; a positive correlation would thicken the right tail instead.

d.reason: Scope error: there was no marked volatility smile for equity options before October 1987; the skew has existed only since the crash, which is why crashophobia is one explanation.

questions.question: A strategist at a UK asset manager is explaining to clients why implied volatility on FTSE 100 options falls as the strike price rises. Which of the following explanations is correctly described?

options.text: Leverage effect: an external rise in volatility makes investors require a higher return, so the equity price falls.
Volatility feedback effect: a fall in the equity price raises the firm’s debt-to-equity ratio, so equity volatility rises.
Crashophobia: traders fear a repeat of the October 1987 crash, which is supported by the skew steepening when the S&P 500 falls and flattening when it rises.
Crashophobia: traders fear sharp equity declines, which is supported by the skew having been equally marked before and after October 1987.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Match each name to its mechanism**

Leverage: price falls → leverage rises → volatility rises. Volatility feedback: volatility rises (external) → required return rises → price falls.

**Step 2 – Crashophobia and its evidence**

Rubinstein’s explanation: traders fear another crash like October 1987 and price options accordingly. Support: the skew steepens when the S&P 500 falls and flattens when it rises.

⇒ C is the only correctly described pairing.

**Interpretation**

A and B are the classic name swap between the two correlation mechanisms. D attaches a false history to the right name.

**LO:** MR-17 e: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.3, Business Snapshot 17.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3 and Business Snapshot 17.2 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 e.2)

a.reason: Sibling swap: this mechanism (volatility first, then price) is the volatility feedback effect.

b.reason: Sibling swap: this mechanism (price first, then leverage and volatility) is the leverage effect.

d.reason: Scope error: the equity skew has existed only since October 1987, which is why crashophobia is a plausible explanation.

questions.question: The CRO of a Japanese bank is preparing a board risk committee briefing on why FRTB replaces 10-day 99% VaR with 97.5% expected shortfall for market risk capital under the internal models approach. One desk head argues the change is cosmetic, since for his desk, whose losses are close to normally distributed, the two measures give almost the same JPY figure. Which of the following statements should the CRO include as correct?

options.text: With loss distributions whose tails are heavier than the normal, 97.5% ES can be considerably lower than 99% VaR, so the change mainly reduces capital for fat-tailed desks.
Like the Basel I VaR measure, the 97.5% ES is a current measure, calibrated to market movements over the one to four years immediately preceding the calculation date.
Because 97.5% ES and 99% VaR are almost exactly equal for any loss distribution, the switch affects capital only through the new liquidity horizons.
For a normal loss distribution the two measures nearly coincide, but with heavier tails 97.5% ES can be considerably greater, and FRTB calibrates the ES to stressed market conditions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Compare the two measures under normality**

For normal losses with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$: 99% VaR $= \mu+ 2.326\sigma$ and 97.5% ES $= \mu+ 2.338\sigma$.

⇒ The desk head is right for his desk: the multipliers differ by only $0.012\sigma$.

**Step 2 – Drop the normality condition**

For non-normal losses the measures are not equivalent; when the loss distribution has a heavier tail than the normal, 97.5% ES can be considerably greater than 99% VaR.

⇒ ES averages the losses beyond the quantile, so it sees the shape of the tail that VaR ignores. The change is not cosmetic for fat-tailed desks.

**Step 3 – The calibration**

The measure is stressed ES at 97.5%: calculated from how market variables moved during stressed market conditions, as for Basel 2.5 stressed VaR.

**Interpretation**

The CRO’s answer to the desk head: near-equality is a property of the normal case only; the capital consequences come from fat tails, stressed calibration and (separately) liquidity horizons.

**LO:** MR-18 a • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Section 18.1

**Source:** Workbook A4.2 • S1 • Aug-2026 • Map #5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 a.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: heavier tails make 97.5% ES considerably greater than 99% VaR, raising capital for fat-tailed desks.

b.reason: Sibling swap: “current” calibration over the preceding one to four years describes the Basel I VaR; the FRTB measure is stressed ES.

c.reason: Scope/condition error: near-equality holds for normal distributions only; extending it to “any” distribution drops the condition.

questions.question:
A market risk manager at an Australian bank is preparing a trading desk for the switch from a 99% VaR to a 97.5% ES under FRTB. The desk’s P/L distribution is heavy-tailed. The desk’s model slices the tail beyond the 97.5% confidence level into 10 equal-probability slices and reports the VaR at each confidence level (AUD million):

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Confidence | 97.50% | 97.75% | 98.00% | 98.25% | 98.50% | 98.75% | 99.00% | 99.25% | 99.50% | 99.75% |
| VaR | 4.29 | 4.50 | 4.75 | 5.04 | 5.39 | 5.84 | 6.42 | 7.26 | 8.60 | 11.43 |

Which of the following is closest to the desk’s 97.5% ES and the change in its headline risk number when the 97.5% ES replaces the 99% VaR?

options.text: ES AUD 5.92 million; change −AUD 0.50 million
ES AUD 6.35 million; change −AUD 0.07 million
ES AUD 6.42 million; change AUD 0.00 million
ES AUD 6.58 million; change +AUD 0.16 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the tail VaRs**

With $n = 10$ slices beyond 97.5% there are $n - 1 = 9$ tail VaRs, at 97.75% through 99.75%. The 97.5% VaR (4.29) marks the start of the tail and is excluded.

**Step 2 – Average the tail VaRs**

ES$_{97.5\%} \approx\frac{4.50 + 4.75 + 5.04 + 5.39 + 5.84 + 6.42 + 7.26 + 8.60 + 11.43}{9} = \frac{59.23}{9} = 6.58$

⇒ On the worst 2.5% of days the desk loses about AUD 6.58 million on average.

**Step 3 – Compare with the 99% VaR**

$$\Delta= \text{ES}_{97.5\%} - \text{VaR}_{99\%} = 6.58 - 6.42 = +0.16$$

**Interpretation**

For a normal distribution the two numbers would almost coincide (2.338$\sigma$ against 2.326$\sigma$); because this desk’s tail is heavy, the 97.5% ES exceeds the 99% VaR, which is the FRTB motivation for capturing tail risk. With only 10 slices the estimate is, if anything, too low: the average-tail-VaR estimate rises towards the true ES as $n$ grows.

**LO:** MR-1 c; MR-1 d; MR-18 a • **Reference:** Dowd, Measuring Market Risk 2e, Ch.3, 1.4, Tables 1.1 and 1.2; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, 18.1

**Source:** Workbook B2.2 • S2 • Map #12 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 a.5)

a.reason: Divided the nine tail VaRs by the number of slices (10) instead of the number of tail VaRs (9): 59.23/10 = 5.92, change 5.92 − 6.42 = −0.50.

b.reason: Included the 97.5% VaR in the average (the off-by-one on tail membership): (59.23 + 4.29)/10 = 6.35, change −0.07.

c.reason: Applied the normal-distribution equivalence to a heavy-tailed desk and set the 97.5% ES equal to the 99% VaR, so the change is zero.

questions.question: A market risk manager at a mid-sized European bank is preparing a briefing note on the FRTB sensitivities-based standardized approach for the bank’s risk committee. Which of the following statements should the manager include as correct?

options.text: Risk weights are set by the Basel Committee as multiples of stressed daily volatility that reflect each risk factor’s liquidity horizon and the 97.5% ES confidence level.
Diversification is recognized between the delta and vega charges within a risk class, and across the seven risk classes, through correlations set by the Basel Committee.
Banks set the risk weights and correlations from their own data, and the regulator then applies a multiplier of at least 1.5 to the resulting charge.
The correlations specified by the Basel Committee are applied exactly as given, so the bank reports a single charge calculated at the prescribed correlation levels.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Who sets what**

In the sensitivities-based method the bank supplies the sensitivities $\delta_{i}$; the Basel Committee sets the risk weights $W_{i}$ and the correlations $\rho_{ij}$.

**Step 2 – How the risk weights are built**

$W_{i}$ = stressed daily volatility $\times\sqrt{LH} \times2.338$: the $\sqrt{LH}$ brings in the liquidity horizon and 2.338 is the normal multiplier for 97.5% ES. Example: $0.02 \times\sqrt{20} \times2.338 = 0.209$.

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 3 – Diversification and correlation scenarios**

There is no diversification across risk classes, nor between delta and vega within a class. Correlations are tested at 1.25, 1.00 and 0.75 times the Basel values and the greatest charge is used.

**Interpretation**

The SA is “standardized” because the regulator fixes the weights and correlations; the bank’s only input is its own sensitivities. This is also how liquidity horizons enter the SA (see Question MR-18 b.3).

**LO:** MR-18 a • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Section 18.2 and footnote 5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, Section 18.2 and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 a.6)

b.reason: Overstates diversification: none is allowed across risk classes or between delta and vega.

c.reason: Sibling swap: banks do not set SA weights or correlations; the multiplier $m_{c} \ge1.5$ belongs to the IMA capital formula.

d.reason: Drops the correlation scenarios: the charge is computed at 1.25, 1.00 and 0.75 times the Basel correlations and the greatest is used.

questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing a one-page comparison of market risk capital under the 1996 Amendment to Basel I, Basel II, Basel 2.5 and FRTB for the chief compliance oﬀicer of a UK bank. The FRTB section discusses two GBP options desks under the standardized approach: one is short a book of at-the-money options and the other is long a similar book. Which of the following statements is correct to include?

options.text: FRTB moves from 99% to 97.5% confidence and from one 10-day horizon to liquidity horizons, but still lets banks scale one-day changes to 10 days with a square-root-of-10 multiplier.
Basel II overhauled market risk capital by adding a stressed VaR term to the current VaR term, alongside the introduction of its three pillars.
Under FRTB’s standardized approach, the long-option desk attracts the curvature risk charge, because its gamma raises value relative to delta for both up and down moves.
Under FRTB’s standardized approach, the short-option desk’s curvature charge is the larger of its two shocked losses net of the delta effect, with negative results set to zero.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Curvature mechanics (Section 18.2.2)**

Shock risk factor $i$ up and down by its risk weight $W_{i}$. Compute $W_{i}\delta_{i} -\Delta V^{+}_{i}$ and $-W_{i}\delta_{i} -\Delta V^{-}_{i}$; the charge is the greater, and a negative result counts as zero.

⇒ Each term is the extra loss from curvature after the linear (delta) effect has been removed.

**Step 2 – Apply to the two desks**

Short options (Figure 4a): both moves are worse than delta predicts, so both terms are positive and the charge is the larger ($AB$ in the figure). Long options (Figure 4b): curvature increases value relative to delta for both moves, both terms are negative, so the charge is zero.

⇒ Illustration: short book terms 21,500 and 26,200 give 26,200; long book terms −17,300 and −14,700 give 0.

**Step 3 – Place the accords**

1996 Amendment: 10-day 99% VaR, usually 1-day VaR $\times\sqrt{10}$, $m \ge3$. Basel II: IRB credit risk, operational risk capital, three pillars; market risk retained. Basel 2.5: stressed VaR, IRC, CRM. FRTB: stressed 97.5% ES from overlapping 10-day changes, liquidity horizons, desk-level approval, SA with delta, vega and curvature.

**Interpretation**

The curvature charge is the standardized approach’s gamma charge, and it falls on the short-gamma desk.

**LO:** MR-18 a; ORR-21 c; ORR-22 a • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Sections 18.1, 18.2.2, 18.3; Carey (GARP), Ch.21 and Ch.22

MR-18 • Fundamental Review of the Trading Book • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A4.4 • S3, S5, S6 • Map #5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 a.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: $\sqrt{10}$ scaling of one-day changes is the Basel I / Basel 2.5 practice; FRTB requires actual overlapping 10-day changes from the stressed period.

b.reason: Wrong accord: stressed VaR is a Basel 2.5 change (end-2011); Basel II’s innovations were credit risk weights, operational risk capital and the three pillars.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the reason given is why a long option book receives a zero curvature charge; it is the short book that attracts it.

questions.question: A market risk analyst at a universal bank is mapping the risk factors of a new multi-asset trading desk to the FRTB liquidity horizon categories before the desk applies for internal models approval. Which of the following assignments is correct?

options.text: Large-cap equity price volatility: 10 days.
Corporate investment-grade credit spread: 40 days.
Foreign exchange volatility: 60 days.
Credit spread volatility: 60 days.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Look up each factor in Table 18.1**

Large-cap equity price volatility: 20. Corporate IG credit spread: 40. FX volatility: 40. Credit spread volatility: 120.

⇒ Only B matches.

**Step 2 – Use the patterns**

Volatilities sit at or above their level (large-cap equity 10, its vol 20; FX up to 40, FX vol 40). Credit spreads lengthen as quality falls (sovereign IG 20, corporate IG 40, corporate non-IG 60), and credit spread volatility is the longest, 120.

**Interpretation**

Each wrong option moves one factor into a neighbouring bucket: the typical GARP distractor for a lookup table.

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, Table 18.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 b.2)

questions.question: A model validation analyst is reviewing a bank’s FRTB internal models implementation, which estimates stressed 97.5% ES by historical simulation over a 250-day stressed period. The first simulation trial uses the changes in all risk factors between Day 0 and Day 10 of the stressed period, the second uses the changes between Day 1 and Day 11, and so on. Which of the following statements about this design is correct?

options.text: Successive trials share most of their daily changes and are not independent; this does not bias the ES estimate, but it reduces the effective sample size and makes the estimate noisier.
Successive trials share most of their daily changes, so the ES estimate is biased upward, and the bank must divide the result by $\sqrt{10}$ before using it for capital.
The design breaches FRTB, which requires non-overlapping 10-day periods so that the observations on losses are independent.
The design is unnecessary under FRTB, which allows the bank to compute 1-day changes and scale them by $\sqrt{10}$, avoiding overlapping periods altogether.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What overlap does**

Adjacent trials (Day 0 to 10, Day 1 to 11) share 9 of their 10 daily changes, so successive trials are not independent.

**Step 2 – What overlap does not do**

GARP: this “does not bias the results, but it reduces the effective sample size, making results more noisy”.

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 3 – Why FRTB accepts it**

Non-overlapping 10-day periods would require a very long history. The Basel Committee judges 10-day changes more relevant than 1-day changes, because successive days may not be independent while successive 10-day periods reasonably can be.

**Interpretation**

The FRTB design trades statistical eﬀiciency (overlap) for relevance (actual 10-day moves in a stressed period).

**LO:** MR-18 b • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Section 18.3 and Problem 18.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, Section 18.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 b.4)

b.reason: Overlap does not bias the estimate, and there is no $\sqrt{10}$ correction.

c.reason: Reversed: FRTB requires overlapping periods; non-overlapping periods are what econometricians would prefer but are infeasible.

d.reason: $\sqrt{10}$ scaling of 1-day changes is the Basel I / II.5 practice that FRTB abandons.

questions.question:
A market risk analyst at a Canadian bank is producing the FRTB internal models approach figures for the bank’s credit trading desk. The desk’s only risk factors are:

- sovereign investment-grade credit spreads
- corporate investment-grade credit spreads
- corporate non-investment-grade credit spreads
- credit spread volatilities

Using overlapping 10-day changes from the stressed period, the analyst has computed stressed 97.5% ES (CAD million): ES$_{1}$ (all risk factors shocked) = 18.0; ES$_{3} = 12.0$; ES$_{4} = 7.5$; ES$_{5} =$ 3.0. The ES$_{2}$ run was dropped from the overnight batch. The desk’s 1-day 99% VaR used for backtesting is CAD 4.6 million. Which of the following is closest to the desk’s liquidity-adjusted ES?

options.text: CAD 27.9 million
CAD 33.2 million
CAD 44.6 million
CAD 70.9 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Map each risk factor to its liquidity horizon (Table 18.1)**

Sovereign IG spread: 20 days (category 2). Corporate IG spread: 40 days (category 3). Corporate non-IG spread: 60 days (category 4). Credit spread volatility: 120 days (category 5).

⇒ The desk has no category 1 (10-day) risk factors at all.

**Step 2 – Infer the missing** ES$_{2}$

ES$_{2}$ shocks categories 2 to 5 and holds category 1 constant. With no category 1 factors, holding them constant changes nothing, so ES$_{2} = \text{ES}_{1} = 18.0$.

⇒ The missing run is not a zero: every factor on this desk still moves in the second 10-day block.

**Step 3 – Cascade weights**

$(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10$: 1, 1, 2, 2, 6.

**Step 4 – Squared, weighted terms**

$1 \times18.0^{2} = 324.0$; $1 \times18.0^{2} = 324.0$; $2 \times12.0^{2} = 288.0$; $2 \times7.5^{2} = 112.5$; $6 \times3.0^{2} = 54.0$.

**Step 5 – Liquidity-adjusted ES**

ES $= \sqrt{324.0 + 324.0 + 288.0 + 112.5 + 54.0} = \sqrt{1102.5} = 33.20$

⇒ CAD 33.2 million, about 1.84 times the 10-day all-factor ES: the long horizons of spreads and spread volatility add capital that a single 10-day horizon would miss.

**Interpretation**

The 1-day 99% VaR is a red herring: it is used only for the desk-level backtest, and scaling it by $\sqrt{10}$ is the Basel I / 2.5 practice that FRTB abandons.

**LO:** MR-18 b • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Section 18.3 and Table 18.1

**Source:** Workbook A4.1 • S2 • Aug-2026 • Map #5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 b.7)

a.reason: Dropped term: treats the missing ES$_{2}$ as zero, $\sqrt{324.0 + 288.0 + 112.5 + 54.0} =$ $\sqrt{778.5} = 27.90$.

d.reason: Adds the scaled ES linearly (perfect correlation): $18.0+18.0+12.0\sqrt{2}+7.5\sqrt{2}+$ $3.0\sqrt{6} = 70.93$.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
questions.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
The head of market risk at an Australian bank is reviewing the FRTB eligibility pack for four trading desks, all of which currently hold internal models approval. Results for the most recent 12 months:

| Desk | 1-day 99% VaR exceptions | 1-day 97.5% VaR exceptions | P&L attribution situations outside ranges |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rates | 11 | 34 | 1 |
| FX | 7 | 22 | 2 |
| Equity | 10 | 27 | 3 |

The credit desk holds a portfolio of illiquid loans that it has documented an intent to trade but is not able to trade or hedge on the desk. Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: The rates desk must calculate capital using the standardized approach, even though its 99% VaR exceptions are within the permitted number.
The equity desk must calculate capital using the standardized approach, because its P&L attribution ratios fell outside the ranges in three situations.
The credit desk may keep the loans in the trading book, because its documented intent to trade them meets the FRTB trading book test.
The FX desk’s internal models approval fully replaces the standardized approach, so no standardized capital needs to be calculated for it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Backtesting test, desk by desk**

Rule: more than 12 exceptions at 99% or more than 30 at 97.5% sends the desk to the standardized approach. Rates: 11 ≤ 12 passes at 99%, but 34 > 30 fails at 97.5%. FX: 7, 22: passes. Equity: 10, 27: passes.

⇒ Either condition alone is enough. The rates desk stays on the standardized approach until neither condition holds.

**Step 2 – P&L attribution test**

Rule: four or more situations in 12 months outside the ranges. Rates 1, FX 2, Equity 3: all below four.

⇒ No desk loses approval on P&L attribution this year; the equity desk is one breach from the threshold.

**Step 3 – Trading book boundary**

Under FRTB, intent to trade is no longer suﬀicient: the bank must be able to trade and manage the risks on a trading desk. The credit desk’s loans fail this test.

**Interpretation**

The recommendation: move the rates desk to standardized capital, keep FX and equity on internal models while watching equity’s attribution, and review the credit desk’s loans for banking book treatment. Because approval is desk by desk, the rates result does not affect other desks. (The 1996 Amendment backtest, 10 or more exceptions in 250 days forcing a multiplier of 4, would have penalised the equity desk; FRTB’s desk-level thresholds do not.)

**LO:** MR-18 c; MR-18 a • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Sections 18.1, 18.3.1, 18.3.2, 18.4

**Source:** Workbook A4.3 • S3, S4 • Map #5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 c.4)

b.reason: Scope/condition error: the trigger is four or more situations in 12 months; three does not trigger the standardized approach.

c.reason: Sibling swap: substitutes the pre-FRTB “intent to trade” test for the FRTB test, which requires the ability to trade and manage the risks on a desk.

d.reason: Absolute claim: even with internal models approval, banks must calculate capital under both approaches; the standardized approach provides a floor.

questions.question: The head of regulatory capital at a bank with a large book of asset-backed securities and collateralized debt obligations is briefing the CFO on how FRTB changes the capital treatment of these positions. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Basel II.5’s comprehensive risk measure let banks use approved internal models; because capital for the same portfolio varied too much across banks, FRTB requires the standardized approach for securitizations.

Basel II.5’s comprehensive risk measure let banks use approved internal models; because those models were found to be systematically too lenient, FRTB applies a higher multiplier to securitization ES.
FRTB allows securitizations to remain under the internal models approach, provided the desk holding them passes both the backtesting and the P&L attribution tests.
FRTB moves securitizations out of the trading book into the banking book, where they attract credit risk capital under the IRB approach.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The Basel 2.5 position**

The CRM charge covered securitization products (ABS, CDOs) and allowed banks, with regulatory approval, to use their own models.

**Step 2 – The problem the Basel Committee found**

Too much variation in the capital charges calculated by different banks for the same portfolio.

**Step 3 – The FRTB response**

The standardized approach must be used for securitizations.

⇒ A is correct.

**Interpretation**

The motivation is consistency, not conservatism: models were judged too variable, not too lenient. The positions stay in the trading book; they simply lose internal models.

**LO:** MR-18 c • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.18, Section 18.3.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, Section 18.3.4 and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-18 c.7)

b.reason: Wrong motivation and wrong mechanism: variability, not leniency; and the $m_{c}$ multiplier applies to WES under the IMA, not to securitizations.

c.reason: Securitizations lose internal models outright, whatever the desk’s test results.

d.reason: Sibling swap with the book boundary: FRTB does not move securitizations to the banking book.

questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Dowd 1.5, Example 1.6)
questions.question: A market risk analyst estimates the 99% VaR of a standardised P/L series at $q = 2.326$ from $n = 1{,}000$ observations and wants a 90% confidence interval using the quantile standard error with a bin width of 0.2. For the fitted distribution, the probability of a loss greater than 2.426 is 0.0076 and the probability of a profit or a loss smaller than 2.226 is 0.9870. Which of the following is closest to the 90% confidence interval for the VaR?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Probability mass in the bin**

$$f(q) = 1 - 0.0076 - 0.9870 = 0.0054$$

⇒ The bin is 2.326 ± 0.1 = \[2.226, 2.426\], and $p = 0.0076$ is the probability beyond its top.

**Step 2 – Standard error**

se$(q) = \frac{\sqrt{0.0076 \times0.9924/1000}}{0.0054} = \frac{0.002747}{0.0054} = 0.5086$

**Step 3 – 90% interval**

2.326 ± 1.645 × 0.5086 = 2.326 ± 0.837 = \[1.49, 3.16\]

⇒ Even with 1,000 observations, the 99% VaR could plausibly lie anywhere from about 1.5 to 3.2.

**Interpretation**

Compare Dowd’s 95% interval with the same bin width, \[1.15, 2.14\] (se 0.30): moving out to 99% makes the estimate markedly less precise (se 0.51).

**LO:** MR-1 e: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors. • **Reference:** Dowd, Measuring Market Risk 2e, Ch.3, 1.5, eqs. 1.26 and 1.27, Example 1.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Dowd 1.5, Example 1.6) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-1 e.4)

a.reason: Used the VaR multiplier 2.326 instead of 1.645 for a 90% interval: 2.326 ± 2.326 × 0.5086 = \[1.14, 3.51\].

b.reason: Used $p = 0.01$ (the VaR’s tail probability) instead of the 0.0076 beyond the bin: se = 0.5827, \[1.37, 3.28\].

d.reason: Forgot the square root, using the variance 0.0014 as if it were the standard error: \[2.324, 2.328\].

questions.question: A risk manager re-runs Dowd’s confidence interval for a 95% VaR estimated from 1,000 observations, widening the bin around the quantile from 0.1 to 0.2. The interval moves from about \[0.61, 2.68\] to about \[1.15, 2.14\]. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The interval narrows because the probability mass in the wider bin roughly doubles; since the bin width is arbitrary, the reported precision partly reflects a modelling choice.
The interval narrows because the left-tail probability $p$ falls from 0.045 to 0.0405, and $p$ is the only input that changes when the bin is widened.
The interval narrows, and because the quantile standard error gives symmetric intervals it is the most reliable approach for extreme quantiles such as the 99.9% VaR.
The interval should have widened, because a wider bin admits more observations and therefore more sampling noise around the quantile.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What changes when** $h$ **doubles**

$f(q)$ goes from 0.0104 to 0.0207 (it roughly doubles), and $p$ falls slightly from 0.045 to 0.0405.

**Step 2 – Effect on the standard error**

se falls from 0.630 to 0.301, driven mainly by the larger $f(q)$ in the denominator.

⇒ The interval narrows. But $h$ is “essentially arbitrary”, so the narrower interval is partly a product of the analyst’s choice.

**Interpretation**

Dowd’s own comment: even with $h = 0.2$ (“probably as wide as we can reasonably go”) the interval is still rather wide.

**LO:** MR-1 e: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors. • **Reference:** Dowd, Measuring Market Risk 2e, Ch.3, 1.5, Example 1.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Dowd 1.5) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-1 e.5)

b.reason: Both $p$ and $f(q)$ change, and the $f(q)$ effect dominates; the fall in $p$ alone would barely move the interval.

c.reason: True fact attached to the wrong conclusion: the intervals are symmetric, which is a weakness for extreme quantiles whose true intervals are asymmetric.

d.reason: Polarity flip: a wider bin raises $f(q)$ and narrows the interval.

questions.loText: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors.

questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.question: A validation team compares the precision of several risk-measure estimators computed from the same 1,000-day history. Which of the following conclusions is consistent with GARP’s reading on standard errors?

options.text: The 99% VaR estimate is less precise than the 95% VaR estimate, because the probability mass around the quantile falls faster than $p(1 - p)$ as the quantile moves into the tail.
The 99% VaR estimate is more precise than the 95% VaR estimate, because $p(1-p)$ is smaller at $p = 0.01$ than at $p = 0.05$.
ES estimators always have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, because averaging tail quantiles removes the effect of large but infrequent losses.
Once the sample exceeds 1,000 observations, the standard error no longer needs to be reported alongside the risk measure.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Tail direction**

Moving from the 95% to the 99% quantile lowers $p(1 - p)$ but lowers $f(q)$ much more, because observations are sparse in the tail. With $n = 1{,}000$ and $h = 0.2$: se 0.30 at 95%, 0.51 at 99%.

⇒ GARP: “the more extreme the quantile, the less precise its estimator”.

**Step 2 – ES versus VaR**

Yamai and Yoshiba found ES standard errors much bigger than VaR’s for heavy-tailed distributions; Acerbi found them roughly comparable in realistic ranges. Neither says ES is always more precise.

**Interpretation**

Dowd’s practical advice is to report the standard error every time, whatever the sample size.

**LO:** MR-1 e: Evaluate estimators of risk measures by estimating their standard errors. • **Reference:** Dowd, Measuring Market Risk 2e, Ch.3, 1.5, Figure 1.9; Standard Errors in Estimators of Coherent Risk Measures

MR-1 • Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Dowd 1.5) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-1 e.6)

b.reason: Reads only the numerator $p(1 - p)$; the shrinking $f(q)$ dominates.

c.reason: Polarity flip: heavy tails make ES estimators more prone to large infrequent losses.

d.reason: Absolute claim: there is no sample size beyond which the standard error stops mattering.

questions.loText: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Dowd 1.6, QQ plots)
questions.question: A risk analyst plots the quantiles of a daily P/L series in USD thousands (vertical axis) against standard normal quantiles (horizontal axis). The points lie very close to a straight line along the whole range, including both tails; the line has an intercept of about 5 and a slope of about 40. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: The P/L is not normal, because the plot does not follow the 45-degree line.
The P/L has fat tails, because its quantiles are about 40 times larger than the normal quantiles.
The P/L is consistent with a normal distribution with a mean of about USD 5,000 and a standard deviation of about USD 40,000.
The P/L is positively skewed, because the intercept of the line is above zero.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – A straight line means the shape fits**

The points lie on a straight line throughout, including the tails, so the empirical distribution has the same shape as the normal reference.

**Step 2 – Read location and scale from the line**

If empirical $= a + b\times$ normal quantile, then $a$ estimates the location and $b$ the scale: mean about 5 and standard deviation about 40, in USD thousands.

⇒ A normal with mean about USD 5,000 and standard deviation about USD 40,000.

**Interpretation**

Dowd: a linear QQ plot means the reference fits “up to a linear transformation”, and the intercept and slope give a rough idea of the location and scale parameters.

**LO:** MR-1 f: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution. • **Reference:** Dowd, Measuring Market Risk 2e, Ch.3, 1.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1 (Dowd 1.6, QQ plots) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-1 f.5)

a.reason: A different slope or intercept does not reject normality; only bending does.

b.reason: Larger quantiles everywhere are a scale effect; fat tails need a bend in the tails.

d.reason: The intercept is the location; skew needs an asymmetric bend.

questions.question:
A credit analyst models two borrowers, B and Caa, with a Gaussian default-time copula and a copula correlation of 0.4. The default probability term structures are:

| Year | B: default prob. in year | B: cumulative | Caa: default prob. in year | Caa: cumulative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6.51% | 6.51% | 23.83% | 23.83% |
| 2 | 7.65% | 14.16% | 13.29% | 37.12% |
| 3 | 6.87% | 21.03% | 10.31% | 47.43% |
| 4 | 6.01% | 27.04% | 7.62% | 55.05% |
| 5 | 5.27% | 32.31% | 5.04% | 60.09% |

Software returns these values of the bivariate standard normal CDF with correlation 0.4: $M_{2}(-1.4855, -1.6410) = 1.20\%$; $M_{2}(-0.8054, -0.0645) = 14.66\%$; $M_{2}(-0.8054, 0.2557) = 16.93\%$; $M_{2}(-0.4590, 0.2557) = 24.93\%$. Which of the following is closest to the probability that B defaults by the end of year 3 and Caa defaults by the end of year 5?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Pick the cumulative PDs at each borrower’s own horizon**

B by year 3: $Q_{B}(3) = 21.03\%$. Caa by year 5: $Q_{Caa}(5) = 60.09\%$.

**Step 2 – Map to standard normal percentiles**

$$N^{-1}(0.2103) = -0.8054, N^{-1}(0.6009) = 0.2557$$

**Step 3 – Read the bivariate normal**

$$M_{2}(-0.8054, 0.2557; 0.4) = 16.93\%$$

⇒ A 16.93% chance that both have defaulted by those dates.

**Interpretation**

The horizons differ, and the method does not change: each borrower is mapped at its own date, and the correlation enters only in the last step. The 24.93% value in the stem is “both by year 5”, a further trap.

**LO:** MR-10 b: Describe the Gaussian copula and explain how to use it to derive the joint probability of default of two assets. • **Reference:** Meissner, Ch.5, Example 10.1 (Question 2)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10 (Meissner, Example 10.1) and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-10 b.4)

a.reason: Used the in-year default probabilities (6.87% and 5.04%) instead of the cumulative ones: $M_{2}(-1.4855, -1.6410) = 1.20\%$.

b.reason: Ignored the copula and multiplied the marginals: 21.03% × 60.09% = 12.64%.

c.reason: Used year 3 for both borrowers: $M_{2}(-0.8054, -0.0645) = 14.66\%$.

questions.question: A quantitative analyst at a Canadian bank is reviewing the documentation of the bank’s portfolio credit model. The model joins each obligor’s default-time distribution with a one-factor Gaussian copula, and its correlation parameter is calibrated so that modelled values of standard index tranches match their market prices. Which of the following statements in the documentation is correct?

options.text: The model assumes that the obligors’ times to default are jointly normally distributed, so each obligor’s marginal default-time distribution must itself be normal.
Conditional on a negative realisation of the common factor, an obligor with a higher factor loading has a lower conditional default probability than an otherwise identical obligor.
The correlation calibrated to the tranche prices is a real-world parameter, estimated from the historical default experience of the obligors in the index.
Once the common factor is realised, the obligors’ defaults are independent, so all default dependence in the model enters through the obligors’ loadings on that factor.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Conditional independence**

In the single-factor model $a_{i} = \beta_{i}m + \sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}} \epsilon_{i}$ (Hull: $x_{i} = a_{i}F + \sqrt{1 - a^{2}_{i}} Z_{i}$) the idiosyncratic shocks are independent of one another and of the factor. Fixing $m$ leaves only $\epsilon_{i}$ random, so defaults are conditionally independent and the pairwise correlation $\beta_{i}\beta_{j}$ comes entirely from the loadings.

**Step 2 – Conditional default probability check**

$p(m) = \Phi((k_{i} - \beta_{i}m)/\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}})$. With $\pi= 1\%$ ($k = -2.33$) and $m = -1$: $\beta= 0.4$ gives 1.78% (Malz Example 11.4); a higher $\beta$ raises the numerator and shrinks the denominator, so the conditional PD is higher.

**Interpretation**

D is correct. Conditional independence is what makes the factor model tractable and underlies the Vasicek large-portfolio result used for Credit VaR and IRB capital.

**LO:** MR-10 b: Describe the Gaussian copula and explain how to use it to derive the joint probability of default of two assets. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8, 8.3 Conditional Default Distributions; Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24, 24.2; Meissner, Ch.5, The Gaussian Copula; Malz, Ch.9, 22.4 Implied Correlation

MR-15 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook B3.3 • S4, S6 • Map #16 • Map #60 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-10 b.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap ($t_{i}$ for $x_{i}$). Hull: a company’s time to default “is not even approximately normal”; the copula maps each $t_{i}$ percentile-to-percentile into $x_{i} = N^{-1}[Q_{i}(t_{i})]$ and assumes only the $x_{i}$ are multivariate normal, so the marginals can take any shape.

b.reason: Polarity flip. When $m < 0$, a higher loading pushes the conditional mean $\beta_{i}m$ further down and the conditional PD up: cyclical firms suffer more in a downturn.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Implied correlation is inferred from market prices using risk-neutral default probabilities from single-name CDS spreads (Malz 22.4); it is a risk-neutral, market rather than credit risk, parameter, not a historical estimate.

questions.question: A model validator compares three short-rate models whose parameters have been chosen so that, ten years ahead, the distribution of the short rate under each model has a mean of 5% and a standard deviation of 2.32%. The models are a normal model, the CIR model and a lognormal model. Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: Because the three distributions share the same mean and standard deviation, the models will give the same prices for out-of-the-money interest rate options.
The normal model assigns a positive probability to negative rates, and this probability shrinks as the forecast horizon lengthens.
The CIR and lognormal distributions are non-negative and right-skewed, so out-of-the-money option prices can differ significantly from the normal model’s.
The CIR distribution is left-skewed with a floor at the long-run level $\theta$, while the lognormal distribution is symmetric around 5%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What matching two moments does and does not fix**

Equal mean and standard deviation fix the centre and spread, not the shape. The normal is symmetric; CIR and lognormal are bounded at zero and right-skewed (Figure 2).

**Step 2 – Consequence for options**

Out-of-the-money options depend on the probability of outcomes far from the mean, which differs across the three shapes.

⇒ Prices of out-of-the-money options can differ significantly even with identical means and standard deviations.

**Interpretation**

This is the “concept of terminal distributions” that Vardeez points to: the shape of the distribution is “an important determinant of that model’s performance”.

**LO:** MR-15 d: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.2, Figure 15.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.15, 15.2 and Figure 15.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 d.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim. Two matched moments do not make the tails equal, and out-of-the-money prices live in the tails.

b.reason: Polarity flip. The normal model’s probability of negative rates grows with the horizon.

d.reason: Sibling swap of shapes: CIR is right-skewed with a floor at zero (not at $\theta$), and the lognormal is right-skewed, not symmetric.

questions.question: A dealer’s rates trader must choose a short-rate model for a book of near-the-money swaptions. She believes that constant volatility describes the current environment well, that the possibility of negative rates has only a small impact on the prices of the securities she trades, and that the computational simplicity of a constant-volatility model is valuable. According to the reading, which choice is most defensible?

options.text: A constant basis-point volatility model, accepting that it allows some probability of negative rates.
The CIR model, because any model that allows negative rates must be rejected regardless of purpose.
A lognormal model, because its basis-point volatility is constant and it cannot produce negative rates.
The CIR model, because its terminal distribution is normal and therefore simpler to compute with.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Match the trader’s three beliefs to the reading**

GARP’s example uses exactly these three beliefs (constant volatility fits now; negative rates matter little for the securities; simplicity has great value) and concludes that such a trader “might very well opt for a model that allows some probability of negative rates.”

**Step 2 – Check the alternatives against the model facts**

Lognormal basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$, not constant; CIR’s terminal distribution is not normal.

⇒ The defensible choice is a constant-volatility model.

**Interpretation**

Non-negativity is “in some respects” an improvement, but “choosing a model depends on the purpose at hand.”

**LO:** MR-15 d: Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.2

MR-15 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.15, 15.2 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 d.7)

b.reason: Absolute claim. The reading explicitly allows models with some probability of negative rates when that probability barely affects prices.

c.reason: Sibling swap. The lognormal model has constant yield volatility; its basis-point volatility rises with the rate.

d.reason: CIR’s terminal distribution is non-negative and right-skewed, and CIR is the more complex model.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Australian bank is simulating monthly paths of the short rate under the risk-neutral Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) process $dr = k(\theta- r) dt + \sigma\sqrt{r} dw$, where $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. For the first step of one path the inputs are:

- Current short rate: 3.60%; long-run value $\theta$: 5.00%; speed of mean reversion $k$: 0.40
- Volatility parameter $\sigma$: 0.05
- Time step: one month ($dt = 1/12$); the standard normal draw for this step is +1.2

Which of the following is closest to the change in the short rate over the month and to the annualized basis-point volatility of the short rate at the start of the month?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Basis-point volatility**

$\sigma\sqrt{r} = 0.05 \times\sqrt{0.036} = 0.05 \times0.18974 = 0.0094868 = 94.9$ bp

⇒ At a 3.60% short rate, one standard deviation of annual rate change is about 95 bp. The parameter 0.05 is not itself a basis-point volatility.

**Step 2 – Drift over the month**

$k(\theta- r) dt = 0.40 \times(0.0500 - 0.0360) \times\frac{1}{12} = 0.000467 = 4.67$ bp

⇒ The rate is below $\theta$, so mean reversion pulls it up.

**Step 3 – Random term**

$dw = 1.2\sqrt{1/12} = 0.34641, \sigma\sqrt{r} dw = 0.0094868 \times0.34641 = 0.003286 = 32.86$ bp

**Step 4 – Rate change**

$\Delta r = 4.67 + 32.86 = 37.53$ bp$, r_{1} = 3.975\%$

**Interpretation**

At the new rate the basis-point volatility is $0.05\sqrt{0.03975} = 99.7$ bp: CIR volatility rises with the square root of the rate. Had the draw driven the rate toward zero, volatility would have shrunk toward zero while the drift $k\theta> 0$ stayed positive, so the rate cannot become negative.

**LO:** MR-15 d; MR-15 e: Calculate the short-term rate change and describe the basis point volatility using the CIR and lognormal models. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 3e, Ch.10, 15.2, eqs. 15.3 and 15.6 to 15.8 (GARP MR Ch.15)

**Source:** Workbook D1.1 • S1, S2 • Map #39 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 e.5)

b.reason: Did not scale the drift by $dt$: 0.40 × 0.014 = 0.0056, plus 0.003286, gives 88.9 bp.

c.reason: Did not scale the shock by $\sqrt{dt}$: 0.000467 + 0.0094868 × 1.2 = 0.011851, or 118.5 bp.

d.reason: Treated the constant parameter $\sigma= 0.05$ as the basis-point volatility (500 bp) and omitted $\sqrt{r}$: 0.000467 + 0.05 × 0.34641 = 0.017787, or 177.9 bp.

questions.question: A rates desk calibrates three short-rate models so that each gives a basis-point volatility of 100 bp when the short rate is 8%: a normal model (constant basis-point volatility), the CIR model (basis-point volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$) and a lognormal model (basis-point volatility $\sigma r$). The parameters are then held fixed while the short rate falls to 2%. Which of the following is closest to the basis-point volatilities of the CIR model and of the lognormal model at the 2% rate?

options.text: CIR 25 bp; lognormal 50 bp
CIR 50 bp; lognormal 25 bp
CIR 100 bp; lognormal 100 bp
CIR 200 bp; lognormal 400 bp

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Calibrate at 8%**

$$\sigma_{CIR}\sqrt{0.08} = 0.01 \Rightarrow\sigma_{CIR} = 0.035355 \sigma_{Y} \times0.08 = 0.01 \Rightarrow\sigma_{Y} = 0.125$$

**Step 2 – Re-evaluate at 2%**

CIR: $0.035355 \times\sqrt{0.02} = 0.0050 = 50$ bp Lognormal: 0.125 × 0.02 = 0.0025 = 25 bp

⇒ Equivalently, CIR scales by $\sqrt{2/8} = 0.5$ and the lognormal by 2/8 = 0.25.

**Interpretation**

When rates fall, the lognormal model’s basis-point volatility shrinks fastest, CIR’s more slowly, and the normal model’s not at all (Figure 1). In yield-volatility terms CIR is now at 50/200 = 25% while the lognormal stays at 12.5%.

**LO:** MR-15 e: Calculate the short-term rate change and describe the basis point volatility using the CIR and lognormal models. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.2, eqs. 15.6 to 15.8 and Figure 15.2

MR-15 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.15, eqs. 15.6 to 15.8 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 e.8)

a.reason: Sibling swap: gave CIR the proportional scaling ($r$) and the lognormal the square-root scaling.

c.reason: Treated both as constant basis-point volatility models, which is only true of the normal model.

d.reason: Scaled in the wrong direction, multiplying by $\sqrt{8/2} = 2$ and 8/2 = 4: a falling rate lowers basis-point volatility in both models.

questions.topic: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution

questions.question: A junior quant describes the lognormal model with deterministic drift (the “Salomon Brothers” model), $dr = a(t) r dt + \sigma r dw$, to a model validation committee. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

options.text: The natural logarithm of the short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with a time-dependent drift, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.
The natural logarithm of the short rate reverts toward a time-dependent central tendency ln $\theta(t)$, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.
The short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with a time-dependent drift, so the short rate is normal and low nodes of its tree may become negative.
The basis-point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the square root of the rate, so the short rate is non-negative but not lognormal.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Apply Ito’s lemma**

$d[\text{ln} r] = [a(t) - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}] dt + \sigma dw = a\tilde{(} t) dt + \sigma dw$: a Ho-Lee process written on ln $r$.

**Step 2 – Consequences**

ln $r$ is normal, so $r$ is lognormal; nodes are $r_{0}\text{e}^{(\cdot)} > 0$.

⇒ “The Ho-Lee model based on the natural logarithm of the short rate.”

**Interpretation**

The drift is deterministic and time-dependent (fitted to bond prices), with no mean reversion. That is what separates it from Black-Karasinski.

**LO:** MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.3, eqs. 15.9 to 15.12

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.15, 15.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 f.2)

b.reason: Sibling swap: reversion toward ln $\theta(t)$ is Black-Karasinski, the lognormal model with mean reversion.

c.reason: Describes Ho-Lee itself, on the rate rather than its logarithm, with normal rates that can go negative.

d.reason: Square-root basis-point volatility is CIR; the lognormal model’s basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$.

questions.question: In a lognormal short-rate tree with $a_{1} = 0$ and $dt = 1$, the up node after one period is $r_{0} \text{e}^{\sigma}$. The model’s volatility parameter is $\sigma= 12.5\%$ and the current short rate is 4.00%. Which statement best explains why volatility in this model is quoted as a percentage of the rate?

options.text: Because e$^{\sigma} \approx1 + \sigma$, the up-state rate is about 12.5% above the current rate, about 4.5%, so the size of the move scales with the level of the rate.
Because e$^{\sigma} \approx1 + \sigma$, the up-state rate is about 12.5 percentage points above the current rate, about 16.5%, so the size of the move is fixed in basis points.
Because the drift is additive, the up-state rate is the current rate plus 12.5% of the long-run level, so the size of the move scales with the long-run level.
Because the tree is built in rates rather than in logs, the up-state rate is the current rate times 12.5%, so the size of the move scales with the level of the rate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Use the small-**$x$ **approximation**

$r_{0}\text{e}^{\sigma} \approx r_{0}(1 + \sigma) = 4.00\% \times1.125 = 4.50\%$ (exactly $4.00\% \times\text{e}^{0.125} = 4.53\%$).

**Step 2 – Interpret**

The move is 12.5% of the rate, about 50 bp here. At a 2% rate the same $\sigma$ would move it by about 25 bp.

⇒ Volatility is a percentage of the rate: yield volatility.

**Interpretation**

GARP: “Volatility is clearly a percentage of the rate…If, for example, $\sigma= 12.5\%$, then the short rate in the up-state is 12.5% above the initial short rate.”

**LO:** MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.3, eq. 15.13

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.15, 15.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 f.3)

b.reason: Reads 12.5% as percentage points (an additive basis-point move), which is the normal-model reading.

c.reason: The lognormal drift is multiplicative, and there is no long-run level in the deterministic-drift model.

d.reason: The tree is built in logs and then exponentiated, and the up node is $r_{0}\text{e}^{\sigma}$, not $r_{0} \times\sigma$ (which would give 0.5%).

questions.question: A Black-Karasinski tree with a fixed time step $dt$ recombines only if $k(2) =$ $[\sigma(1) - \sigma(2)] / [\sigma(1) dt]$. Instead of imposing this restriction, the model lets the length of the time step vary. Which of the following best explains why?

options.text: Mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility while time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate, so the two must be chosen independently.
Mean reversion controls the future volatility of the short rate while time-dependent volatility controls the term structure of volatility, so the two must be chosen independently.
Imposing the restriction would make the model an equilibrium model, while varying the time step keeps the drift deterministic and removes mean reversion.
Varying the time step always makes the tree recombine, whatever mean reversion and volatility functions are chosen, so no restriction on $dt_{2}$ is needed.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the restriction would do**

Imposing $k(2) = [\sigma(1) - \sigma(2)]/[\sigma(1)dt]$ “would require that the mean reversion speed be completely determined by the time-dependent volatility function.”

**Step 2 – Why that is unacceptable**

The two serve distinct purposes: mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility; time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate, and hence the prices of options expiring at different times.

⇒ Letting $dt$ vary keeps both free.

**Interpretation**

The length of the first step is arbitrary; the second is set to satisfy eq. 15.23.

**LO:** MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.15, 15.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-15 f.6)

b.reason: Sibling swap of the two roles.

c.reason: Black-Karasinski is arbitrage-free and keeps mean reversion; varying $dt$ removes neither.

d.reason: Absolute claim: $dt_{2}$ is not free; it must be chosen to satisfy eq. 15.23.

questions.question: A quant is estimating the Gauss+ model from daily US data and must choose the empirical proxy for the short-term rate $r$. Which choice, with its justification, follows the reading?

options.text: The fed funds target rate, because general collateral repo rates show occasional idiosyncratic jumps that complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages.
A general collateral repo rate, because it is theoretically more consistent with a Treasury term structure and its jumps make the estimated volatility more realistic.
The two-year zero yield, because the short-term rate in the Gauss+ model is fitted each day to the one-year rate two years forward.
The fed funds target rate, because the short-term rate in the Gauss+ model carries its own random shock that must match fed funds volatility.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The reading’s choice**

“The short-term rate, $r$, is taken each day as equal to the fed funds target rate on that day.”

**Step 2 – The reason**

A GC repo rate is “theoretically more consistent” with a Treasury term structure, but repo rates “exhibit occasional idiosyncratic jumps that complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages.”

⇒ Fed funds target, for practical reasons.

**Interpretation**

The choice also fits the model’s story: $r$ reflects central bank policy, pegged at a target that moves with the business cycle.

b.reason: Takes the theoretical argument for repo but inverts the conclusion: the jumps are the reason not to use it.

c.reason: Confuses the proxy for $r$ with the daily fitting targets; the two-year forward is fitted through the factors, not used as $r$.

d.reason: The short rate has no random shock in Gauss+ (that is the “+”); fed funds is chosen as a proxy, not to match a volatility.

questions.question: In the estimation data, a regression of changes in the 3-year zero yield gives a coeﬀicient of 0.91 on changes in the 2-year yield and 0.22 on changes in the 10-year yield; for the 15-year yield the coeﬀicients are −0.20 and 1.10. Which of the following statements about this stage of the estimation is correct?

options.text: These coeﬀicients are used to choose $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $\alpha_{l}$ so that the model’s implied coeﬀicients match them as closely as possible.
These coeﬀicients are used to choose $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ and $\rho$ so that the model’s implied coeﬀicients match them as closely as possible.
These coeﬀicients are used to choose $\mu$, because the coeﬀicients shift with the level of long-term yields.
These coeﬀicients cannot be matched by the model, so the speeds are instead taken from maximum likelihood estimates.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the coefficients are**

They are the empirical sensitivities of each zero yield’s changes to changes in the 2-year and 10-year zero yields (Figure 16.5).

**Step 2 – What they identify**

“All these regression coeﬀicients implicitly describe the mean reversion parameters of the model.” This stage chooses $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$, $\alpha_{l}$ so the model’s implied coeﬀicients match the empirical ones “as closely as possible.”

⇒ The match is very close and within statistical confidence intervals.

**Interpretation**

Short maturities load mostly on the 2-year yield; long maturities load mostly on the 10-year yield (even negatively on the 2-year), which is the term-structure footprint of fast and slow mean reversion.

**LO:** MR-16 d: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.16, 16.3, Figure 16.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.16, 16.3 and Figure 16.5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 d.5)

b.reason: Sibling swap: volatilities and $\rho$ are matched to the volatility term structure, not to regression coeﬀicients.

c.reason: $\mu$ is found last, from yield levels; the coeﬀicients do not identify it.

d.reason: Polarity: the model matches the coeﬀicients very closely; maximum likelihood is the standard alternative the reading avoids.

questions.question: After estimation, a trading desk uses the Gauss+ model for relative value. Each day the factors are chosen so that the model matches the fed funds target rate and the one-year rates two and ten years forward. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The medium- and long-term factors $m$ and $l$ are, by construction, equal to the one-year rates two and ten years forward.
The fitted forwards are fair by construction, and the relation of every forward rate to $m$ and $l$ depends on the estimated parameters, especially the mean reversion speeds.
Because the fitted forwards are fair by construction, every other point on the curve is also fair, so the model cannot identify rich or cheap securities.
The short-term rate $r$ is fitted to the one-year rate two years forward, and $m$ and $l$ are both fitted to the ten-year forward.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What is fitted each day**

The factors are chosen to match the fed funds target and the one-year rates two and ten years forward, so “these two- and 10-year forward rates \[are\] fair by construction.”

**Step 2 – What** $m$ **and** $l$ **are**

They are “in no way those forward rates themselves.” The relation of every forward rate to $m$ and $l$ depends on the estimated parameters, in particular the mean reversion speeds.

⇒ B combines both facts.

**Interpretation**

Fitting a few points and reading the rest of the curve off the model is exactly what makes Gauss+ a relative value tool: securities away from the fitted points can be rich or cheap to the model.

a.reason: The factors are not the forward rates, unlike $r$, which does equal fed funds.

c.reason: Absolute claim: only the fitted points are fair by construction; the model is used to trade value elsewhere on the curve.

d.reason: $r$ is set to the fed funds target, not to a forward rate.

questions.question: The Gauss+ estimates on US Treasury data are $\alpha_{r} = 1.0547$, $\alpha_{m} = 0.6358$, $\alpha_{l} = 0.0165$, $\sigma_{m} = 109.2$ bp, $\sigma_{l} = 96.4$ bp, $\rho= 0.212$ and $\mu= 10.555\%$. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The half-lives are about 0.66, 1.09 and 42 years, in the order the economics predicts, and $\mu$ seems high because it includes a risk premium and the long-term factor reverts to it very slowly.
The half-lives are about 0.66, 1.09 and 42 years, and the 109 and 96 bp volatility parameters translate into higher zero-yield volatilities because the factors mean revert.
The half-lives are about 1.05, 0.64 and 0.02 years, so the long-term factor reverts fastest of all, toward a $\mu$ that is a pure expectation of the short rate.
The half-lives are about 0.66, 1.09 and 42 years, and the long-term factor’s slow reversion shows that $\mu$ was estimated first, from the regression stage.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Half-lives**

$\frac{\text{ln} 2}{1.0547} = 0.66, \frac{\text{ln} 2}{0.6358} = 1.09, \frac{\text{ln} 2}{0.0165} = 42.0$ years

⇒ About 8 months, 13 months and 42 years: central bank reaction fastest, then $m$ to $l$, then $l$ to $\mu$.

**Step 2 – Interpret** $\mu$ **and the volatilities**

$\mu$ “might seem high at over 10%, but the long-term factor reverts very slowly to this target, and that target includes a risk premium.” The 109 and 96 bp volatility parameters translate into lower zero-yield volatilities because of mean reversion.

**Interpretation**

The estimates come out in exactly the order the model’s economic story predicts, which is a check on the estimation.

**LO:** MR-16 d: Explain how the parameters of the Gauss+ model can be estimated from empirical data. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.16, 16.3, Table 16.1

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.16, Table 16.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-16 d.7)

b.reason: Polarity flip: mean reversion makes zero-yield volatilities lower than the factor volatility parameters.

c.reason: Reports the speeds themselves as half-lives and reverses the order; $\mu$ includes a risk premium.

d.reason: $\mu$ is estimated last, by least squares on yield levels, not at the regression stage.

questions.question: A risk analyst plots implied volatility against the strike price for a stock index on two dates. Between the dates the index rose about 10%, and the whole curve now sits further to the right. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The curve moved right because the at-the-money strike rises with the asset price; this is why implied volatility is usually plotted against $K/S_{0}$ instead.
The curve moved right because implied volatility rose at every strike when the index rose; the strike axis shows this rise correctly.
Plotting against the strike is preferred, because the strike is fixed by contract while $K/S_{0}$ changes every day.
The shift shows that index prices are lognormal, because a lognormal smile moves one-for-one with the asset price.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why the strike-axis curve drifts**

The relationship between implied volatility and $K$ depends on the asset price. As the asset price rises, the central at-the-money strike rises, so the curve moves right (left when the price falls).

**Step 2 – The fix**

Plot against $K/S_{0}$: the curve no longer drifts with the asset price (Figure 1).

⇒ A is GARP’s argument.

**Interpretation**

The movement is horizontal, not vertical. Reading it as a change in the level of volatility is the trap in B.

**LO:** MR-17 f: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 f.3)

b.reason: Polarity of the axis: the curve moved sideways because the ATM strike moved, not because volatility rose at every strike.

c.reason: Reversed preference: the drift of the strike axis is exactly why $K/S_{0}$ is preferred.

d.reason: A lognormal world gives a flat smile; the drift says nothing about lognormality.

questions.question: An FX options desk plots its smiles against $K/F_{0}$, where $F_{0}$ is the forward rate for the options’ maturity, and defines an at-the-money option as one with $K = F_{0}$. Which of the following is the justification for this convention?

options.text: $F_{0}$, not $S_{0}$, is the expected value of the underlying on the option’s maturity date in a risk-neutral world.
$F_{0}$ equals $S_{0}$ whenever interest rates are positive, so the two at-the-money definitions always coincide.
$K = F_{0}$ is the only strike at which a call has a delta of exactly 0.5 and a put a delta of exactly +0.5.
Using $K/F_{0}$ makes the smile independent of the option’s maturity without any further adjustment.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The refinement**

Hull calculates the smile against $K/F_{0}$, with $F_{0}$ the forward price for the option’s maturity, and traders often define at-the-money as $K = F_{0}$.

**Step 2 – The argument**

$F_{0}$, not $S_{0}$, is the expected asset price on the maturity date in a risk-neutral world.

⇒ A is the stated justification.

**Interpretation**

The convention centres the smile on where the asset is expected to be at expiry, not where it is today.

**LO:** MR-17 f: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 f.4)

b.reason: $F_{0} = S_{0}\text{e}^{(r-q)T}$ differs from $S_{0}$ whenever the carry is not zero, so the two definitions generally differ.

c.reason: Put deltas are negative; the 50-delta put has delta −0.5. The delta definition of ATM is a different convention.

d.reason: Removing the maturity dependence needs the scaled measure $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \text{ln}(K/F_{0})$, not $K/F_{0}$ alone.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile.
questions.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
questions.topic: Volatility Smiles
questions.question: When the volatility smile is defined as the relationship between implied volatility and the delta of the option, how is an at-the-money option defined?

options.text: As a call with a delta of 0.5 or a put with a delta of −0.5.
As a call with a delta of 0.5 or a put with a delta of +0.5.
As any option whose strike equals the current asset price, whatever its delta.
As the call or put whose implied volatility is the lowest point on the smile.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The delta convention**

When the smile is defined against delta, an at-the-money option is a call with delta 0.5 or a put with delta −0.5. These are “50-delta options”.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Because put delta = call delta −1 (no dividends), a 0.5 call and a −0.5 put at the same strike are consistent with each other.

**LO:** MR-17 f: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 f.5)

b.reason: Sign error: a European put’s delta is negative.

c.reason: That is the strike-based definition ($K = S_{0}$); under the delta approach the 50-delta option is generally not the $K = S_{0}$ option.

d.reason: The lowest point of a smile is a market outcome, not a definition of at-the-money; for an equity skew there is no interior minimum at all.

questions.question: A financial engineer wants the smiles for 1-month, 1-year and 5-year options on the same asset to lie as close to one another as possible, so that one curve can serve all maturities. Defining $T$ as time to maturity and $F_{0}$ as the forward price for the option’s maturity, which horizontal axis does GARP’s reading suggest?

options.text: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \text{ln}(\frac{K}{F_{0}})$
$\sqrt{T} \text{ln}(\frac{K}{F_{0}})$
The strike price $K$

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The maturity problem**

Smiles become less pronounced as maturity increases, so curves for different maturities differ when plotted against $K$ or $K/S_{0}$.

**Step 2 – The scaled measure**

Some financial engineers define the smile against $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \text{ln}(K/F_{0})$; the smile is then usually much less dependent on maturity.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Dividing by $\sqrt{T}$ puts moneyness in units that grow with the square root of time, the same way the standard deviation of returns grows.

**LO:** MR-17 f: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.5

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 f.6)

b.reason: Multiplies by $\sqrt{T}$ instead of dividing: it stretches long maturities further apart rather than bringing them together.

c.reason: $K/S_{0}$ removes the drift with the asset price but not the dependence on maturity.

d.reason: The strike axis also drifts with the asset price, so it is the least stable choice.

questions.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles
questions.topic: Volatility Smiles
questions.question: A model validation team asks how the desk’s FX volatility surface is populated before it is used to price new options. Which of the following describes standard practice?

options.text: Entries for options with reliable market data are implied volatilities calculated directly from their market prices; the rest of the table is typically filled by interpolation.
All entries are historical volatilities measured over a window equal to each option’s maturity, then adjusted for the strike.
All entries are derived from the at-the-money implied volatility, scaled by $\sqrt{T}$ for maturity and held constant across strikes.
Entries are BSM option prices rather than volatilities, and a trader reads the price of a new option straight from the table.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the numbers come from**

At any time some entries correspond to options with reliable market data; their implied volatilities are calculated directly from market prices.

**Step 2 – The rest**

The remaining entries are typically determined by interpolation.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The surface is therefore anchored to traded prices; interpolation fills the gaps so any strike and maturity can be priced.

**LO:** MR-17 g: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 g.6)

b.reason: The surface holds implied volatilities, not historical ones.

c.reason: Holding volatility constant across strikes would erase the smile the surface exists to capture.

d.reason: The table holds volatilities; the price comes from putting the looked-up volatility into BSM or a binomial tree.
