questions.question: A hedger is short a large position in at-the-money calls on a stock index that shows the usual equity skew, and delta-hedges by buying the index using the Black-Scholes-Merton delta. Implied volatilities on the index tend to fall when the index rises. Relative to the minimum variance hedge, which of the following best describes her position?

options.text: She holds more of the index than the minimum variance hedge requires, because the BSM delta is higher than the minimum variance delta.
She holds less of the index than the minimum variance hedge requires, because the BSM delta ignores the rise in implied volatility along the skew.
Her hedge equals the minimum variance hedge, because positive vega offsets any change in implied volatility.
She holds more of the index than required when it rises and less when it falls, because the curve shifts in both directions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which delta is larger**

For equity options $\Delta_{MV} = \Delta_{BSM} + \nu\partial E(\sigma_{imp})/\partial S < \Delta_{BSM}$ , since $\nu> 0$ and implied volatility falls when the index rises.

**Step 2 – Translate into the hedge**

Short calls are hedged by buying $\Delta$ units of the index. Using the larger BSM delta means buying more than the minimum variance hedge.

⇒ A: she is over-hedged relative to the minimum variance hedge.

**Interpretation**

When the index rises, the calls gain less than BSM predicts because their implied volatility falls, so fewer units of the index are needed to offset them.

**LO:** MR-17 h: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the calculation of an option’s Greek letter risk measures. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.6

MR-17 • Volatility Smiles • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.6 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 h.6)

b.reason: Uses effect 1 alone; the dominant effect is the downward shift of the whole curve.

c.reason: Positive vega is the reason the hedges differ, not a reason they coincide.

d.reason: The comparison has one sign: the curve moves against the price in both directions, so the BSM delta is too high whichever way the index moves.

questions.reading: MR-17: Volatility Smiles

questions.question: A biotech stock trades at \$50. A regulatory decision due in two days will move it to about \$58 if approval is granted or to about \$42 if it is refused. An analyst compares the distribution of the stock price in one month with a lognormal distribution that has the same mean and standard deviation. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The true distribution is bimodal, with probability concentrated around the two post-decision prices rather than around \$50.
The true distribution is unimodal with heavier tails on both sides than the lognormal, as for an exchange rate.
The true distribution is unimodal with a heavier left tail and a thinner right tail, as for an equity index.
The true distribution is bimodal, and its standard deviation must exceed that of any lognormal with the same mean.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Model the news**

The 1-month price is a mixture of two lognormals: one around \$58 (approval), one around \$42 (refusal).

**Step 2 – Compare with the lognormal**

The mixture is bimodal, and it can share its mean and standard deviation with a unimodal lognormal; only the shape differs.

⇒ A (Figure 5a).

**Interpretation**

This bimodal shape, not fat tails, is what drives the frown.

**LO:** MR-17 i: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.8, Figure 17.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.8 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 i.1)

b.reason: Heavier tails on both sides is the random-jump, exchange-rate picture, which gives a smile.

c.reason: Heavier left tail and thinner right tail is the equity-index picture, which gives a skew.

d.reason: The mixture can have the same standard deviation as a lognormal; the difference is shape, not spread.

questions.question:
A stock trades at \$50 and will be worth either \$42 or \$58 in one month, depending on a court ruling. A trader values one-month European options on a two-point tree and backs out BSM implied volatilities:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strike (\$) | 44 | 46 | 48 | 50 | 52 | 54 | 56 |
| Implied volatility (%) | 58.8 | 66.6 | 69.5 | 69.2 | 66.1 | 60.0 | 49.9 |

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The pattern is a frown, so using the implied volatility of the \$50-strike option would overprice the \$44 and \$56 options.
The pattern is a smile, so using the implied volatility of the \$50-strike option would under-price the \$44 and \$56 options.
The pattern is a skew, with implied volatility falling as the strike rises, as for equity index options.
The pattern is a frown, so using the implied volatility of the \$50-strike option would under-price the \$44 and \$56 options.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the shape**

Implied volatility peaks near \$48–\$50 (69.5%, 69.2%) and falls both ways, to 58.8% at \$44 and 49.9% at \$56.

⇒ A frown: the opposite of the currency smile.

**Step 2 – Consequence for pricing**

The \$44 and \$56 options have lower implied volatilities than the \$50 option. Pricing them at the \$50 option’s 69.2% would use too high a volatility.

⇒ Overpricing, as GARP states.

**Interpretation**

This is the polarity of the frown: the wings are cheap relative to the at-the-money option.

**LO:** MR-17 i: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.20 (GARP MR-17), 17.8, Table 17.3 (recomputed)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.8 and Table 17.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-17 i.2)

b.reason: Wrong shape and wrong direction: the wings have lower implied volatility here.

c.reason: Volatility rises from \$44 to \$48 before falling, so this is a hump, not a monotone skew.

d.reason: Right shape, wrong consequence: too high a volatility overprices, it does not underprice.

questions.question: A volatility strategist is matching causes to implied volatility patterns. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: A single anticipated price jump produces a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest; heavy tails on both sides produce a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest.
A single anticipated price jump produces a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest; heavy tails on both sides produce a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest.
A single anticipated price jump produces a downward skew; a heavier left tail alone produces a frown.
A single anticipated price jump produces a frown, with at-the-money implied volatility the lowest; heavy tails on both sides produce a smile, with at-the-money implied volatility the highest.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Single anticipated jump**

Bimodal distribution ⇒ ATM options are the dear ones ⇒ frown, ATM implied volatility highest.

**Step 2 – Heavy tails on both sides**

Extreme moves more likely in both directions ⇒ deep ITM and OTM options are dear ⇒ smile, ATM implied volatility lowest.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

This is the polarity pair in Section 3. Option D keeps the labels but flips what each label means.

b.reason: Swaps the two causes.

c.reason: A downward skew comes from a heavy left tail and thin right tail (equities), not from a single jump; a heavy left tail alone does not give a frown.

d.reason: Right labels, wrong definitions: in a frown ATM implied volatility is highest, in a smile it is lowest.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.4, Table 4.2 (Kupiec, 1995)
questions.question:
A model validator at a regional bank reviews a one-day 97.5% VaR model. Over the last 510 trading days the desk recorded 6 exceptions. The validator uses the following excerpt of Kupiec’s nonrejection regions, at the 95% test confidence level:

| VaR confidence | $T = 252$ | $T = 510$ | $T = 1{,}000$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 99% | $N < 7$ | $1 < N < 11$ | $4 < N < 17$ |
| 97.5% | $2 < N < 12$ | $6 < N < 21$ | $15 < N < 36$ |
| 95% | $6 < N < 20$ | $16 < N < 36$ | $37 < N < 65$ |

Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: Do not reject the model: 6 exceptions lies inside the nonrejection region $2 < N < 12$.
Reject the model: 6 exceptions is at the lower limit of $6 < N < 21$, so the VaR model is overly conservative.
Reject the model: 6 exceptions exceeds the Basel green-zone limit of 4, so the VaR understates risk.
Do not reject the model: 6 exceptions is close to the expected count of 0.025 × 252 = 6.3.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Pick the right cell**

VaR confidence 97.5% ($p = 0.025$) and $T = 510$: the nonrejection region is $6 < N < 21$, so $N = 7, \dots, 20$ pass.

**Step 2 – Locate the observation**

$N = 6$ is not strictly greater than 6, so it falls in the lower rejection region. (Check: Kupiec’s $LR_{uc} = 4.55 > 3.841$.)

⇒ Too few exceptions: the expected count is 0.025 × 510 = 12.75, and 6 is too far below it.

**Step 3 – Interpret**

A count below the region means VaR is set too high: the model is overly conservative and ties up excess capital.

**Interpretation**

The table rejects in both directions. Reading the correct column matters: the same 6 exceptions would pass at $T = 252$, where 6.3 are expected.

**LO:** MR-4 c: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.6, 4.2, Table 4.2 (adapted from Kupiec, 1995), eq. 4.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.4, Table 4.2 (Kupiec, 1995) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-4 c.6)

a.reason: Read the $T = 252$ column ($2 < N < 12$) instead of $T = 510$.

c.reason: Applied the Basel green-zone rule (0 to 4 exceptions of a 99% VaR over 250 days) to a 97.5% VaR over 510 days, and read the direction wrongly.

d.reason: Computed the expected count with $T = 252$ instead of 510; over 510 days 12.75 are expected.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.4 (JPM 1998 example) and Vardeez
questions.question: A risk manager reviews a 95% VaR model over 252 trading days with 20 exceptions. Of these, 14 occurred on a day following a day with no exception (232 such days) and 6 occurred on a day following an exception (20 such days). The unconditional coverage statistic is $LR_{uc} = 3.91$ and the independence statistic is $LR_{ind} = 9.53$. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: $\pi_{1} = 30.0\%$ versus $\pi_{0} = 6.0\%$ and $LR_{ind} = 9.53 > 3.841$ indicate clustering, and $LR_{cc} =$ 13.44 > 5.991 rejects conditional coverage.
$\pi_{1} = 6/252 = 2.4\%$ is below $\pi_{0} = 14/252 = 5.6\%$, so exceptions are less likely after an exception day and independence is not rejected.
$LR_{cc} = 13.44$ is compared with the $\chi^{2}(1)$ cut-off 3.841; since $LR_{uc}$ alone already exceeds 3.841, the independence test adds no information.
$LR_{cc} = 9.53 - 3.91 = 5.62$ is below 5.991, so the model passes conditional coverage even though it fails unconditional coverage.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Conditional probabilities**

$$\pi_{0} = \frac{T_{01}}{T_{00} + T_{01}} = \frac{14}{232} = 6.0\%, \pi_{1} = \frac{T_{11}}{T_{10} + T_{11}} = \frac{6}{20} = 30.0\%$$

⇒ An exception is five times as likely after an exception day.

**Step 2 – Independence**

$LR_{ind} = 9.53 > 3.841$: reject independence; exceptions cluster.

**Step 3 – Conditional coverage**

$$LR_{cc} = LR_{uc} + LR_{ind} = 3.91 + 9.53 = 13.44 > 5.991 (\chi^{2}(2))$$

**Interpretation**

The model fails on both counts: too many exceptions ($LR_{uc} = 3.91 > 3.841$) and bunched ones. GARP’s conclusion is to explore models that allow for time variation in risk.

**LO:** MR-4 e: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.6, 4.2 Conditional Coverage Models, Table 4.5, eqs. 4.4 and 4.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.4 (JPM 1998 example) and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-4 e.6)

b.reason: Divided by all 252 days instead of conditioning on the previous day’s state.

c.reason: Used the $\chi^{2}(1)$ cut-off for the $\chi^{2}(2)$ joint statistic, and wrongly dismissed the independence test, which carries different information from the count.

d.reason: Subtracted instead of adding: $LR_{cc}$ is the sum of the two statistics.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the need to consider conditional coverage in the backtesting framework.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing the backtesting report for a desk’s 99% VaR model. Over 250 days the desk recorded 3 exceptions, on three consecutive trading days of a volatile month. The auditor drafts comments for the risk committee. Which of the following comments is correct?

options.text: Kupiec’s proportion of failures test should reject the model, because exceptions bunched within two weeks raise the failure rate measured by the test.
If the model is in fact correct and is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 2 error, the risk that the Basel zones are designed to keep low.
Christoffersen’s independence test would also reject a model whose exceptions occur exactly one week apart, because it detects dependence between exceptions at any lag.
The conditional coverage statistic adds Kupiec’s $LR_{uc}$ to Christoffersen’s $LR_{ind}$ and can reject this model even though its exception count is acceptable.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Unconditional coverage**

Expected exceptions: 0.01 × 250 = 2.5. Three exceptions lies inside the nonrejection region ($N < 7$ at $T = 252$), so Kupiec’s test does not reject: $LR_{uc} = 0.095 < 3.841$. The count is fine.

**Step 2 – Independence**

Exceptions “could cluster or bunch closely in time, which also should invalidate the model”. Here $T_{00} = 245$, $T_{01} = 1$, $T_{10} = 1$, $T_{11} = 2$: $\pi_{0} = 1/246 = 0.4\%$ but $\pi_{1} = 2/3 = 66.7\%$, giving $LR_{ind} = 15.65 > 3.841$.

**Step 3 – Conditional coverage**

$$LR_{cc} = LR_{uc} + LR_{ind} = 0.095 + 15.651 = 15.75 > 5.991 = \chi^{2}_{0.95}(2)$$

**Interpretation**

D is correct. The joint test checks whether the proportion of violations following an exceedance equals the proportion following a non-exceedance, while also checking the level. It catches a model whose exceptions are right in number but wrong in timing: the signal that VaR is not responding to changing volatility.

**LO:** MR-4 c, d, e; MR-7 a: Identify the properties of an exceedance-based backtest that indicate a VaR model is accurate, and describe how these properties are reflected in a PIT-based backtest. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.6, 4.2 (Model Verification, Conditional Coverage Models), Tables 4.1 and 4.2; Iercosan et al., Ch.4, 7.5

MR-4 • Backtesting VaR • Vardeez: IMPORTANT (refer to crash-course notes)

**Source:** Workbook C2.3 • S3, S4 • Map #21 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-4 e.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap. Kupiec counts exceptions only and “ignores the time variation in the data”; three consecutive exceptions have the same failure rate as three spread-out ones.

b.reason: Polarity flip. Rejecting a correct model is a Type 1 error (the 10.8% probability of five or more exceptions under a correct model); Type 2 is failing to reject an incorrect model.

c.reason: Scope error. Christoffersen’s test is a first-order Markov chain and “does not allow for the possibility that independence may be violated at a distance greater than one lag”; breaches a week apart need Ljung-Box or the duration test.

questions.question:
A regulatory analyst at a German bank is computing the market risk capital charge for a trading book under the internal models approach. Over the last 250 trading days the one-day 99% VaR was exceeded on 8 days, with the following causes identified:

- 4 days: markets were particularly volatile and correlations changed
- 2 days: the model uses too few maturity buckets for the yield curve
- 1 day: positions changed materially during the day through intraday trading
- 1 day: a major earthquake caused large losses across local markets

The supervisor will exclude any exception that the Basel rules allow to be excluded. The 10-day 99% VaR for the previous day is EUR 52 million and the average 10-day 99% VaR over the last 60 days is EUR 40 million. Which of the following is closest to the multiplier $k$ and the market risk capital charge?

options.text: $k = 3.00$; EUR 120 million
$k = 3.50$; EUR 140 million
$k = 3.65$; EUR 146 million
$k = 3.75$; EUR 150 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Count the exceptions that remain**

Exceptions “may be excluded if they are the result of such occurrences as sudden abnormal changes in interest rates or exchange rates, major political events, or natural disasters”. Only the earthquake qualifies. Volatile markets and changed correlations are bad luck that should “be expected to occur at least some of the time”; model accuracy and intraday trading exceptions are penalised.

$$N = 8 - 1 = 7$$

**Step 2 – Zone and plus factor**

Seven exceptions fall in the yellow zone (5 to 9); Jorion’s Table 4.3 gives an increase in $k$ of 0.65:

$$k = 3 + 0.65 = 3.65$$

⇒ With a correct 99% model the expected count is 2.5; the probability of seven or more under a correct model is only 1.4% (Table 4.4), so a penalty is appropriate.

**Step 3 – Capital charge**

MR $= \text{max} (\text{VaR}_{t-1}, k \times\overline{\text{VaR}}_{60}) = \text{max}(52, 3.65 \times40) = \text{max}(52, 146) = 146$

**Interpretation**

The bank holds EUR 146 million, EUR 26 million more than with $k = 3$. Fixing the maturity buckets (“model accuracy could be improved”) is the actionable item: those exceptions carry a penalty that “should” apply.

**LO:** MR-4 f: Describe the Basel rules for backtesting. ORR-21 c: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.6, The Basel Rules, Tables 4.3 and 4.4; Carey, Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis, 21.1

MR-5 • VaR Mapping • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook C2.1 • S1, S5 • Map #21 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-4 f.7)

a.reason: Excluded every bad-luck exception as well as the earthquake: 8 − 1 − 4 = 3, green zone, 3 × 40 = 120.

b.reason: Read the plus factor one row too high (0.50 belongs to 6 exceptions): 3.50 × 40 = 140.

d.reason: Did not exclude the earthquake: 8 exceptions, $k = 3.75$, 3.75 × 40 = 150.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is preparing a report comparing principal, duration and cash-flow mapping for a bond portfolio, using the textbook example of a 5-year 6% bond and a 1-year 4% bond held in equal amounts at par. Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to include in the report?

options.text: Principal mapping understates the true risk of the portfolio, because it maps the market value to the average maturity of principal and ignores the intervening coupon payments.
Duration mapping places the present value of each cash flow on the vertex nearest its payment date, which allows it to capture imperfect correlation along the curve.
Cash-flow mapping is preferred because it preserves the market value of the portfolio, a property that principal mapping and duration mapping do not have.
The diversified cash-flow VaR is below the duration VaR, because risk is not linear in maturity and because correlations between the vertices are below one.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three numbers**

Principal (3-year vertex): USD 2.97 million. Duration (2.733 years, interpolated risk 1.351%): USD 2.70 million. Cash flow: USD 2.63 million undiversified, USD 2.57 million diversified.

**Step 2 – Decompose the duration to cash-flow gap**

$$2.70 - 2.57 = 0.13 = \underbrace{(2.70 - 2.63)}_{\text{0.07 non-linear risk in maturity}} + \underbrace{(2.63 - 2.57)}_{\text{0.06 correlations below one}}$$

**Interpretation**

D is correct. The ranking of fidelity runs from cash-flow mapping (finest, captures both effects), through duration mapping (one vertex, ignores the curvature of risk across maturities and assumes perfect correlation), to principal mapping (crudest, ignores coupons).

**LO:** MR-5 c: Differentiate among the three methods for mapping portfolios of fixed-income securities. MR-5 d: Summarize how to map a fixed-income portfolio into positions of standard instruments. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.11, 5.2 Mapping Approaches, Tables 5.2 to 5.4

MR-5 • VaR Mapping • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook C3.2 • S1, S3 • Map #22 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-5 c.7)

a.reason: Polarity flip. Principal mapping “overstates the true risk because it ignores intervening coupon payments”: it gives the highest VaR, USD 2.97 million.

b.reason: Sibling swap. Grouping each cash flow on term-structure vertices is cash-flow mapping; duration mapping replaces the whole portfolio by one zero-coupon bond with maturity equal to the portfolio duration.

c.reason: Scope/condition error. All three methods preserve market value (USD 200 million is mapped in each case); “ideally, it also should preserve its market risk”, and it is risk preservation that separates them.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Mumbai-based insurer maps a USD 200 million bond portfolio onto zero-coupon vertices. It holds USD 100 million of a 2-year 5% annual-coupon bond and USD 100 million of a 4-year 5% annual-coupon bond, both priced at par on a flat 5% curve. The analyst has computed:

- Average maturity of principal: 3.00 years
- Portfolio Macaulay duration: 2.84 years

Monthly 95% VaR percentages for zeros:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maturity (years) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| VaR (%) | 0.4696 | 0.9868 | 1.4841 | 1.9714 | 2.4261 |

Using duration mapping with linear interpolation, which of the following is closest to the portfolio’s monthly 95% VaR?

options.text: USD 1.40 million
USD 1.97 million
USD 2.81 million
USD 2.97 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Locate the duration on the grid**

$D = 2.84$ years lies between the 2-year and 3-year vertices.

**Step 2 – Interpolate the VaR %**

$V_{2.84} = 0.9868 + (1.4841 - 0.9868) \times(2.84 - 2) = 0.9868 + 0.4973 \times0.84 = 1.4045\%$

**Step 3 – Duration-mapping VaR**

VaR $= 200 \times1.4045\% = \text{USD} 2.81$ million

⇒ Slightly below the principal-mapping figure, as the ranking predicts.

**Interpretation**

The average maturity of principal (3.00 years) is the input for principal mapping, not duration mapping; it is there to lure you to option D. (For reference: the 2-year 5% par bond has Macaulay duration 1.952 years and the 4-year one 3.723 years; their equal-weighted average is 2.838.)

**LO:** MR-5 d: Summarize how to map a fixed-income portfolio into positions of standard instruments. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.11, 5.2 (duration mapping by linear interpolation); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 1, LO 5.d

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.5 (Jorion 11.5.2) and Vardeez MR-5 d (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-5 d.3)

a.reason: Correct interpolated VaR %, but applied to one bond only: 100×1.4045% = 1.40.

b.reason: Did not interpolate; read the 2-year vertex: 200 × 0.9868% = 1.97.

d.reason: Used the average maturity of principal (3 years), which is principal mapping: 200 × 1.4841% = 2.97.

questions.loText: Explain how VaR can be calculated and used relative to a performance benchmark.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a German pension fund must track a government bond index with EUR 250 million. The index’s monthly 95% absolute VaR is EUR 4.80 million. The risk team has built five candidate portfolios, all with the same duration as the index, and computed their monthly 95% VaRs (EUR million):

| Portfolio | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vertices used | 4Y, 5Y | 3Y, 7Y | 2Y, 9Y | 1Y, 10Y | 1M, 30Y |
| Absolute VaR | 5.40 | 5.10 | 4.95 | 4.75 | 4.10 |
| Tracking error VaR | 1.05 | 0.62 | 0.38 | 0.55 | 1.95 |

The manager’s mandate is to track the index as closely as possible. Which portfolio should the manager choose, and what is its variance improvement relative to the index?

options.text: Portfolio 3; variance improvement 99.4%
Portfolio 3; variance improvement 92.1%
Portfolio 4; variance improvement 98.7%
Portfolio 5; variance improvement 83.5%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Choose the right risk measure**

The mandate is relative, so the selection criterion is the tracking error VaR, $\alpha\sqrt{(x - x_{0})^{'}\Sigma(x - x_{0})}$, not the absolute VaR. Portfolio 3 has the lowest TE-VaR, EUR 0.38 million.

**Step 2 – Variance improvement for each candidate**

2

VI $= 1 - (\frac{\text{TE-VaR}}{\text{VaR}_{\text{index}}})$

Portfolio 1: $1 - (1.05/4.80)^{2} = 95.2\%$; portfolio 2: 98.3%; portfolio 3: $1 - (0.38/4.80)^{2} =$ 1 − 0.00627 = 99.4%; portfolio 4: 98.7%; portfolio 5: 83.5%.

⇒ The ranking by variance improvement is the same as the ranking by TE-VaR, and portfolio 3 wins.

**Interpretation**

Like an $R^{2}$, a 99.4% variance improvement means the portfolio reproduces all but 0.6% of the variance of the index’s returns; the residual comes from non-parallel moves in the term structure. Spreading the two positions to 2 and 9 years comes closest to the index’s cash-flow profile, which is why it beats the narrow 4- and 5-year bracket even though all five have the same duration. The EUR 250 million size is not needed.

**LO:** MR-5 f: Explain how VaR can be calculated and used relative to a performance benchmark. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.11, 5.2 Benchmarking, Table 5.5 and eq. 5.8

MR-6 • Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT (new topic, highly testable)

**Source:** Workbook C3.1 • S2 • Map #22 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-5 f.8)

b.reason: Right portfolio, but used the ratio of VaRs instead of the ratio of variances: 1 − 0.38/4.80 = 92.1%.

c.reason: Picked the portfolio whose absolute VaR is closest to the index’s (4.75 against 4.80) instead of the lowest tracking error; matching absolute risk is not matching the index.

d.reason: Picked the lowest absolute VaR (the barbell of 1-month bills and 30-year zeros). “Minimizing absolute market risk is not the same as minimizing relative market risk”: its TE-VaR is the worst, $1 - (1.95/4.80)^{2} = 83.5\%$.

questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.3 (Lo 2001; Jorion 2007)
questions.question: A risk manager at a multi-strategy fund reviews a desk that has earned small, steady profits for three years by selling deep out-of-the-money index puts. The desk’s 99% VaR is estimated by fitting a GARCH(1,1) model to the desk’s daily actual P&L, and it has stayed low throughout. The validation team has flagged the model. Which of the following is the most appropriate reason?

options.text: A GARCH model fitted to actual P&L cannot respond to volatility clustering, so the reported VaR is too stable over time.
The P&L history does not reflect the risk of the positions now held, so VaR would neither reveal the tail risk in the puts nor fall when positions are cut.
A 99% confidence level is too low for an option-selling desk, so raising it to 99.9% on the same P&L history would make the model sound.
A P&L-based GARCH VaR is known to be less accurate than banks’ positional VaR models, so it would fail a backtest.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the model**

A GARCH VaR on the desk’s actual P&L history: the same type of model Berkowitz and O’Brien found to be accurate.

**Step 2 – Apply the fit-for-purpose test**

The P&L of a short deep out-of-the-money put book is a run of small gains until the market moves. That history does not show the tail risk of the puts now held, and it does not change when the positions change.

⇒ This is Lo’s “Capital Decimation Partners” case: only a VaR on the current positions (Jorion) shows the risk and responds to position changes.

**Interpretation**

The model fails conceptual soundness because it is not fit for purpose, not because it is inaccurate. The confidence level and GARCH’s volatility dynamics are not the issue.

**LO:** MR-6 a: Describe some important considerations for a bank in assessing the conceptual soundness of a VaR model during the validation process. • **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.3 (Berkowitz and O’Brien 2002; Lo 2001; Jorion 2007)

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.3 (Lo 2001; Jorion 2007) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 a.6)

a.reason: Wrong model fact: GARCH is designed to capture volatility clustering. The problem is the input (actual P&L), not the volatility dynamics.

c.reason: Raising the confidence level on the same P&L history leaves the position-change problem in place.

d.reason: Sibling swap: Berkowitz and O’Brien found the GARCH model on actual P&L more accurate than banks’ VaR models.

questions.question: A model validation analyst at a US bank holding company is writing the validation report for the trading desk’s historical-simulation VaR model, covering conceptual soundness, sensitivity analysis, confidence intervals and benchmarking. Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to include in the report?

options.text: A VaR model fitted by applying a GARCH model to the desk’s actual P&L history would fail the conceptual soundness test, because its VaR would not fall when the trader cuts positions.
Confidence intervals for historical-simulation VaR are typically narrower than those for filtered historical simulation, and they become narrower still when estimated over stress periods.
Under the regulatory loss function, which penalizes only exceedances, a P&L-based GARCH VaR outperformed the banks’ positional VaR models at most of the banks studied.
The component VaR of a position with scarce valuation data is best estimated by regressing changes in portfolio value on the full time series of that position’s value changes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Purpose test (Section 6.3)**

“A crucial aspect of VaR modeling; its key purpose is to show how risk changes when positions change.” A VaR built on actual P&L history is unaffected when positions are cut, because the history does not change; a VaR on the pseudo history of the current portfolio does fall.

⇒ Such a model “is not fit for purpose and thus fails a crucial conceptual soundness test”, even though Berkowitz and O’Brien found the P&L GARCH model more accurate as a forecast.

**Step 2 – Check the remaining validation claims**

Confidence intervals (Section 6.5, Table 6.1): FHS narrowest; HS “particularly wide” in stress periods. Benchmarking (Section 6.8): positional VaR wins under the regulatory loss function at every bank; P&L VaR wins under the check loss at 16 of 19. Sensitivity (Section 6.4): with scarce data the regression approach “is diﬀicult to implement”; Tasche and Hallerbach use the position’s change on the day that determines the HS VaR.

**Interpretation**

A is correct. It is the reason a validator may use the P&L GARCH VaR as a benchmark but not as the risk management model. The other three options are tested again in MR-6 b, c and d.

**LO:** MR-6 a, b, c, d (all four LOs of the reading). • **Reference:** Lynch, Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk, Sections 6.3, 6.4, 6.5, 6.8

MR-6 • Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT (new topic, highly testable)

**Source:** Workbook D10.2 • S3 • Map #53 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 a.7)

b.reason: Polarity flip: HS intervals are wider than FHS intervals (FHS “provides more eﬀicient estimates of VaR”), and HS intervals widen, not narrow, in stress periods.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the P&L VaR outperformed on accuracy under the check loss function; under the regulatory loss function the positional VaR “significantly outperforms the P&L VaR in every case”, reflecting conservatism.

d.reason: Scope/condition error: the regression of Equation 6.5 “requires that you have a full time series of the change in value of the positions”, which is what is missing; the component is instead estimated from the position’s loss on the VaR-determining day, or an average of ordered observations near it.

questions.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.
questions.reading: MR-6: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
questions.topic: Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk
questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.4
questions.question: A risk manager explains to a trading head how the VaR model’s sensitivity to a single position is measured. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Because VaR is linear homogeneous in positions, component VaRs sum to total VaR, and a position’s sensitivity depends on its portfolio share and on how its value moves with the portfolio.
Because VaR is subadditive, component VaRs sum to more than total VaR, and the excess measures each position’s contribution to diversification.
Marginal VaR measures the change in portfolio value caused by a small change in a position’s price, so it does not depend on the position’s share of the portfolio.
Supervisors ask for risks not in VaR on a component basis only, because stand-alone VaR changes whenever the portfolio’s composition changes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Linear homogeneity and Euler**

VaR is linear homogeneous in positions, so VaR$(V_{P} ) = \sum_{i}(\partial\text{VaR}/\partial V_{i})V_{i}$: the component VaRs add up to total VaR.

**Step 2 – What drives a position’s component**

Component VaR$_{i} = \text{VaR} w_{i}\beta_{i}$: the position’s share $w_{i}$ and the sensitivity $\beta_{i}$ of its value to the portfolio value.

⇒ A is the reading’s statement.

**Interpretation**

This decomposition is what makes sensitivity analysis to positions possible. It also explains why supervisors ask for a stand-alone view too: component VaR moves with the portfolio’s composition.

**LO:** MR-6 b: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis. • **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.4, Euler equation and Equation 6.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 b.5)

b.reason: Wrong property: Euler’s equation makes the components sum exactly to total VaR; subadditivity is a different property of risk measures.

c.reason: Marginal VaR is the change in VaR for a small change in the size of the position, and it does depend on the position’s weight through $\beta_{i}$ and the portfolio.

d.reason: Reversed: supervisors ask for both component and stand-alone measures, because stand-alone VaR is independent of the portfolio’s composition.

questions.question: A validation team wants to measure how much a thinly traded structured note, which was valued on only a few days in the past year, contributes to the desk’s 99% historical-simulation VaR. Which approach is most consistent with the methods described for this situation?

options.text: Regress the note’s value changes on the portfolio’s value changes over the full year, estimate $\beta$, and set component VaR equal to VaR times the note’s weight times $\beta$.
Replace the note with a liquid proxy and use the proxy’s beta, since a proxy is at least as volatile and as correlated with the portfolio as the note.
Use the change in the note’s value on the day that determines the historical-simulation VaR, or an average of ordered observations near that day.
Exclude the note, since a material omission would already have produced an unexpected cluster of exceptions in the desk’s backtest.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why the regression fails here**

Equation 6.5 needs a full time series of the position’s value changes. The note was valued on only a few days, so that series does not exist.

**Step 2 – Apply Tasche and Hallerbach**

On the scenario that sets the HS VaR, the portfolio loss equals the sum of the positions’ changes. So a position’s component VaR can be estimated by its change in value on that day.

⇒ One day is noisy, so an average of the ordered observations near the HS VaR may be used instead.

**Interpretation**

The method is “especially easy to implement when using historic simulation”, which is the model in the stem.

**LO:** MR-6 b: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis. • **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.4 (Tasche 2000; Hallerbach 2003)

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.4 (Tasche 2000; Hallerbach 2003) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 b.6)

a.reason: The regression needs exactly the full time series that is missing.

b.reason: Polarity flip: a proxy may be less volatile or less correlated, and so understate the contribution.

d.reason: A backtest does not show whether a specific position’s omission is material; that is what the sensitivity analysis is for.

questions.loText: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis.

questions.question: A bank’s VaR pseudo history values an options book with a first-order (delta) Taylor approximation and omits basis risk on several emerging-market bonds. The head of validation asks what sensitivity analysis can achieve in this situation. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: It tests whether the assumption that the omitted terms and positions are immaterial holds, and gives a consistent way to prioritise which risk factors or higher-order terms to add.
It proves that the omissions are immaterial whenever the VaR model passes its backtest with fewer than five exceptions over the past 250 days.
It removes the need to track data proxies, because supervisors accept sensitivity results in place of an inventory of the risks not in VaR.
It estimates the omitted risks precisely, because the scarcer the data on a position, the easier its effect on VaR is to isolate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the analysis tests**

It tests the assumption that the omitted positions or risk factors (here, basis risk and the next Taylor term) are immaterial.

**Step 2 – What it delivers**

A consistent framework for quantifying omitted risks and a more rigorous way to prioritise model changes: more risk factors or higher-order terms.

⇒ This is Jarrow’s view of validation: check whether the model is sensitive to its assumptions.

**Interpretation**

Sensitivity analysis complements, rather than replaces, backtesting and the tracking of proxies that supervisors require.

**LO:** MR-6 b: Explain how to conduct sensitivity analysis for a VaR model, and describe the potential benefits and challenges of performing such an analysis. • **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.4

MR-6 • Validating Bank Holding Companies’ Value-at-Risk Models for Market Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT (new topic, highly testable)

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 b.7)

b.reason: A backtest result does not prove that a particular omission is immaterial.

c.reason: Supervisors increasingly require banks to track their data proxies and risks not in VaR; sensitivity analysis supports that, it does not replace it.

d.reason: Reversed: with scarce data it is hard to make a precise estimate of the omission’s effect.

questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.5 (Jorion 1996)
questions.question: A bank holding company’s validation team proposes to place a 90% confidence interval around its one-day 99% historical-simulation VaR using Jorion’s asymptotic standard error of a quantile, $SE = \frac{1}{f(\text{VaR})}\sqrt{c(1 - c)/T}$. Which of the following is the main challenge in applying this formula?

options.text: The coverage level $c$ and the sample size $T$ are unknown and must first be estimated from the pseudo history.
The density at the VaR, $f(\text{VaR})$, must be specified, and assuming a normal density is probably a mistake because returns are non-normal.
The formula gives intervals that are too narrow whenever more data are used, so $T$ must be kept to one year or less.
The formula cannot be applied to VaR at all, because VaR is not a quantile of the distribution of portfolio value changes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which inputs are known**

VaR, $T$ and $c$ are known, so the calculation is “seemingly straightforward”.

**Step 2 – Which input is hard**

$f(\text{VaR})$, the probability density at the VaR. Imposing a distribution, usually normal, is convenient, but financial returns are non-normal, so “imposing a normal distribution would probably be a mistake”.

⇒ The challenge is specifying $f(\cdot)$; non-parametric methods (order statistics, bootstrap) avoid it.

**Interpretation**

Jorion also suggests basing the interval on more than the single quantile point, using the variance of the distribution of pseudo returns.

**LO:** MR-6 c: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.

- **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.5 (Jorion 1996)

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.5 (Jorion 1996) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 c.4)

a.reason: $c$ and $T$ are chosen and known, not estimated.

c.reason: More data narrows the interval correctly; nothing in the formula makes it “too narrow”.

d.reason: VaR is a quantile of the distribution of value changes; that is why a quantile standard error applies.

questions.question: A risk analyst bootstraps confidence intervals for two VaR models of the same trading book: a historical-simulation VaR and a GARCH(1,1) VaR. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: For the historical-simulation VaR, resampling the pseudo history with replacement assumes daily value changes are independent, so dependence over time is not reflected.
For the GARCH VaR, the analyst should resample the raw daily value changes directly, because the GARCH model already accounts for their dependence.
For the GARCH VaR, the parameters estimated on the original sample should be held fixed in every bootstrap sample, so that estimation risk is kept out.
Filtered historical simulation typically yields the widest intervals of the three, because it combines GARCH volatility with an empirical distribution.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – HS bootstrap**

Drawing observations from the pseudo history with replacement treats the changes as independent over time.

⇒ It is non-parametric, like HS itself, but it does not reflect dependence.

**Step 2 – GARCH bootstrap**

The standardised residuals $z_{t}$ are IID, so resample them, rebuild the series, and re-estimate the GARCH equation on each sample so that estimation risk enters the interval.

**Interpretation**

The two bootstraps are designed differently because the bootstrap must mimic the dependence of the data. FHS, which keeps the re-estimated residuals, gives the narrowest intervals in Table 6.1.

**LO:** MR-6 c: Describe the challenges a financial institution could face when calculating confidence intervals for VaR.

- **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.5 (Christoffersen and Goncalves 2005)

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.5 (Christoffersen and Goncalves) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 c.5)

b.reason: Raw value changes are not IID under GARCH; it is the standardised residuals that are resampled.

c.reason: Reversed: the equation is re-estimated precisely to include estimation risk.

d.reason: Polarity flip: FHS gives the narrowest intervals.

questions.question: A validation analyst compares the bank’s positional VaR with a GARCH(1,1) VaR estimated on the bank’s trading P&L, both one-day 99%, using the sign test under two loss functions. Based on the evidence reported for US bank holding companies, which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: Under the regulatory loss function the P&L VaR outperformed the positional VaR at most banks, showing that positional VaR models are too aggressive.
Under the regulatory loss function the positional VaR outperformed in every case, while under the check loss function the P&L VaR was more accurate at 16 of 19 banks.
Under the check loss function the positional VaR outperformed at 16 of 19 banks, because conservatism is rewarded when accuracy is measured.
Under both loss functions the two models were statistically indistinguishable, so a plot of the two VaR series is suﬀicient benchmarking.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Regulatory loss function**

“The positional VaR model significantly outperforms the P&L VaR in every case.”

⇒ This shows the conservative nature of banks’ positional VaR models, often attributed to regulatory oversight.

**Step 2 – Check loss function**

“The P&L VaR outperforms the positional VaR at sixteen out of nineteen banks.” One bank’s positional VaR won; two were insignificant.

**Interpretation**

Conservatism wins under a loss that penalises only exceedances; accuracy wins under the check loss (Figure 1). The same pair of facts is option C of Question MR-6 a.7.

**LO:** MR-6 d: Discuss the challenges in benchmarking VaR models and various approaches proposed to overcome them. • **Reference:** Lynch, Section 6.8

MR-7 • Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.6, 6.8 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-6 d.7)

a.reason: Reversed: under the regulatory loss the positional VaR won every time, which shows conservatism, not aggressiveness.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the 16 of 19 result belongs to the P&L VaR under the check loss.

d.reason: The differences were significant in most cases; and a plot only shows relative conservatism.

questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.7 (Iercosan et al.), 7.5
questions.question: A validation team has confirmed that a desk’s one-day 99% VaR model passes both Kupiec’s unconditional coverage test and Christoffersen’s independence test. A senior validator asks what further exceedance-based evidence could still reveal a misspecified model. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Kupiec’s test would have rejected the model if exceedances had bunched together, so clustering can be ruled out.
The Christoffersen–Pelletier duration test models the time between exceedances, which is memoryless under a correct model, so it can flag clustering beyond a one-day lag.
The Ljung-Box test examines a single lag of the hit series, so it adds nothing beyond Christoffersen’s independence test.
The joint conditional coverage test is more powerful than either individual test when only one of the two properties is violated.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the two passed tests cannot see**

Kupiec ignores timing. Christoffersen uses a first-order Markov chain, so it “does not allow for the possibility that independence may be violated at a distance greater than one lag”.

**Step 2 – Tests that look further**

The Christoffersen–Pelletier duration test models $D_{i} = t_{i} - t_{i-1}$. Under a correct model Pr$(D = d) = (1 - p)^{d-1}p$, an exponential (memoryless) distribution; it is tested against a Weibull alternative. Clustering produces too many short and too many long durations, whatever the lag.

⇒ Statement B is correct.

**Interpretation**

GARP stresses that passing Kupiec and Christoffersen is not the end of the story: the duration test, Ljung-Box and logit regressions of hits on lagged information can all reveal a model that does not respond to market changes.

**LO:** MR-7 a • **Reference:** Iercosan et al., GARP MR Ch.7, 7.5, eqs. 7.12 to 7.21

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.7 (Iercosan et al.), 7.5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-7 a.6)

a.reason: Sibling swap: Kupiec counts exceedances only; bunched exceedances give the same $LR_{uc}$ as spread-out ones.

c.reason: Ljung-Box tests $m$ lags jointly, $Q = T (T + 2) \sum^{m}_{k=1} r^{2}_{k}/(T - k) \sim\chi^{2}(m)$; that is precisely what it adds beyond one lag.

d.reason: GARP notes the opposite: joint tests “have significant limitations in their ability to detect misspecifications when only one of the two properties is violated”.

questions.question: A model validation analyst at a US bank holding company is presenting to newly hired analysts on how the bank’s subportfolio VaR models are validated. The bank stores, for each day, the one-day 99% VaR, the clean P&L and the corresponding probability integral transform (PIT). Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to make?

options.text: A hump-shaped PIT histogram, with realised P&L clustering in the middle of the forecast distribution, signals aggressive misspecification because the model distribution is too narrow.
Uniformity of the PITs on the interval from 0 to 1 is the counterpart of unconditional coverage, so a PIT test uses information from every percentile of the forecast distribution.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the preferred uniformity test for a 99% VaR model, because it places more weight on the tails of the PIT distribution than the Anderson-Darling test.
Because PITs use the whole forecast distribution, a subportfolio that passes Kupiec’s unconditional coverage test will also pass a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of PIT uniformity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the PIT is**

$p_{t+1} = F_{t}(P \&L_{t+1})$: the previous day’s forecast distribution evaluated at the realised P&L. A correctly specified model produces i.i.d. $U(0, 1)$ PITs.

**Step 2 – Map the two exceedance properties**

Unconditional coverage (exceedances at 1% VaR observed 1% of the time, at 3% VaR 3% of the time, and so on) “is analogous to the uniformity distributional property of a series of PITs”; independence of exceedances maps to independence of the PITs.

**Interpretation**

B is correct. An exceedance count tests the model at a single percentile; PITs, when well estimated, “provide information on the accuracy of the risk model at any percentile of the forecast distribution”. That is why PIT tests can reveal misspecifications that pure exceedance analysis misses.

**LO:** MR-7 a, b, c, d • **Reference:** Iercosan, Shcherbakova, McArthur and Alper, GARP MR Ch.7, 7.1, 7.2, 7.6, 7.7

MR-7 • Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook C2.2 • S2 • Map #21 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-7 a.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip. P&L clustering in the middle is conservative misspecification: the model distribution is too wide. Aggressive misspecification (too narrow) shows realised P&L in the tails.

c.reason: Sibling swap. The KS test lacks sensitivity at the extremes; Anderson-Darling is the modification that puts more weight on the tails and so better detects tail misspecification of a 99% VaR model.

d.reason: Absolute claim. In the study 67% of subportfolios passed Kupiec but only 21% passed KS: banks perform better on exceedance tests than on tests of the distribution.

questions.question: A junior analyst is drafting the definition of a probability integral transform (PIT) for the bank’s VaR validation manual. Which of the following definitions is correct?

options.text: The PIT for day $t + 1$ is the realised P&L for day $t + 1$ divided by the standard deviation forecast for that day.
The PIT for day $t + 1$ is the previous day’s forecast CDF evaluated at the realised P&L of day $t + 1$, i.e. the model’s probability of a P&L at or below the one realised.
The PIT is a point-in-time version of the exceedance indicator, equal to 1 when the loss exceeds VaR and 0 otherwise.
The PIT for day $t + 1$ is the forecast CDF re-estimated after observing day $t + 1$’s P&L, evaluated at the VaR threshold.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The definition**

$p_{t+1} = F_{t}(P \&L_{t+1})$: the forecast distribution made on day $t$, evaluated at day $t + 1$’s realised P&L. GARP: the model’s probability of observing a loss below the actual P&L, “often called the p-value”.

⇒ It is a cumulative probability, so it always lies in \[0,1\].

**Interpretation**

Two details carry the definition: the CDF (not the density, not the $z$-score) and the forecast made before the outcome.

**LO:** MR-7 b: Explain how to derive probability integral transforms (PITs) in the context of validating a VaR model. • **Reference:** Iercosan et al., GARP MR Ch.7, 7.1 and 7.2, eq. 7.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.7, 7.1 and 7.2 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-7 b.1)

a.reason: That is the $z$-score (for a zero-mean forecast). It still has to go through the CDF to become a PIT.

c.reason: PIT is not “point in time”, and the 0/1 indicator is the exceedance (hit) series of the exceedance-based approach.

d.reason: A forecast re-estimated after the outcome is no longer a forecast, and the CDF is evaluated at the realised P&L, not at the VaR threshold.

questions.question:
A validation analyst reviews two recent days for a desk whose VaR model forecasts normally distributed daily returns with a mean of zero:

| Day | Forecast s.d. | Realised return | $z$ | PIT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | 3.25% | −3.00% | −0.92 | 0.178 |
| 15 | 1.00% | −2.00% | −2.00 | 0.023 |

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Day 14 is the more extreme outcome for the model, because its loss of 3.00% is the larger of the two.
Day 15 is the more extreme outcome relative to its own forecast; the PIT puts days with different forecast distributions on one comparable \[0,1\] scale.
Neither PIT is informative, because PITs can only be compared when the forecast standard deviation is the same every day.
A PIT close to zero indicates a large gain relative to the forecast, so Day 15 was an unusually good day for the desk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Compare each loss with its own forecast**

Day 14: −3.00/3.25 = −0.92, PIT $= N (-0.92) = 0.178$. Day 15: −2.00/1.00 = −2.00, PIT $= N (-2.00) = 0.023$.

⇒ Day 15’s smaller loss sits much deeper in the left tail of its forecast.

**Step 2 – Why that is the right comparison**

The forecasts differ (3.25% vs 1.00%), so raw returns are not comparable. The PIT maps each outcome to \[0,1\] under its own forecast.

**Interpretation**

A PIT of 0.023 means the model gave only a 2.3% chance to a day at least that bad; Day 14’s loss was a roughly one-in-six event for its wider forecast.

**LO:** MR-7 b • **Reference:** Iercosan et al., GARP MR Ch.7, 7.2; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 1, Reading 7, LO 7.b

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.7, 7.2 and Vardeez’s PIT table (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-7 b.5)

a.reason: Compares raw losses across days with different forecasts, exactly what the PIT is designed to avoid.

c.reason: Reverses the purpose: the PIT exists because forecasts change day to day.

d.reason: Polarity flip: low PITs are losses in the left tail; a large gain would give a PIT near 1.

questions.loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
questions.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models

questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.7, 7.3 and 7.4
questions.question: Iercosan et al. pooled the PITs of hundreds of US bank subportfolios, each with a one-day 99% regulatory VaR model, into a single histogram. The histogram was humped across the middle deciles but also showed visible spikes in the 0.0–0.1 and 0.9–1.0 bins. Which interpretation is most consistent with this shape?

options.text: The models are uniformly conservative: the forecast distributions are too wide everywhere, including the tails.
The models are conservative in the body of the distribution, but their tails are thinner than realised P&L requires, so extreme outcomes are understated.
The models are aggressive in the body but conservative in the tails, so the 99% VaR overstates extreme losses.
The shape reflects serial dependence of the PITs rather than any miscalibration of the forecast distribution.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the body**

A hump across the middle deciles: outcomes cluster near the centre of the forecasts, so in the body the forecasts are too wide (conservative).

**Step 2 – Read the ends**

Spikes at both ends: extreme outcomes land beyond the forecast tails more often than predicted, so the tails are too thin.

⇒ Conservative in the body, but tails thinner than realised P&L requires.

**Interpretation**

This is exactly GARP’s finding for subportfolio PITs: models are “fairly conservative in the body” while “the tails of these risk models are thinner than is required by the realizations of P&L”. It also matches the moment results: models overstate variance and understate kurtosis.

**LO:** MR-7 c • **Reference:** Iercosan et al., GARP MR Ch.7, 7.3 and 7.4

MR-7 • Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of Value-at-Risk Models • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.7, 7.3 and 7.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-7 c.8)

a.reason: Ignores the spikes: a model too wide everywhere would have thin ends, not spikes.

c.reason: Reverses both halves.

d.reason: A histogram describes the distribution of PITs, not their order in time; dependence needs a separate test.

questions.question: A validator wants to test whether a desk’s daily PITs are independent over time, following the approach described by Berkowitz (2001). Which procedure is correct?

options.text: Apply the Anderson-Darling test to the PITs, because it weights the tails where clustered losses show up.
Transform each PIT into a standard normal value with the inverse normal CDF, then test the transformed series for dependence, for example by regressing it on its own lag and on lagged P&L.
Count the exceedances of the 99% VaR and apply Kupiec’s proportion of failures test to the count.
Regress the raw PITs directly on their lags, because their \[0,1\] support makes the normal transformation unnecessary.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why transform**

PITs live on the bounded interval \[0,1\]. Berkowitz notes it is easier to test independence outside that range, so each PIT is mapped to a standard normal value, $\Phi^{-1}(p_{t})$ (e.g. 0.046 becomes −1.69), to “avoid problems of inference due to bounded support”.

**Step 2 – Then test dependence**

The transformed series is tested with log-likelihood methods; GARP regresses it on its lag and on lagged P&L. Significant coeﬀicients mean the forecasts ignore information already available.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

Uniformity tests (KS, AD, CvM) and independence tests are separate steps; together they check i.i.d. uniformity, the PIT version of conditional coverage.

**LO:** MR-7 d • **Reference:** Iercosan et al., GARP MR Ch.7, 7.6, Table 7.10; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 1, Reading 7, LO 7.d

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.7, 7.6 (Berkowitz) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-7 d.6)

a.reason: AD is a goodness-of-fit test of the PIT distribution; it says nothing about the order of PITs in time.

c.reason: Kupiec tests the exceedance count (unconditional coverage), not independence of PITs.

d.reason: Reverses the reason: the bounded \[0,1\] support is exactly why the normal transformation is used.

questions.question: In Iercosan et al.’s study of 597 US bank subportfolios, the share whose PITs passed (did not reject) each uniformity test at the 1% level was about 21% for Kolmogorov-Smirnov, 11% for Anderson-Darling and 21% for Cramér-von Mises, against 67% passing Kupiec’s unconditional coverage test. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Because the most tail-sensitive test rejected the most subportfolios, the models’ main weakness lies in the centre of the forecast distribution.
The models perform better on exceedance tests than on tests of the whole distribution, and Anderson-Darling, which weights the tails, has the most power to detect the misspecification.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises tests are the more reliable, because they agree with each other and reject fewer models.
The PIT tests must be wrong, because a model that passes Kupiec’s test has a correctly specified forecast distribution.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Exceedance tests vs distribution tests**

67% pass Kupiec, but only 11% to 21% pass the PIT uniformity tests.

⇒ The models do better at the single VaR percentile than across the whole distribution.

**Step 2 – Rank the tests**

AD rejects the most (only 11% pass). GARP: “as the power of the test increases, we are able to find fewer subportfolios which exhibit the desired properties”.

⇒ AD, the tail-weighted test, is the most powerful here.

**Interpretation**

Passing an exceedance test is weak evidence that the whole forecast distribution is right; PIT tests, especially AD, reveal the tail misspecification the counts miss.

**LO:** MR-7 d • **Reference:** Iercosan et al., GARP MR Ch.7, 7.5, 7.6 and 7.7

a.reason: The most tail-sensitive test rejecting the most points to the tails, not the centre.

c.reason: Agreement between two less powerful tests is not reliability; they reject less because they are less sensitive.

d.reason: Kupiec checks one percentile only; passing it does not validate the full distribution.

questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.9 (Meissner 9.2, 9.3)
questions.question: A risk analyst replicates Meissner’s study of the 30 Dow stocks. Regressing the monthly change in the average correlation on the previous month’s level gives $y = 0.256 - 0.7903x$, with $R^{2} =$ 0.3948. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The long-run mean correlation implied by the regression is 25.6%, the value of the intercept.
The one-month-lag autocorrelation is about 79.0%, and the mean reversion rate is about 21.0%.
The negative slope of −0.7903 means correlations tend to move away from their long-run mean, so the series shows no mean reversion.
The mean reversion rate is 79.03%, the implied long-run mean is about 32.4%, and the one-month-lag autocorrelation is about 21.0%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Mean reversion rate**

$$a = -\beta= 0.7903 = 79.03\%$$

**Step 2 – Long-run mean**

$$\mu= \frac{\alpha}{a} = \frac{0.256}{0.7903} = 32.4\%$$

**Step 3 – One-lag autocorrelation**

$$AC = 1 - a = 20.97\% \approx21.0\%$$

**Interpretation**

These are exactly Meissner’s figures for the Dow, 1972 to 2017. The $R^{2}$ describes how well the regression fits; it is not a parameter of the mean reversion model.

**LO:** MR-9 b: Calculate a mean reversion rate using standard regression and calculate the corresponding autocorrelation. • **Reference:** Meissner, Correlation Risk Modeling and Management 2e, Ch.2, 9.2 and 9.3, eqs. 9.4 to 9.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.9 (Meissner 9.2, 9.3) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-9 b.7)

a.reason: The intercept is $a\mu$, not $\mu$: dividing by $a$ gives 32.4%.

b.reason: Sibling swap: 79.03% is the mean reversion rate and 20.97% the autocorrelation, not the other way round.

c.reason: A negative slope of the change on the level is exactly what mean reversion means: above the mean, the expected change is negative.

questions.question:
A quantitative analyst at a Hong Kong asset manager models the monthly average pairwise correlation of a regional equity basket. Regressing the monthly change in the average correlation, $\rho_{t} - \rho_{t-1}$, on the previous month’s level, $\rho_{t-1}$, gives:

- Intercept: 0.217; slope coeﬀicient: −0.62; $R^{2}$: 0.31
- Current (last month’s) average correlation: 24%

Ignoring the stochastic term, which of the following is closest to the one-lag autocorrelation of the correlation series implied by the regression and the expected average correlation for next month?

options.text: Autocorrelation 38%; expected correlation 30.8%
Autocorrelation 38%; expected correlation 28.2%
Autocorrelation 38%; expected correlation 22.6%
Autocorrelation 62%; expected correlation 30.8%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Mean reversion rate**

In $\rho_{t} - \rho_{t-1} = a\mu_{\rho} - a\rho_{t-1}$, the slope is $-a$:

$$a = -\beta= -(-0.62) = 0.62$$

⇒ Each month, 62% of the gap between the current level and the long-term mean is closed.

**Step 2 – Long-term mean from the intercept**

$$\mu_{\rho} = \frac{\text{intercept}}{a} = \frac{0.217}{0.62} = 0.35$$

**Step 3 – Autocorrelation**

$$AC = 1 - a = 1 - 0.62 = 0.38$$

⇒ Mean reversion and one-lag autocorrelation are reverse properties; in Meissner’s study they sum to 1 (79.03% and 20.97%).

**Step 4 – Expected correlation next month**

$E[\rho_{t}] = \rho_{t-1} + a(\mu_{\rho} - \rho_{t-1}) = 0.24 + 0.62 \times(0.35 - 0.24) = 0.24 + 0.0682 = 0.3082$

**Interpretation**

The basket’s correlation, currently well below its long-term mean of 35%, is expected to jump to about 30.8% next month. For a book that is short correlation (for example, sold basket options), that strong pull back towards the mean is the risk to hedge. The $R^{2}$ of 0.31 describes the regression’s fit and is not an input.

**LO:** MR-9 b: Calculate a mean reversion rate using standard regression and calculate the corresponding autocorrelation. • **Reference:** Meissner, Correlation Risk Modeling and Management 2e, Ch.2, 9.2 and 9.3, eqs. 9.2 to 9.6, Example 9.1

MR-9 • Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World? • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook D11.1 • S2, S3 • Map #54 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-9 b.8)

b.reason: Used the autocorrelation (0.38) as the speed of mean reversion: 0.24 + 0.38 × 0.11 = 0.2818.

c.reason: Took the intercept (0.217) as the long-term mean instead of $a\mu_{\rho}$: 0.24 + 0.62 × (0.217 − 0.24) = 0.2257.

d.reason: Reported the absolute slope (0.62), which is the mean reversion rate, as the autocorrelation; the forecast is right but the autocorrelation is the sibling quantity.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations.
questions.reading: MR-9: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
questions.topic: Empirical Properties of Correlation: How Do Correlations Behave in the Real World?
questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.9 (Meissner 9.4)
questions.question: A model validator asks what kind of distribution the Johnson SB is, since it was identified as the best fit for equity correlations in Meissner’s study. Which description is correct?

options.text: A one-parameter distribution defined on positive values only, like the chi-squared distribution.
A three-parameter distribution (location, scale and shape) used to model block maxima in extreme value theory.
An unbounded, heavy-tailed distribution like the Pareto, chosen because correlations have fat right tails.
A four-parameter distribution with two shape parameters, one location and one scale parameter, flexible enough to fit the bounded, skewed shape of correlations.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The parameters**

Meissner describes the Johnson SB as a versatile distribution with four parameters: $\gamma$ and $\delta$ (shape), $\mu$ (location) and $\sigma$ (scale).

**Step 2 – Why it suits correlations**

It is bounded and can take skewed shapes, so it can match a variable that lives in an interval and leans to one side, which is what the histogram of Dow correlations looks like.

**Interpretation**

The distractors describe the distributions the Johnson SB is set against in this and other readings: chi-squared (a test name), GEV (the bond-correlation fit and the EVT block-maxima distribution) and Pareto (EVT tails).

**LO:** MR-9 c: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations. • **Reference:** Meissner, Correlation Risk Modeling and Management 2e, Ch.2, 9.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.9 (Meissner 9.4) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-9 c.3)

a.reason: Describes a chi-squared distribution: one parameter, positive values only. Correlations can be negative.

b.reason: Describes the GEV distribution (the best fit for bond correlations, and the block-maxima distribution of MR-3).

c.reason: Describes a Pareto-type tail; correlations are bounded, not unbounded.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a UK bank is calibrating a correlation simulation engine that will draw correlation scenarios for three books: an equity basket options book, a corporate bond portfolio, and a credit book whose losses depend on default probability correlations. Following Meissner’s empirical study, which of the following recommendations should the analyst make?

options.text: Use the Johnson SB distribution for all three correlation types, since it gave the best fit for equity, bond and default probability correlations alike.
Use the Johnson SB distribution for equity and default probability correlations, and the generalised extreme value distribution for bond correlations.
Use the Johnson SB distribution for equity and bond correlations, and the generalised extreme value distribution for default probability correlations.
Use the Johnson SB distribution for equity correlations in expansions, but switch to the normal distribution in recessions when correlations are high.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Equity correlations**

Of 61 distributions tested (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, chi-squared), the four-parameter Johnson SB gave the best fit; normal, lognormal and beta fit poorly.

**Step 2 – Default probability correlations**

“The default probability correlation distribution is similar to equity correlation distribution … and can be replicated best by the Johnson SB distribution.”

**Step 3 – Bond correlations**

“The bond correlation distribution shows a more normal shape and can be best fitted with the generalised extreme value distribution and quite well with the normal distribution.”

**Interpretation**

B is correct. The engine should use Johnson SB for the equity and credit books and the generalised extreme value distribution for the bond portfolio. The bond and default results are preliminary and “currently being verified with a larger sample”, so the analyst should flag them for periodic review.

**LO:** MR-9 c: Identify the best-fit distribution for equity, bond, and default correlations. MR-9 a: Describe how equity correlations and correlation volatilities behave throughout various economic states. • **Reference:** Meissner, Correlation Risk Modeling and Management 2e, Ch.2, 9.4 and 9.6, Summary

MR-11 • Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D11.2 • S1 • Map #54 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-9 c.7)

a.reason: Absolute claim. Johnson SB is not the best fit for every type: bond correlations have a more normal shape and are best fitted by the generalised extreme value distribution.

c.reason: Sibling swap. The bond and default probability fits are exchanged; it is default probability correlations that resemble equity correlations.

d.reason: Scope/condition error. Fitting equity correlations by state of the economy gave results that were “slightly but not significantly different”, and the normal distribution fits equity correlations poorly in any state.

questions.question:
A market maker buys USD 100 million face of the JNJ 2.450s of 2060 (DV01 0.2124) from a client and plans to sell USD 111.2 million of the Treasury 1.625s of 2050 (DV01 0.1910), a DV01-neutral hedge. A risk analyst regresses daily changes in the JNJ yield on daily changes in the Treasury yield over the past four months:

|  | Value | Std. error |
|---|---|---|
| Constant ($\alpha\hat{)}$ | 0.060 | 0.223 |
| Slope ($\beta\hat{)}$ | 0.842 | 0.051 |
| $R^{2}$ | 77.5% |  |
| Standard error of regression | 2.00 bp |  |

Which of the following statements best describes the planned DV01-neutral hedge?

options.text: It over-hedges: the 95% interval for the slope, about 0.740 to 0.944, excludes one, so the data reject the parallel-shift assumption on which the hedge rests.
It under-hedges: because the $R^{2}$ is only 77.5%, the Treasury position should be scaled up by 1/0.775 to cover the unexplained variance.
It is appropriate: the 95% interval for the constant includes zero, so the data are consistent with parallel shifts in the two yields.
It is appropriate: equal DV01s on the two legs make it the hedge that minimizes the variance of the hedged P&L.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Test the slope against one**

95% interval: 0.842 ± 2 × 0.051 = (0.740, 0.944). One lies outside it.

⇒ The hypothesis of parallel shifts ($\beta= 1$) is rejected: the JNJ yield moves only about 0.842 bp per Treasury basis point.

**Step 2 – Direction of the error**

The regression hedge sells 111.2 × 0.842 = \$93.6 million. The DV01 hedge sells \$111.2 million, about \$17.6 million too much.

⇒ With $\hat{\beta} < 1$ the DV01-neutral hedge over-hedges.

**Interpretation**

The constant’s interval, 0.060 ± 0.446, does include zero, but the constant has nothing to do with parallel shifts and does not enter the hedge. The $R^{2}$ and standard error describe how much risk is left, not the hedge size.

**LO:** MR-11 a: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.1, Tables 11.1 and 11.2, eq. 11.9

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Tuckman), Tables 11.1 and 11.2 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 a.5)

b.reason: $R^{2}$ measures the share of variance explained; it never scales the hedge. Dividing by 0.775 would only increase the over-hedge.

c.reason: Tests the wrong coeﬀicient: parallel shifts concern the slope, not the constant.

d.reason: Sibling swap: variance minimisation is the property of the regression hedge. Equal DV01s minimise variance only if $\beta= 1$, which the data reject.

questions.question: A trader at a dealer hedges a long position in a 40-year corporate bond by selling a 30-year Treasury bond in a DV01-neutral amount. The hedge has lost money on several days when Treasury yields moved by only a few basis points. Which of the following is the most accurate explanation?

options.text: DV01 is a first-order measure, so the hedge fails only when yields move by large amounts; for small daily moves it is exact.
The hedge assumes the two yields change by the same number of basis points, but the corporate bond trades at a changing spread to Treasuries and 40- and 30-year rates are not perfectly correlated.
The hedge sets the face amounts of the two bonds equal, so it ignores the difference in their price sensitivities to yield changes.
The hedge relies on a regression estimated over a historical window, so it becomes unreliable when the relationship between the two yields changes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The assumption**

A DV01-neutral hedge is exact only if both yields move by the same number of basis points.

**Step 2 – Why it fails here**

GARP gives two reasons for this exact pair: the corporate bond trades at a changing spread to Treasuries, and 40-year and 30-year rates are not perfectly correlated.

⇒ Losses on small moves are the signature of a wrong relationship between the yields, not of a second-order (convexity) effect.

**Interpretation**

The losses on days of small Treasury moves point to basis risk between the two yields, which a DV01 hedge cannot address.

**LO:** MR-11 a: Explain the drawbacks to using a DV01-neutral hedge for a bond position. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.1

MR-11 • Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Tuckman), 11.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 a.6)

a.reason: The parallel-shift assumption fails on small moves too; convexity is not this LO’s drawback.

c.reason: A DV01 hedge equates DV01s, not face amounts; here it sells \$111.2m against \$100m.

d.reason: Caveat swap: dependence on a historical regression is a weakness of the regression hedge, not of the DV01 hedge.

questions.question: The head of a rates desk is reviewing an analyst’s regression hedge, which was estimated from four months of daily yield changes. Which of the following statements should the head of the desk accept?

options.text: A longer estimation window is always preferable, because more observations reduce the standard errors of the regression coeﬀicients.
Because least-squares estimates are unbiased, the in-sample standard error of the regression is a reliable guide to future hedged P&L volatility, so out-of-sample tests add little.
Too short a window may not give statistically reliable estimates and too long a window may include less relevant data, and an earlier episode can be more relevant than the recent past.
The most recent period is the relevant one by definition, because a regression hedge assumes that beta changes each day with the latest data.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – GARP on the estimation window**

“Choosing the length of the observation or estimation window is also part of the art of regression hedging. Too short a window might fail to furnish statistically reliable estimates, but too long a window might include less relevant historical data.”

**Step 2 – GARP on which period is relevant**

If the Fed is expected to raise rates, an earlier tightening episode may be more relevant than a recent period of unchanged rates.

**Interpretation**

C states the trade-off and the possibility that an earlier period is more relevant. The other three statements each turn a judgement into an absolute.

**LO:** MR-11 b: Describe a regression hedge and explain how it can improve a standard DV01-neutral hedge. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Tuckman), 11.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 b.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim: more data reduce standard errors but may bring in irrelevant regimes.

b.reason: Unbiasedness is an in-sample property under the model’s assumptions; poor out-of-sample performance is exactly how unstable coeﬀicients show up, so out-of-sample tests matter.

d.reason: The regression hedge assumes a constant beta, and the recent past is not relevant “by definition”.
