questions.question:
A risk analyst has four months of daily yield changes for a 40-year corporate bond, which is to be hedged, and for a 30-year Treasury bond, the hedging instrument. The summary statistics are:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Standard deviation of corporate yield changes | 4.20 bp |
| Standard deviation of Treasury yield changes | 4.40 bp |
| Mean daily change, corporate / Treasury | 0.10 bp / 0.05 bp |
| $R^{2}$ of the regression of corporate on Treasury yield changes (positive slope) | 77.5% |

Which of the following is closest to the regression hedge adjustment factor, $\beta$?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Correlation from** $R^{2}$

In a one-variable regression $R^{2} = \rho^{2}$: $\rho= \sqrt{0.775} = 0.8803$ (positive slope).

**Step 2 – Beta**

$$\hat{\beta} = \rho\frac{\sigma_{\text{corp}}}{\sigma_{\text{Tsy}}} = 0.8803 \times\frac{4.20}{4.40} = 0.840$$

⇒ The corporate yield moves about 0.84 bp per Treasury basis point, close to GARP’s 0.842 for JNJ.

**Interpretation**

The mean daily changes are a red herring: they determine the intercept, not the slope.

**LO:** MR-11 c: Calculate the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.1 (in a one-variable regression $R^{2}$ is the squared correlation)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Tuckman), 11.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 c.3)

c.reason: Took the correlation as the hedge ratio: $\sqrt{0.775} = 0.880$.

d.reason: Inverted the volatility ratio: 0.8803×4.40/4.20 = 0.922, which is what a reverse regression of the Treasury on the corporate would give.

questions.question:
A relative value trader at a Canadian dealer buys CAD 50 million face amount of a 30-year provincial bond for a client and hedges the interest rate risk by selling the Government of Canada 30-year benchmark bond. The desk’s risk analyst supplies the following:

- DV01 per 100 face: provincial bond 0.1835; Government of Canada bond 0.2010
- Regression of daily changes in the provincial yield on daily changes in the Government of Canada yield (bp), 90 observations: constant 0.08 (std. error 0.21); slope 0.91 (std. error 0.04); $R^{2}$ 81%; standard error of the regression 1.6 bp

Which of the following is closest to the face amount of the Government of Canada bond the trader should sell under a regression hedge, and to the standard deviation of the daily P&L of the hedged position?

options.text: CAD 41.54 million; CAD 133,588
CAD 41.54 million; CAD 146,800
CAD 45.19 million; CAD 146,800
CAD 45.65 million; CAD 146,800

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – DV01 ratio**

$P$

$$\frac{\text{DV01}}{\text{DV01}^{H}} = \frac{0.1835}{0.2010} = 0.91294$$

⇒ Per unit of face, the provincial bond moves 0.913 times as much as the benchmark for the same yield change.

**Step 2 – Regression hedge face amount**

$P$

$$F^{H} = -F^{P} \frac{\text{DV01}}{\text{DV01}^{H}} \hat{\beta} = -50 \times0.91294 \times0.91 = -41.54$$

⇒ Sell CAD 41.54 million. The hedge ratio per unit of face is 0.91294 × 0.91 = 0.831, and the risk weight (hedge DV01 over position DV01) equals $\hat{\beta} = 91\%$.

**Step 3 – DV01 of the hedged position**

$$\frac{F^{P} \text{DV01}^{P}}{100} = \frac{50{,}000{,}000 \times0.1835}{100} = 91{,}750$$

**Step 4 – Hedged P&L volatility**

$$\sigma_{P \&L} = 91{,}750 \times1.6 = 146{,}800$$

⇒ Each 1 bp residual (the provincial yield moving 1 bp more than 0.91 times the benchmark change) costs CAD 91,750, so a 1.6 bp residual volatility gives about CAD 146,800 per day.

**Interpretation**

The slope’s 95% interval, 0.91 ± 2(0.04) = (0.83, 0.99), excludes one, so the data reject parallel shifts and the DV01-neutral hedge over-hedges. The constant’s interval, 0.08 ± 0.42, includes zero and the constant plays no part in the hedge. Whether CAD 146,800 per day is acceptable depends on the spread the trader earns and the holding period.

**LO:** MR-11 c: Calculate the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta. MR-11 d: Calculate the face value of an offsetting position needed to carry out a regression hedge. MR-11 a. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.1, eqs. 11.8 to 11.12, Tables 11.1 and 11.2

**Source:** Workbook C1.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #23 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 c.4)

a.reason: Correct face amount, but computed the P&L volatility with the DV01 of the hedge leg: $41.54\text{m} \times0.2010/100 \times1.6 = 133{,}588$, which is $\hat{\beta}$ times the right answer.

c.reason: Added the intercept to the slope: 50 × 0.91294 × (0.08 + 0.91) = 45.19. The constant is a red herring for the hedge ratio.

d.reason: Dropped $\beta\hat{:} 50 \times0.91294 = 45.65$ is the DV01-neutral hedge, which assumes parallel yield shifts.

questions.question: A portfolio manager is short USD 80 million face of a 10-year agency bond (DV01 0.0870 per 100 face) and hedges with the 10-year Treasury note (DV01 0.0905 per 100 face). A regression of daily changes in the agency yield on daily changes in the Treasury yield gives a constant of −0.03, a slope of 1.15, an $R^{2}$ of 88% and a standard error of 1.4 bp. Which trade implements the regression hedge?

options.text: Buy USD 66.88 million of the Treasury note.
Buy USD 76.91 million of the Treasury note.
Buy USD 88.44 million of the Treasury note.
Sell USD 88.44 million of the Treasury note.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Sign of the position**

$F^{P} = -80$ (short), so $F^{H} = -F^{P} \times\cdots$ is positive: **buy** the Treasury.

**Step 2 – DV01 hedge**

80 × 0.0870/0.0905 = 76.91.

**Step 3 – Regression hedge**

$76.91 \times1.15 = \text{USD} 88.44$ million.

⇒ The agency yield moves 1.15 bp per Treasury basis point, so the hedge needs 15% more Treasury DV01 than the position’s DV01.

**Interpretation**

The constant, $R^{2}$ and standard error do not enter the face amount (the standard error gives the hedged P&L volatility: $80\text{m} \times0.0870/100 \times1.4 = \$97{,}440$ per day).

**LO:** MR-11 d: Calculate the face value of an offsetting position needed to carry out a regression hedge. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.1, eqs. 11.7 and 11.8

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Tuckman), eq. 11.8 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 d.4)

a.reason: Divided by beta: 76.91/1.15 = 66.88.

b.reason: Dropped beta: 76.91, the DV01 hedge.

d.reason: Right size, wrong direction: a short position is hedged by buying.

questions.question:
A risk manager reviews the PCA of USD swap rates below (share of each rate’s variance, in percent):

| Term | Level | Slope | Short rate | Three PCs / total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-year | 32.7 | 15.0 | 52.3 | 74.54 |
| 4-year | 69.1 | 29.7 | 1.2 | 99.72 |
| 9-year | 99.3 | 0.2 | 0.6 | 99.92 |
| 30-year | 87.9 | 11.3 | 0.8 | 99.93 |
| All 13 rates | 91.3 | 7.8 | 0.8 | 99.84 |

Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with these results?

options.text: A trader of 8- to 10-year swaps can reasonably defend a one-factor (level) hedge, while traders in the 3- to 6-year sector or at the long end may need two factors and the very short end may need three.
Because the level PC explains over 90% of the total variance, a single-factor hedge is adequate at every point of the curve, including the one-year sector.
The short-rate PC is most important at the long end of the curve, where it explains the largest share of each rate’s variance.
Because three PCs explain 99.84% of the total variance, hedging a position with any three swaps removes all but 0.16% of its risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where one factor is enough**

At 9 years the level PC explains 99.3% of the variance (GARP: 98.2 to 99.5% from 8 to 10 years), so a one-factor hedge is defensible there.

**Step 2 – Where it is not**

At 4 years the slope PC explains 29.7%; at 30 years 11.3%: two factors may be needed. At 1 year the short-rate PC explains 52.3% and three PCs together only 74.54%: the very short end may need three.

**Interpretation**

A is GARP’s own conclusion from Table 11.5.

**LO:** MR-11 h: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.5, Table 11.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11 (Tuckman), Table 11.5 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 h.4)

b.reason: The 91.3% is a total across all rates; at the one-year point the level PC explains only 32.7%.

c.reason: The short-rate PC matters at the short end (52.3% at 1 year, 0.8% at 30 years).

d.reason: The 99.84% describes the rates’ variance, not the risk left after an arbitrary three-swap hedge; a hedge must be solved to neutralise the PC exposures.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the hedging methodology of a bank’s swap desk. Single-bond positions are currently hedged DV01-neutral, and the desk proposes to hedge its 10s/20s/30s butterflies using principal component analysis (PCA) of swap rates, with the 10-year and 30-year swaps as the two hedging instruments. Which of the following statements should the consultant include in the report?

options.text: A DV01-neutral hedge minimizes the variance of the hedged P&L, because by construction the DV01 of the hedge equals the DV01 of the position being hedged.
A PCA hedge is eﬀicient because the principal components are constructed to be highly correlated, so neutralizing the level PC also neutralizes the others.
A PCA hedge using two hedging swaps can neutralize exposure to only two PCs, so the residual exposure to the third PC must be measured and either accepted or hedged.
A PCA hedge of the butterfly sets the risk weights of the two hedging swaps so that they always sum to 100% of the DV01 of the position being hedged.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a DV01-neutral hedge assumes**

Equal DV01s on both sides (risk weight 100%) is the right hedge only if the two yields move in parallel. The book rejects $\beta= 1$ for JNJ versus the 30-year Treasury (interval 0.740 to 0.944).

**Step 2 – Which hedge minimises variance**

The regression hedge, with risk weight $\beta\hat{,}$ minimises the variance of the hedged P&L (Appendix A6.1). The DV01 hedge does so only in the special case $\hat{\beta} = 1$.

**Step 3 – How many PCs two securities can hedge**

Each hedged PC adds one equation (11.30, 11.31); two hedging swaps solve two equations. The book measures the residual short-rate exposure at 0.007 per 100 and notes the trader may accept it or add a 15-year swap and a third equation.

**Interpretation**

C is correct: it states the counting rule and the follow-up decision that the book models.

**LO:** MR-11 a, MR-11 b; MR-11 h: Describe principal component analysis and explain how it is applied to constructing a hedging portfolio. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.6, 11.1 and 11.5, eqs. 11.30 to 11.34

**Source:** Workbook C1.2 • S3, S4, S5 • Map #23 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-11 h.5)

a.reason: Sibling swap. Variance minimisation is the property of the regression hedge; equal DV01s minimise variance only if yields shift in parallel.

b.reason: Polarity flip. PCs are constructed to be uncorrelated; that is why each needs its own neutralising equation.

d.reason: Absolute claim. Only under parallel shifts do risk weights always sum to 100%; the book’s PCA butterfly needs 27.1% + 74.1% = 101.2%.

questions.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
questions.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
questions.topic: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.12, 12.2 to 12.3
questions.question: A fixed-income analyst values a call option that expires in six months and gives the right to buy USD 1,000 face value of a then six-month zero-coupon bond at USD 990. The six-month rate is 2.00% today and will be 2.50% or 1.50% in six months, each with a true probability of 0.50. The one-year zero trades at USD 978.842, and on date 1 a six-month zero is worth USD 987.654 in the up state and USD 992.556 in the down state. Which of the following is closest to the option’s price, with the correct reason?

options.text: USD 1.27, because expected discounted value under the true probabilities is the arbitrage price.
USD 0.50, because the risk-neutral up probability of 0.8009 leaves a weight of 0.1991 on the only state where the option pays.
USD 0.50, because investors’ risk aversion lowers the true probability of the down state below 0.50.
USD 2.53, because the option pays USD 2.556 in the down state, discounted at the six-month rate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Option payoffs on date 1**

Up: max(987.654 − 990, 0) = 0. Down: 992.556 − 990 = 2.556.

**Step 2 – Risk-neutral probability from the one-year zero**

$$\frac{p(987.654) + (1 - p)(992.556)}{1.01} = 978.842 \Rightarrow p = 0.8009, 1 - p = 0.1991$$

⇒ The market prices the one-year zero below its true expected discounted value (980.302), and $p$ captures that penalty.

**Step 3 – Price by expected discounted value under** $p$

$\frac{0.8009 \times0 + 0.1991 \times2.556}{1.01} = \$0.504$

**Interpretation**

The same \$0.504 comes from the replicating portfolio (long 521.4375 face of one-year zeros, short 515.00 of six-month zeros). The true probabilities of 0.50 never enter the arbitrage price; they matter only through the one-year zero’s market price.

**LO:** MR-12 d: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e (GARP MR Ch.12), 12.2 and 12.3, eqs. 12.5 to 12.8

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.12, 12.2 to 12.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-12 d.1)

a.reason: Used the true probabilities: 0.5×2.556/1.01 = 1.27. That is expected discounted value, not the arbitrage price.

c.reason: Right number, wrong reason: risk aversion does not change the true probabilities. It is the risk-neutral probabilities that shift weight to the up (high-rate) state.

d.reason: Discounted the down-state payoff as if it were certain: 2.556/1.01 = 2.53.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift.
questions.reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
questions.topic: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
questions.source: New • built from GARP MR Ch.12, 12.2 to 12.4
questions.question: A junior analyst is reviewing a binomial tree for the six-month rate that a desk uses to price interest rate derivatives. Which of the following statements about true and risk-neutral probabilities is correct?

options.text: Risk-neutral probabilities are the market’s best forecasts of future rate moves, which is why they recover market prices.
Any tree whose up probability differs from 0.50 is a risk-neutral tree, since true probabilities are always 0.50.
Risk-neutral probabilities put extra weight on high-rate, low-price states, so the risk-neutral drift exceeds the true drift.
The arbitrage price of an option on a zero depends directly on the true probabilities of the up and down moves.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What risk-neutral probabilities are**

They are the probabilities that make expected discounted values equal market prices. Because investors pay less than expected discounted value for risky bonds, these probabilities must put more weight on states where bond prices are low, that is, where rates are high.

⇒ Higher weight on the up-rate move means a positive risk-neutral drift: GARP’s 30.09 bp against 0 under the true 0.5.

**Step 2 – Test each statement**

A calls them forecasts; B turns the textbook’s 0.5 into a rule; D says option prices depend directly on true probabilities. Only C survives.

**Interpretation**

The gap between risk-neutral and true drift is the tree’s way of carrying the risk premium for bearing rate risk.

**LO:** MR-12 d: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e (GARP MR Ch.12), 12.2 to 12.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.12, 12.2 to 12.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-12 d.2)

a.reason: Risk-neutral probabilities are not forecasts. They embed investors’ aversion to price risk, which is exactly why they differ from true probabilities.

b.reason: Absolute claim. True probabilities need not be 0.5; a probability is risk-neutral because it recovers market prices, not because of its value.

d.reason: The replicating portfolio, and so the arbitrage price, does not depend directly on true probabilities; they enter only through current bond prices.

questions.question: A risk manager uses a recombining tree in which the six-month rate is 2.00% today and moves up or down by 50 bp every six months. The true probability of an up move is 0.50 at every node. The risk-neutral probability of an up move, solved to recover the one-year and 1.5-year zero prices, is 0.8009 from date 0 and 0.6520 from either date-1 node. Under the risk-neutral process, which of the following is closest to the expected six-month rate one year from now (date 2) and its cumulative drift relative to the true process?

options.text: 2.00%; zero drift, because the up and down moves are symmetric
2.30%; drift of 30 bp
2.45%; drift of 45 bp
2.60%; drift of 60 bp

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Drift from date 0 to date 1**

(2 × 0.8009 − 1) × 50 = +30.09 bp $\Rightarrow E[r_{1}] = 2.3009\%$

**Step 2 – Drift from date 1 to date 2 (its own probability)**

(2 × 0.6520 − 1) × 50 = +15.20 bp from either date-1 node

**Step 3 – Expected rate on date 2**

$$E[r_{2}] = 2.00\% + 0.3009\% + 0.1520\% = 2.4529\% \approx2.45\%$$

⇒ Cumulative risk-neutral drift of about 45 bp, against zero under the true probabilities.

**Interpretation**

The true probabilities (0.50) are in the stem only as a temptation. The second-step probability is solved from the 1.5-year zero and is lower than the first.

a.reason: Used the true probabilities: symmetric moves, zero drift.

b.reason: Stopped after the first step: 2.00% + 0.30%.

The swap is quoted in the market at an OAS of −10 bp. Which of the following is closest to its market price, and how does it trade?

options.text: USD 2,719.83; the swap trades rich
USD 3,699.18; the swap trades rich
USD 3,705.03; the swap trades cheap
USD 3,705.03; the swap trades rich

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Payments (unshifted rates)**

Date 1: +2,500 (2.50%) and −2,500 (1.50%). Date 2: +5,000, 0, −5,000.

**Step 2 – Date-1 values, discounting at the node rate minus 10 bp**

$$V_{1,u} = \frac{0.6520(5{,}000) + 0.3480(0)}{1 + 0.0240/2} + 2{,}500 = 5{,}721.11$$

$$V_{1,d} = \frac{0.6520(0) + 0.3480(-5{,}000)}{1 + 0.0140/2} - 2{,}500 = -4{,}228.14$$

**Step 3 – Date-0 value at 1.90%**

$$V_{0} = \frac{0.8009(5{,}721.11) + 0.1991(-4{,}228.14)}{1 + 0.0190/2} = 3{,}705.03$$

⇒ The market price is USD 2.92 above the model value: negative OAS, rich.

**Interpretation**

GARP’s model and Figure 12.8 use the unrounded $q = 0.65195$; with $q = 0.6520$ each value is about USD 0.2 higher. Either way the answer is closest to D.

b.reason: Added +10 bp instead of −10 bp: 3,699.18 is GARP’s value at a positive OAS.

c.reason: Right price, wrong label: a negative OAS means the market price is above the model value, so rich.

questions.question: A relative value analyst models a mortgage-related security on a semiannual binomial tree. The six-month rate today is 4.00%, and the security trades at an option-adjusted spread of −20 bp. Assuming the OAS is expected to stay constant, which of the following is closest to the security’s expected return over the next six months under the risk-neutral process?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Expected return with an OAS**

$$E[\frac{dP}{P}] = (r_{0} + \text{OAS}) dt = (4.00\% - 0.20\%) \times\frac{1}{2} = 1.90\%$$

⇒ A rich security (negative OAS) is expected to earn less than the short rate.

**Interpretation**

GARP’s version: 2% short rate and +10 bp OAS give 1.05% over six months. “Mortgage-related” is background only.

b.reason: Ignored the OAS: 4.00%/2.

c.reason: Added the spread with the wrong sign: (4.00% + 0.20%)/2.

d.reason: Gave the annual rate $r_{0} + \text{OAS} = 3.80\%$, not the six-month return.

questions.question: A relative value trader identifies a bond that trades at an OAS of +15 bp under the desk’s term structure model. She buys it, hedges all of its factor (interest rate) risk so that $\partial P /\partial r = 0$, and finances the purchase by borrowing at the short-term rate. If the model is correct, what does the position’s expected return consist of?

options.text: The OAS plus any gain from the OAS converging toward zero.
The short-term rate plus the OAS, whatever the financing cost.
The risk premium on interest rate risk plus the OAS.
The short-term rate only, because the factor risk is hedged.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Attribution**

$dP = (r_{0} + \text{OAS})P dt + \frac{\partial P}{\partial r}(dr - E[dr]) + \frac{\partial P}{\partial\text{OAS}}d$OAS.

**Step 2 – Apply the trade**

Hedged: $\partial P /\partial r = 0$, so the rate term drops. Financed at $r_{0}$: the short-rate part of the carry is paid away.

⇒ What is left is the OAS, plus the gain $\frac{\partial P}{\partial\text{OAS}} d$OAS if the OAS converges toward zero.

**Interpretation**

This is why the OAS is used as a relative value measure: a model with predictive power implies cheap securities converge to fair value.

**LO:** MR-12 f: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e (GARP MR Ch.12), 12.7, eqs. 12.36 and 12.37

MR-12 • Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.12, 12.7 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-12 f.6)

b.reason: Financing at the short rate cancels the short-rate component.

c.reason: Risk premium terms cancel when factor risk is hedged away.

d.reason: Ignores the OAS that the cheap security earns.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a European bank values a one-year stylized CMT swap on the six-month yield with notional USD 2,000,000 and strike 4.00%. The bank receives USD $2{,}000{,}000\times(y_{\text{CMT}} -$ 4.00%)/2 every six months (a negative amount is paid). The model’s recombining tree has the six-month rate at 4.00% today, moving up or down by 40 bp each six months. The risk-neutral probability of an up move is 0.65 from date 0 and 0.58 from either date-1 node; the desk’s estimate of the true probability is 0.50 at every node. Which of the following is closest to the value of the swap?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Payments**

Date 1: 2,000,000 × (±0.40%)/2 = ±\$4,000. Date 2: +\$8,000 (4.80%), \$0 (4.00%), −\$8,000 (3.20%).

**Step 2 – Date-1 values (probability 0.58)**

$$V_{1,u} = \frac{0.58(8{,}000) + 0.42(0)}{1.022} + 4{,}000 = 8{,}540.12$$

$$V_{1,d} = \frac{0.58(0) + 0.42(-8{,}000)}{1.018} - 4{,}000 = -7{,}300.59$$

**Step 3 – Date-0 value (probability 0.65)**

$V_{0} = \frac{0.65(8{,}540.12) + 0.35(-7{,}300.59)}{1.02} = \$2{,}937.13$

**Interpretation**

The swap is struck at today’s rate, yet worth about USD 2,900 to the receiver of the floating yield, because the risk-neutral process drifts up (+12 bp, then +6.4 bp). The true probabilities are a red herring.

b.reason: Left out the date-1 payments of ±\$4,000: \$1,760.66.

d.reason: Reused 0.65 at date 1 instead of 0.58: \$3,475.07.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a US insurer is checking the desk’s mark on a one-year stylized constant-maturity Treasury (CMT) swap on the six-month yield. The insurer receives, every six months for one year, USD $5{,}000{,}000 \times(y_{\text{CMT}} - 2.80\%)/2$, where $y_{\text{CMT}}$ is the six-month rate on the payment date (a negative amount is paid). The desk’s recombining tree of six-month rates (semiannually compounded) and its probabilities are:

- Date 0: 3.00%. Date 1: 3.60% (up) or 2.40% (down). Date 2: 4.20%, 3.00% or 1.80%
- Risk-neutral probability of an up move: 0.70 from date 0; 0.60 from either date-1 node
- Estimated true probability of an up move at every node: 0.50

The pricing system reports that the swap trades in the market at an option-adjusted spread (OAS) of +25 bp. Which of the following is closest to the swap’s market price, and how does it trade relative to the model?

options.text: USD 24,328; the swap trades cheap
USD 24,328; the swap trades rich
USD 9,719; the swap trades cheap
USD 36,523; the swap trades cheap

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – CMT payments (from the unshifted tree rates)**

Date 1: $5{,}000{,}000 \times\frac{3.60\%-2.80\%}{2} = 20{,}000$; $5{,}000{,}000 \times\frac{2.40\%-2.80\%}{2} = -10{,}000$.

Date 2: 35,000 (4.20%); 5,000 (3.00%); −25,000 (1.80%).

⇒ The OAS does not touch these: rates are shifted only for discounting.

**Step 2 – Date-1 values, discounting at the tree rate plus 25 bp**

$$V_{1,u} = \frac{0.60(35{,}000) + 0.40(5{,}000)}{1 + 0.0385/2} + 20{,}000 = \frac{23{,}000}{1.01925} + 20{,}000 = 42{,}565.61$$

$V_{1,d} = \frac{0.60(5{,}000) + 0.40(-25{,}000)}{1 + 0.0265/2} - 10{,}000 = \frac{-7{,}000}{1.01325} - 10{,}000 = -16{,}908.46$

⇒ Each node value is the discounted risk-neutral expectation of the next payment plus the payment made at that node.

**Step 3 – Date-0 value at the OAS**

$$V_{0} = \frac{0.70(42{,}565.61) + 0.30(-16{,}908.46)}{1 + 0.0325/2} = \frac{24{,}723.39}{1.01625} = 24{,}328.06$$

**Step 4 – Compare with the model value (zero OAS)**

Repeating Steps 2 and 3 at the unshifted rates gives date-1 values 42,593.32 and −16,916.99 and a model value of USD 24,374.61. The market price, 24,328, is USD 46.55 below the model value, consistent with a positive OAS: the swap trades cheap.

**Interpretation**

The swap is worth far more than zero although its strike, 2.80%, sits below a 3.00% starting rate and the true probabilities are symmetric. The reason is the risk-neutral drift: (2×0.70−1)×60 = 24 bp from date 0 and (2 × 0.60 − 1) × 60 = 12 bp from date 1, against zero under the true probabilities. If the model is right, a hedged, financed long position earns the 25 bp OAS plus any convergence of the OAS to zero; under the risk-neutral process the expected six-month return is (3.00% + 0.25%)/2 = 1.625%.

**LO:** MR-12 h: Calculate the value of a constant-maturity Treasury swap, given an interest rate tree and the risk-neutral probabilities. MR-12 f: Define option-adjusted spread (OAS) and apply it to security pricing. MR-12 d: Explain the difference between true and risk-neutral probabilities and apply this difference to interest rate drift. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.7 (GARP MR Ch.12), 12.3, 12.5 and 12.6, eqs. 12.18 to 12.31, Figure 12.8

MR-13 • Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook C7.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #33 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-12 h.6)

b.reason: Polarity flip on the OAS sign. A positive OAS means the market price is below the model price, so the swap is cheap, not rich.

c.reason: Used the true probabilities of 0.50 at every node (with the OAS): date-1 values 39,622.27 and −19,869.23, date-0 value 9,718.59. Real-world probabilities do not recover market prices.

d.reason: Added the OAS to the CMT yields that set the payments as well as to the discount rates: payments become 26,250, −3,750, 41,250, 11,250 and −18,750, giving 36,522.75.

questions.question: A rates strategist assumes that the current one-year rate is 8%, that investors know with certainty that the one-year rate will be 7% in one year and 6% in two years, and that investors are risk neutral. Which of the following statements about the term structure implied by these assumptions is correct?

options.text: The one-year forward rates are 8%, 7% and 6%, so the forward curve slopes downward and is completely determined by expectations.
The spot curve is flat, because each spot rate is an average of the same three expected one-year rates.
Forward rates lie below the expected one-year rates, because bond prices are convex in interest rates.
Forward rates lie above the expected one-year rates, because investors demand compensation for holding longer bonds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Price the zeros on the certain path**

$P (1) = 1/1.08$, $P (2) = 1/(1.08 \times1.07)$, $P (3) = 1/(1.08 \times1.07 \times1.06)$.

**Step 2 – Read off the forward rates**

$1 + f_{t} = P (t - 1)/P (t)$ gives forwards of 8%, 7% and 6%: exactly the expected one-year rates.

⇒ With certainty, the term structure is completely determined by expectations; here it slopes downward.

**Interpretation**

The spot rates are 8%, $\sqrt{1.08 \times1.07} - 1 = 7.50\%$ and $(1.08 \times1.07 \times1.06)^{1/3} - 1 = 7.00\%$: also falling. The assumptions remove both other forces on the curve: certainty removes volatility (so no convexity effect), and risk neutrality removes the premium.

**LO:** MR-13 a: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Fixed Income Securities 4e, Ch.8, 13.1, eq. 13.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.13, 13.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 a.1)

b.reason: Each spot rate averages a different set of expected rates (one, two or three of them), so the spot curve falls: 8.00%, 7.50%, 7.00%.

c.reason: The convexity effect needs volatility; with certain rates there is none, so forwards equal expected rates exactly.

d.reason: A risk premium is excluded by the risk-neutrality assumption, and in any case it is not what makes this curve slope.

questions.question: A strategist at a pension fund is building a 30-year forward curve. Her team has detailed views on the next four central bank meetings, on tax payment dates and on quarter-end funding pressure. Her economist estimates a long-run real rate of 1% and long-run inflation of 3%. Which of the following is the most appropriate use of these views?

options.text: Use the short-horizon views to shape the front of the curve, and the 4% macroeconomic estimate to anchor the level of long-horizon expected rates.
Use the short-horizon views to project how the expected one-year rate in 29 years differs from the expected one-year rate in 30 years.
Use the macroeconomic estimate to set both the level and the detailed shape of the long end, because inflation forecasts are as granular as meeting-date views.
Ignore expectations beyond one year, because the long end of the curve is determined by convexity alone.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What short-horizon views can do**

Views tied to central bank meeting dates and the supply and demand for funds (tax dates, issuance calendar, quarter-end balance sheets) are specific, so they can shape the front of the curve.

**Step 2 – What long-horizon views can do**

Expectations far out are not granular, but macroeconomics can anchor the long-run level: 1% + 3% = 4% for the expected short rate.

⇒ Short-horizon views for shape at the front, the macro anchor for the level at the back.

**Interpretation**

This is GARP’s own example: the long-run expected short rate of 4% is “1% due to the long-run real rate of interest and 3% due to long-run inflation”.

**LO:** MR-13 a: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.13, 13.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 a.3)

b.reason: Money market analysis is “unlikely to reveal” a difference between the expected one-year rate in 29 and in 30 years.

c.reason: Macroeconomic estimates anchor the level; they are not granular enough to give the long end a detailed shape.

d.reason: Absolute claim: expectations still set the level of the long end, and the risk premium also acts there.

questions.question: An analyst explains two theories of the term structure using the decomposition $f(T ) = r_{0} +$ $D E[dr]/dt + \lambda D - \frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2}$, setting the convexity term aside. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Under the pure expectations hypothesis, $\lambda= 0$, and the natural no-change scenario is that short-term rates evolve as expected so that forward rates are realized.
Under the pure expectations hypothesis, $E[dr/dt] = 0$, and the natural no-change scenario is that the term structure stays unchanged.
Under the pure risk premium hypothesis, forward rates are set by expected rate changes, so an upward-sloping curve signals that rates are expected to rise.
Under the pure risk premium hypothesis, the natural no-change scenario is that short-term rates evolve so that forward rates are realized.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Pure expectations**

$\lambda= 0$, so forwards are set by expectations, $E[dr/dt]$. The natural no-change scenario: short rates evolve as expected and **forward rates are realized**.

**Step 2 – Pure risk premium**

$E[dr/dt] = 0$, so forwards are set by the risk premium. The natural no-change scenario: short rates stay the same and the **term structure is unchanged**.

⇒ A matches Step 1 exactly.

**Interpretation**

GARP notes that reality lies between the two extremes: the curve is set by a mix of expectations and risk premium (plus convexity).

**LO:** MR-13 a: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.3, eq. 13.20

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.13, 13.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 a.4)

b.reason: Sibling swap: $E[dr/dt] = 0$ and an unchanged curve belong to the pure risk premium hypothesis.

c.reason: Under pure risk premium there are no expected rate changes, so an upward slope reflects the premium, not expected rises.

d.reason: Sibling swap: “forward rates are realized” is the pure expectations no-change scenario.

questions.question: After a central bank announcement, a portfolio manager observes that forward rates have risen, by more at longer terms. She wants to attribute the move between a higher expected path of short-term rates and a higher risk premium. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Forward rates alone cannot split the move, because a drift of a given number of basis points has the same pricing effect as a risk premium of that number per year of duration.
The move must be a higher risk premium, because a higher expected path of short-term rates would raise all forward rates by the same amount.
The move must reflect higher expected rates, because a risk premium depends on the characteristics of individual bonds rather than on duration.
The two can be separated by comparing forward rates with the risk-neutral probabilities used in a pricing tree.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Both terms scale with duration**

Expectations enter $f(T )$ as $D E[dr]/dt$ and the risk premium as $\lambda D$. Both raise forwards more at longer terms.

**Step 2 – They are indistinguishable in prices**

“Increasing the risk premium or increasing the expected short-term rate by the same amount are indistinguishable from the observation of forward rates.”

⇒ The split is not observable from a cross-section of bond prices alone; only the risk-neutral drift is.

**Interpretation**

The split may be useful for economic analysis or macro trading, but it cannot be read from the curve. From a modelling perspective, only the risk-neutral process matters for pricing.

**LO:** MR-13 a: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.3, eqs. 13.18 and 13.20

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.13, 13.3 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 a.5)

b.reason: The expectations term is scaled by duration too, so expected rate rises do not move all forwards equally.

c.reason: The premium depends on time and the level of rates, “but not on the characteristics of any individual bond”; it enters as $\lambda D$.

d.reason: Risk-neutral probabilities embed the combined drift; they do not reveal how much of it is expectation and how much premium.

Using the decomposition of forward rates into expectations, risk premium and convexity, which of the following statements should the analyst include in the report?

The higher risk premium raises all forward rates by the same number of basis points, because the premium per unit of duration does not depend on any individual bond.
Observed forward rates allow the analyst to fully separate the part of the move due to higher expected inflation from the part due to a higher risk premium.
Higher expected short-term rates and a higher risk premium each raise forward rates in proportion to duration, so long-dated gilts lose more value than short-dated gilts.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Expectations term**

Expectations part of $f(T )$: $r_{0} + D E[dr]/dt$.

⇒ Higher expected inflation raises expected short rates; the effect on the forward rate is scaled by the duration of the zero of that term, so it is largest at the long end.

**Step 2 – Risk premium term**

Risk premium part of $f(T )$: $\lambda D$.

⇒ A higher $\lambda$ raises every forward rate by $\lambda$ times its duration: again largest at the long end.

**Step 3 – Convexity term**

Convexity part of $f(T )$: $-\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2}$.

⇒ Higher volatility pushes long forwards down, partly offsetting Steps 1 and 2 for long bonds; it does not add to their losses.

**Step 4 – Effect on bond values**

From $dP /P = f(T ) dt-D dr + \frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2} dt$, a rise in rates reduces value in proportion to duration, so long-dated gilts lose more than short-dated gilts. IM-2 b reaches the same direction from the asset-pricing side: high inflation is bad for bonds because their payments are fixed.

**Interpretation**

A climate shock has no formula of its own in the 2026 readings; it is read through the same three terms: expected inflation (expectations), uncertainty (volatility, convexity) and required compensation (risk premium).

**LO:** MR-13 a: Explain the role of interest rate expectations in determining the shape of the term structure. MR-13 b, c, d. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.1 to 13.3, eqs. 13.15 to 13.20; Ang, Ch.7 (IM-2 b), Table 2.1

MR-13 • Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook D18.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #72 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 a.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip. The convexity term $-\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2}$ lowers long forward rates when volatility rises; volatility supports long bond prices rather than cheapening them.

b.reason: Scope/condition error. $\lambda$ is common to all bonds, but the premium enters as $\lambda D$; dropping the duration condition makes the effect look parallel.

c.reason: Absolute claim. The term structure cannot, on its own, separate expectations of rate changes from risk premium; only their combined risk-neutral drift is observable.

questions.question: A risk analyst prices a two-year zero-coupon bond on a risk-neutral tree with no risk premium. The one-year rate is 8% today and will be 10% or 6% in one year with equal probability. To stress volatility she widens the year-1 nodes to 11% or 5%, keeping the expected one-year rate at 8%. Which of the following is closest to the change in the implied two-year spot rate caused by the stress?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Base tree (10% or 6%)**

$P (2) = 0.5(1/1.10 + 1/1.06)/1.08 = 0.857633$; spot $= (1/0.857633)^{1/2} - 1 = 7.9815\%$.

**Step 2 – Stressed tree (11% or 5%)**

$P (2) = 0.5(1/1.11 + 1/1.05)/1.08 = 0.858000$; spot $= (1/0.858000)^{1/2} - 1 = 7.9583\%$.

**Step 3 – Change**

7.9583% − 7.9815% = −0.023% = −2.3 bp.

⇒ More volatility, same expectations: higher price, lower yield.

**Interpretation**

The value of convexity rises from about 1.85 bp to about 4.2 bp. The question asks for the change in the spot rate, which is the difference between the two.

**LO:** MR-13 b: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure.

questions.question: A portfolio manager uses a risk-neutral binomial tree with annual steps and 50% transition probabilities. The one-year rate is 9% today; in one year it is 13% or 5%; in two years it is 17%, 9% or 1%. The expected one-year rate is therefore 9% at every date. The tree prices the two-year zero at 0.842815 and the three-year zero at 0.776366. Which of the following is closest to the one-year rate one year forward implied by the tree?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – One-year zero**

$P (1) = 1/1.09 = 0.917431$.

**Step 2 – Forward from zero prices**

$$1 + f(2) = \frac{P (1)}{P (2)} = \frac{0.917431}{0.842815} = 1.088532 \Rightarrow f(2) = 8.85\%$$

⇒ Below the 9% expected rate, exactly as Jensen’s inequality requires ($f < 9\%$).

**Interpretation**

The forward curve is 9.00%, 8.85%, 8.56%: it slopes down although expectations are flat, purely because volatility interacts with the convexity of bond prices. The 400 bp per-step volatility is exaggerated on purpose to make this visible.

**LO:** MR-13 c: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.2, Figure 13.1, Table 13.1, eqs. 13.6 to 13.8

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.13, Figure 13.1 and Table 13.1 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 c.5)

a.reason: 8.56% is the next forward, 0.842815/0.776366 − 1: the rate two years forward, not one.

c.reason: 8.93% is the two-year spot rate, $(1/0.842815)^{1/2} - 1$, an average of 9.00% and 8.85%, not the forward.

d.reason: The expected rate: it ignores Jensen’s inequality, which puts the forward below the expectation.

questions.question: A risk-neutral tree has a one-year rate of 8% today; 10% or 6% in one year; and 12%, 8% or 4% in two years, with 50% probabilities on every branch. On this tree the value of convexity for the two-year zero-coupon bond is about 1.85 basis points. Which of the following is closest to the value of convexity for the three-year zero-coupon bond?

options.text: 1.9 bp
2.8 bp
4.9 bp

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Date-2 prices of a one-year zero**

1/1.12 = 0.89286, 1/1.08 = 0.92593, 1/1.04 = 0.96154.

**Step 2 – Date-1 prices of the then two-year zero**

Up (10%): 0.5(0.89286 + 0.92593)/1.10 = 0.82672; down (6%): 0.5(0.92593 + 0.96154)/1.06 = 0.89031.

**Step 3 – Today’s price and spot rate**

$P (3) = 0.5(0.82672 + 0.89031)/1.08 = 0.79492$; $(1/0.79492)^{1/3} - 1 = 7.9506\%$.

**Step 4 – Value of convexity**

8% − 7.9506% = 0.0494% ≈ 4.9 bp.

⇒ Against 1.85 bp for the two-year zero: the value of convexity increases with maturity (shape D12 S3).

**Interpretation**

Schweser rounds this to “5 basis points”. Going from two to three years more than doubles the effect (1.85 bp to 4.9 bp): convexity grows faster than maturity.

**LO:** MR-13 c: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 1, LO 13.c (Figures 13.3 and 13.4); Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.2

**Source:** New • built from Schweser LO 13.c, Figures 13.3 and 13.4 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 c.6)

a.reason: Reported the two-year value of convexity.

b.reason: Scaled the two-year value linearly by maturity: 1.85 × 3/2 = 2.8 bp. Convexity grows faster than that.

d.reason: Forgot the cube root and compared cumulative growth factors: $1.08^{3} -$ 1/0.79492 = 0.173%, or 17.3 bp, a three-year total, not an annual rate.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a German insurer is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts. She uses a risk-neutral binomial tree with annual steps in which the expected one-year rate is the same at every future date, the one-year rate is volatile, and investors require no risk premium. She then compares the forward rates implied by the tree’s zero-coupon bond prices with the flat expected rate. Which of the following statements is correct for her to make?

options.text: Because bond prices are convex in rates, the price of a zero at the expected rate exceeds its expected price, so forward rates lie above the expected short rate.
Convexity lowers every forward rate by the same number of basis points, because the volatility of each one-year rate transition in the tree is the same at every node.
The value of convexity increases with rate volatility and with maturity, so forward rates lie below the expected short rate and fall further at longer terms.
A position that is long convexity earns an expected return above the short rate in every scenario, because convexity adds to return whether rates rise or fall.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Jensen’s inequality**

$E[\frac{1}{1 + r}] > \frac{1}{1 + E[r]} : 0.5 \times\frac{1}{1.13} + 0.5 \times\frac{1}{1.05} = 0.918668 > \frac{1}{1.09} = 0.917431$

⇒ Averaging over volatile rates raises bond prices above the price at the average rate, which lowers the yields and forward rates they imply.

**Step 2 – Effect grows with maturity**

In the book’s tree (expected rate 9% at every horizon, 400 bp per transition) the forward rates are 9.0000%, 8.8532% and 8.5590%: about 15 bp below 9% for year two and 44 bp for year three. In the decomposition the reduction is $\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2}$, and $C$ rises with term.

**Step 3 – Effect grows with volatility**

The same $\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2}$ term rises with $\sigma$. The MR-14 tables show it: lowering long-rate volatility through mean reversion cuts the 30-year par-rate convexity effect from −135.3 bp (Model 1) to −74.7 bp (Vasicek).

**Interpretation**

With flat expectations and no risk premium, the forward curve slopes down purely because of convexity, more at longer terms and more in more volatile markets.

**LO:** MR-13 c: Estimate the convexity effect using Jensen’s inequality. MR-13 b: Apply a risk-neutral interest rate tree to assess the effect of volatility on the shape of the term structure. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat 4e, Ch.8, 13.2 and 13.3, eqs. 13.5 to 13.8 and 13.20, Table 13.1; Tuckman and Serrat 3e, Ch.9, Tables 14.1 and 14.2

MR-13 • Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook D12.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #55 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-13 c.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip of Jensen’s inequality: the expected price exceeds the price at the expected rate, so forwards lie below the expected rate.

b.reason: Scope/condition error: equal per-transition volatility does not make the effect equal across terms; $\frac{1}{2}C\sigma^{2}$ grows with the convexity of longer zeros (15 bp versus 44 bp in the book).

d.reason: Absolute claim: the forward rate is reduced by exactly the convexity gain, so the expected return condition leaves no net advantage of convexity; nothing is earned “in every scenario”.

questions.question: A fixed-income strategist decomposes the forward rate for a term whose zero-coupon bond has a duration of 7. The short-term rate is 2.5%, the expected change in the short-term rate is 0.3% per year, the risk premium is 15 basis points per year of duration risk, and the convexity effect is 0.65%. Which of the following is closest to the forward rate?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Expectations term**

$D \times E[dr]/dt = 7 \times0.3\% = 2.10\%$.

**Step 2 – Risk premium term**

$\lambda D = 7 \times0.15\% = 1.05\%$.

**Step 3 – Assemble**

$$f = 2.50\% + 2.10\% + 1.05\% - 0.65\% = 5.00\%$$

⇒ Both expectations and premium scale with duration; convexity comes off.

**Interpretation**

Figure 5 shows the same numbers as a waterfall. Convexity enters the forward rate with a minus sign even though it adds to bond returns.

a.reason: Did not scale the expected rate change by duration: 2.5 + 0.3 + 1.05 − 0.65 = 3.20%.

b.reason: Did not scale the risk premium by duration: 2.5 + 2.1 + 0.15 − 0.65 = 4.10%.

d.reason: Added the convexity effect instead of subtracting it: 2.5 + 2.1 + 1.05 + 0.65 = 6.30%.

questions.question: A fixed-income analyst calibrates Tuckman’s Model 1 (normal rates, no drift) with $r_{0} = 6.18\%$ and $\sigma= 1.13\%$ per year, so the terminal standard deviation of the short rate is 1.13% after one year and about 3.57% after ten years. She will use the model to value (i) a 10-year coupon bond and (ii) a 10-year option to buy a long-term bond at a yield of 0%. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Negative rates can be ignored for both securities, because the one-year terminal distribution, three standard deviations either side of 6.18%, does not reach zero.
At ten years a negative shock of only about 1.73 standard deviations takes the rate below zero; this matters most for the option, which the model overvalues, and much less for the bond.

At ten years a negative shock of only about 1.73 standard deviations takes the rate below zero; this matters most for the bond, whose value depends on the average rate path, and little for the option.
The probability of negative rates falls as the horizon lengthens, because the recombining tree pulls the short rate back toward its starting level of 6.18%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Horizon**

At one year, 6.18% is 6.18/1.13 = 5.5 standard deviations above zero: negligible. At ten years, 6.18/3.573 = 1.73 standard deviations.

⇒ A modest negative shock now takes the rate below zero (Figure 1).

**Step 2 – Which security suffers**

The coupon bond depends mostly on the average rate path, so a small probability of negative rates does not rule the model out. The option to buy at a 0% yield is asymmetrically sensitive to very low rates, so the model assigns it much too high a value.

**Interpretation**

Whether negative rates make a model unusable “depends on the application”. This is GARP’s own pair of examples.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14), Model 1 and Figure 14.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.14, 14.2 (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 c.2)

a.reason: Uses only the one-year horizon; both securities run for ten years, where the probability is material.

c.reason: Sibling swap: it is the option, not the coupon bond, that is asymmetrically sensitive to low rates.

d.reason: Reversed, and recombining is not mean reversion: Model 1 has no force pulling rates back to $r_{0}$.

questions.question: A rates strategist builds a normal short-rate tree and then sets every negative node to zero, following Black’s shadow-rate approach. Which of the following statements about this method is correct?

options.text: The rates in the original tree are the observed rates and the floored rates are the shadow rates, so the shadow rate can never fall below zero.
When the observed rate reaches zero it can stay there for several periods, until the shadow rate moves back above zero.
The justification is that aggregate saving and investment decisions can never produce a negative equilibrium rate, so the floor recovers the true rate.
Flooring changes the dynamics of the rate across the entire range of rates, which is why it is less attractive than switching to a lognormal model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Names**

The original tree holds the shadow rates; the adjusted tree holds the observed rates.

**Step 2 – Dynamics at zero**

When the observed rate hits zero it can remain there until the shadow rate crosses back to a positive value.

⇒ B is GARP’s description.

**Step 3 – Justification**

The observed rate is constrained to be positive only because investors can hold cash; the shadow rate, the result of aggregate saving, investment and consumption, may well be negative.

**Interpretation**

The change from flooring is localised around zero and negative rates; changing the distribution changes dynamics across the entire range.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14); Black, “Interest Rates as Options”, 1995

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.14, 14.2 (Black 1995) (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 c.6)

a.reason: Name swap: the floored rates are the observed rates; the shadow rate can be negative.

c.reason: Reversed justification: the shadow (equilibrium) rate may well be negative; the floor reflects the cash alternative.

d.reason: Sibling swap: global change in dynamics is the cost of changing the distribution, not of flooring.

questions.question: Rates are close to zero and a desk needs a short-rate model to price interest rate options across a wide range of strikes. One modeller proposes switching from a normal model to a lognormal model to remove negative rates; a colleague proposes keeping the normal model and flooring negative rates at zero. Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.text: The lognormal switch is preferable, because it rules out negative rates without changing the model’s volatility at any level of rates.
Flooring is preferable here, because its effect is localised around zero, whereas changing the distribution alters rate dynamics, including volatilities, across all rates.
Neither is needed, because adding time steps to the normal tree makes the terminal distribution continuous and so removes the negative rates.
The two are equivalent, because any distribution that rules out negative rates has the same volatility structure as a floored normal model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cost of the lognormal switch**

Building the model around a distribution that rules out negative rates “may result in volatilities that are unacceptable for the purpose at hand”, and it changes dynamics across the entire range of rates, which matters when pricing options at many strikes.

**Step 2 – Cost of the floor**

Only rates near and below zero change.

⇒ With rates close to zero, the floor is the less disruptive fix; Vardeez notes it is preferred in very low-rate environments.

**Interpretation**

The choice depends on purpose. Here the desk prices options across strikes, so it should avoid a fix that distorts volatility at every rate level.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14); Vardeez notes MR-14 c

**Source:** New • built from GARP MR Ch.14, 14.2 and Vardeez (Market Risk Workbook, Question MR-14 c.7)

a.reason: Absolute claim: a lognormal model does change volatility behaviour (basis-point volatility proportional to $r$).

c.reason: A finer normal tree still has mass below zero.

d.reason: The two methods have different volatility structures; that is the whole trade-off.
